Nothing Headphone (1) Pro review: Price & release date
- Released on September 28, 2026
- Priced $399 / £349 / (approx. AU$655)
Now then. This is premium territory for Nothing and then some, isn't it?
Given that the Nothing Headphone (1) launched in July 2025 for $299 / £299 / AU$549, and the follow-up Nothing Headphone (a) arrived in March 2026 for half that (at $199 / £149 / AU$329) Nothing essentially has to upsell its fans to the tune of $200 — or £200 — more than the most recent and very highly rated Headphone (a) release, to get you to look over at the Pro-suffixed set. And that is a big ask.
Now, consider the five-star CMF Headphone Pro, which I called "as good as $99 / £79 / AU$179 headphones can possibly look and sound" shortly after their release in September 2025. Hard not to think that the big ask just got even bigger, no?
Then again, $399 / £349 is not an unreasonable asking fee if they're that good; there's plenty at this level to pit them against in the wider flagship headphone space (Sony's WH-1000XM6 are $50 / £50 pricier, at $449 / £399 / AU$699, for example).
It's just that rarely have I seen three sets of headphones from a single brand, all released all within the same 15-month period, that a) look so similar (see attached photos) in terms of design and shape, save for the case you put them in; and b) that vary so much in price.
So let's delve a little deeper, to see where the money's gone.
Nothing Headphone (1) Pro review: Specs
| Drivers | 1x 40 mm bass dynamic driver, 1x precision dynamic driver and 1x treble xMEMS driver per ear cup | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes (adaptive, tweakable static, ambient passthrough) | 
| Battery life | Up to 68 hours with ANC off; up to 30 hours with ANC on | 
| Weight | Headphones: 327g; Case: 383.5g | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0 with LDAC, USB-C, Auracast | 
| Frequency range | 20Hz – 40kHz | 
| Waterproofing | IP52 | 
| Other features | Certified hi-res for wireless listening up to 24-bit/96kHz; wired listening up to 24-bit/192kHz; 5 dynamic spatial audio modes in collab with Metropolis, dual device connection; auto-wear detection; low latency mode; advanced EQ per driver tabs; Personal Sound | 
Nothing Headphone (1) Pro review: Features
- 5 Spatial Audio modes (Standard, Studio B by Metropolis, Live House, Club, Concert Hall) are fairly light touch
- Flat EQ switch to toggle between neutral and everyday listening (meant for pro mixing) is interesting, if hard to access… and not to my taste
- 5 mics per ear cup for ANC is a big improvement, aided by better passive NC
The headline-grabber here is the addition of Spatial Audio profiles that can either be deployed with or without head-tracking. If you're hoping for AirPods Max to Apple Music iPhone levels of head-turning immersive audio trickery, you'll be disappointed, but I did find the profiles added a sense of "OK, the live gig feels like it's in front of me" or "Oh I'm in a recording studio in leafy Chiswick, I get it" to the sound profiles.
As if to really emphasize the new audio architecture under the hood, Nothing has gone particularly specific with the EQ tabs here. If you bypass 'Simple' (which offers the usual 'vocal boost' presets and the option to create your own) and head to 'Advanced' within the Equaliser page on the Nothing X app, you can actually tweak the various settings per driver — well, for the 'precision driver' (ie. the midrange dynamic driver) and the 'main drivers' (which would be the 40mm bass dynamic unit and the xMEMS treble driver). Yes, really.
Add to this Nothing's Q Factor tab (to define the width or sharpness of the frequency band being boosted or cut), Gain (the loudness in decibels of a specific frequency band being toyed with) and Frequency (you can choose a specific frequency from 20Hz up to 40kHz to tweak) and essentially, if you're quite sure that 11,595Hz is where you need a boost you can have at it. And you can have it sharply, and with a modified jolt to the loudness, if you so want — by first locating the Precision dynamic driver dot on the stave, because that handles frequencies between 5 kHz–15 kHz.
While impressive to toy with, the above sonic tweaks pale into relative insignificance once you locate Personal Sound, in my opinion. It's not new to this product, but I've long been a fan. This is a test of your actual hearing, in whatever environment you find yourself. It takes around three minutes, during which you listen to ever-decreasing tones of different frequencies in each ear, until you cannot hear them. At the end of it, a personalized profile will be added to your cans and this, to me, makes a lot more difference than the tweaks I made without it. My hearing is good, but still, this test finds the areas that could be subtly bumped or eased off, for me.
Now, Nothing's 'Flat' EQ toggle, on the top inner edge of the left ear cup, developed alongside Metropolis Studios. Honestly, it's hard to find and difficult to switch on or off while wearing the headphones, but since you can't do so within the app, you will need to use said switch. The feature is billed as a "neutral profile that removes coloration and processing" and "designed for specific listening situations — like reviewing tracks or comparing mixes". Nothing even suggests that the type of situations in which you'll need it: "a clean setup to make critical listening decisions about how a track behaves before it reaches audiences." You should note that Transparency Mode, Spatial Audio and EQ settings are disabled when Flat EQ is on.
For me, Flat EQ is a miss. Deploy it and there's an odd sense of being in a tunnel with a bit of a warm veil and even a slight echo to the audio. It's novel, but neutral and useful for critical listening? During my testing, not so much.
What of the ANC? It's much better. Nothing has put three feed-forward and two feedback mics on each ear cup capture noise. The mics are also now positioned inward in a bid to better avoid direct wind exposure and airflow interference. Basically, Headphone (1) Pro does a better job at understanding your surroundings and adjusting things according to extraneous sounds in your immediate environment.
You can select Adaptive Active Noise Cancellation, which automatically adjusts between Low, Medium and High levels based on your surroundings for a claimed maximum of 46 dB of noise reduction, or manually select it yourself — and when deploying 'High' I was very impressed. My hunch is that the claimed "40% broader noise cancellation coverage across the frequency range" and "5 dB stronger average noise reduction than Headphone (1)" are true, but that aside from the mics and software, said improvements also have plenty to do with the stepped-up padding and new silicone ‘baffle wall’ around the cups to create a better seal around the ear.
Transparency mode? It's good. It really does do what it says on the tin: lets the world in (particularly my voice and the voices of those around me, vying for my attention), but without any tinniness to my music.
Elsewhere, you can "start a broadcast" to other Auracast-enabled devices nearby simply by playing music and toggling on 'Broadcast Audio' in the ap. You can also receive or join broadcasts (with or without a password, if you or your sharer has set one), which is fun and still relatively novel, despite Auracast having launched a few years ago now. Dual connection and a low-lag mode are here, and during my tests wearer-detection (which can be switched on or off in the device settings) was very reliable.
Lastly, call quality: very good indeed. My testing involved taking calls on a particularly windswept day on the Dorset coastline, yet callers said I sounded remarkably clear.
- Features score: 4.5 / 5
Nothing Headphone (1) Pro review: Sound quality
- LDAC support, plus hi-res wired via USB-C or 3.5mm bundled cables
- Highly tweakable sound (if hard to understand via the driver EQ tabs)
- Integrated and neutral by default — if you want 'fun' they may not be ideal
If you're in a rush, know that much of what I'm about to impart in this section can be boiled down to: "They're very good for sound, but better than the cheaper Nothing Headphone (a)? Not especially — unless you always listen with wires".
There are of course the additional spatial audio modes (all five of them, with the option of head-tracking) in this new product, whereas the Headphone (a) only offers a concert mode or cinema mode — and both of those can only move with your head, rather than giving you the option of using your device as a fixed source. However, I found each of the profiles within the Headphone (1) Pro quite light touch, rather than the "Wait, that's so good!" experience you get when sonic passages slip under your chin, past your left ear and down to the small of your back with the AirPods Max 2.
There's nothing wrong with subtlety and faithfulness to a recording (in fact I really like these attributes in headphones) but when listening to my specific reference tracks in an a/b test against the older Nothing headphones, I actually found the bite, attack and general zeal across the frequencies of the cheaper Headphone (a) marginally more fun to listen to than the integrated, studious, hi-fi approach of the Headphone (1) Pro.
That will of course be a matter of taste and may depend on which genres of music you most enjoy. Both sonic recipes are valid — and when listening via USB-C audio to hi-res tracks on my FiiO DAP, greater detail through the leading edges of notes can certainly be had in the Headphone (1) Pro, which makes sense when you realize that the Headphone (a) tops out at 24-bit/96kHz, whereas the Headphone (1) Pro lists resolutions at up to 24-bit/192 kHz when going wired with USB-C.
I cue up The Killers' In the Car Outside and there's a beautiful circumaural presentation to the audio. I have to commend Nothing on the multi-driver integration (the company is proud to have created one of the first over-ear headphones to use an xMEMS driver), with a treble that's particularly sparkling, easy and natural when Brandon Flowers starts to unfurl his vocal folds.
The Nothing Headphone (1) Pro also dig an extra ounce of texture and emotion from within John Frusciante's hard-lived but defiant vocal in Omission, alongside (but never at the expense of) the tambourine and female backing vocals. Switch to an instrumental or classical piece, such as Roberto Cacciapaglia's Universal Dance, and the Headphone (1) Pro are at their happiest, celebrating the rhythmic depression of keys in a cohesive and expansive mix. Head to BackRoad Gee's raucous, rough and ready grime track Live in the Flesh, however, and you may just think these headphones are playing a little safe through a clean, but perhaps marginally over-sanitized, low end.
That said, this is less about any sonic shortfalls with the product itself and more about the well-documented talents of Nothing's own previous (a)-suffixed cans which, however you slice it, are $200 (or £200) cheaper than these. And I'm just not sure the sound is that much better.
- Sound quality score: 4 / 5

Nothing Headphone (1) Pro review: Design
- Slightly firmer but still comfortable clamping force, which helps with ANC
- Triple-driver array is well handled
- Battery life is middling; the half-case is a sore point
I'm a big fan of the adjusted clamping force and general comfort levels here, despite the nominal additional weight (these weigh 327g; the older-generation set weigh 310g).
Nothing products are known for their forward-thinking design language and so if this section feels a tad longer than is traditional for a set of headphones, there’s your reason: there’s plenty to get through.
Visually as well as under the hood, the Headphone (1) Pro’s ear cups can be seen as a refinement on those in the Headphone (1) in the same way that the MiniDisc was a refinement on the cassette tape; much better technically, but perhaps unable to command the recognition or longevity it deserved. To be clear, yes, I have lived through both physical formats' respective heydays.
A lot of work has been done on this ear cup design and Nothing wants you to know it; the padding around each cup is dual-layer and much better; the hinges feel more premium (and are silent); the headband padding means said band never gets tender across the top of my head.
Sadly, we do need to talk about the case, though. It’s hard to find good things to say about it. At a time when Apple AirPods Max 2 arrived still wearing their ‘headphones bra’ idea in lieu of a much-wanted hard-shell case, it’s odd that Nothing didn’t read the room. Instead, Nothing unveiled something like that but bigger, heavier and clunkier, and that only covers the ear cups so your cans look like they’ve been dropped (and are still partially suspended) in wet cement.
And if you’re thinking that at least there’ll be room for your USB-C cable or even replacement batteries in that thing, surely, sadly no. The hinge isn’t especially premium and so the case simply clatters open, which is neither easy to use nor especially useful. It is also heavy at 383.5g (much heavier than the cans themselves) and, I believe, has been an expensive extra. I’d have preferred to opt out. For those who want to wear their headphones in places other than over their ears or draped around their neck, there are holes to fit your own shoulder strap to the Nothing case, so the whole thing can be worn like a cross-body handbag.
I can imagine Nothing's design team excitedly saying “It’s never been done before!” and the market research focus groups coming back with the reason why. This case makes the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro heavy, bulky and cumbersome.
Yes, there is a glass top plate to each driver housing, but Nothing took great pains to tell us how sturdy and shatter-proof this solution is, so there’s no need for such a bulky case, surely? I recently took a very long-haul flight — a great opportunity to test the active noise cancellation here, and very good it was. But let me tell you that once they were in my carry-on bag, I’d have given a lot of money not to have committed to this plan. And it’s a shame, because the actual audio architecture is really good here.
There are also a lot of buttons of varying shapes and sizes on the Headphone (1) Pro. The left ear cup is where you’ll find Nothing’s new ‘flat’ sound profile button slider, on the inner edge of the rectangular top corner of the softly rectangular earpiece. It’s a little hard to access and slide across during wear, but it’s there. The right earpiece, however, is a lot busier. It's a solution Nothing fans will know well, involving a button, a roller and a paddle — and I really like it. Said buttons are snappy and responsive, and the roller is a great way to tweak volume.
Where the design lets itself down, aside from the case, is when it comes to stamina. Where the older Nothing Headphone (a) could go for up to 135 hours without ANC on, or up to 75 hours with noise cancellation, you'll only get up to 68 hours — and that's without ANC. Switch on noise-nixing and you'll only get up to 30 hours of playtime; add LDAC to the mix and it drops to just 28 hours. See how it's hard to make a case for the newer set being a better buy, as well as being much more expensive?
- Design score: 3.5 / 5
Nothing Headphone (1) Pro review: Value
- Very good-looking headphones (until you put the case over them)
- Stuffed with features and sonically up to par, if low on stamina
- That case has eaten into Nothing's budget, though…
The looks and style of these headphones (aside from the case) make them seem worthy of their price — and the sound is up to scratch. The ANC, too, is very good, as is the Transparency and extra whistles and bells.
There are two thorns in the Headphone (1) Pro's side: the stamina (which is a long way short of the cheaper cans they supersede) and the heavy unlikeable case. If there were a third, it would be the talents of the cheaper Headphone (a), which includes most of what makes the Headphone (1) Pro special, and delivers it for a lot less.
- Value score: 3 / 5

You want a fashion statement as well as headphones

You have a Sony or Samsung phone

You want to level up on ANC 
These cans are just better at passive and active isolation than Nothing's previous efforts, and I like that a lot.
Don't buy them if...
You want extra-special spatial audio
Nothing has added five spatial audio options here, in conjunction with Metropolis Studios, and with the option of dynamic head-tracking in each. For me, though, it's all a little bit lightweight. Want AirPods Max performance with Apple's head-tracked Spatial Audio? You'll need to buy those products.

What I'm saying is, pack them in your backpack and you'll notice the weight. 
You need stamina for a long-haul flight and back

How I tested the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro

- Listened at home, on a long-haul flight, in a hotel room in Tokyo and while walking alone along a blustery seafront, in the rain
- Listened to Tidal Masters, Qobuz and Apple Music Lossless tracks via USB-C to my FiiO player and streamed to my iPhone 15 Pro, MacBook Pro and Sony Xperia smartphone
The Nothing Headphone (1) Pro became my primary travel companions for two weeks — after a 24-hour run-in period. And to be honest, there were times when I wished I hadn't brought their heavy case along, in my hand luggage.
They accompanied me to the airport (walking brusquely to Heathrow's T5 from the Airport Express train) and even on the hotel balcony in Tokyo during a minor 5.0 earthquake — no really, I promise I'm telling the truth.
To assess comfort levels (very good), ANC (also very effective) and battery life claims (less impressive), I followed TechRadar's meticulous methodology testing and found much to report back on — including their slightly underwhelming stamina.
To check the audio chops across the frequencies, I listened for many hours, in various environments, to my own reference playlists on Apple Music, Qobuz and Tidal, alongside TechRadar's reference tracks, plus podcasts and movies.
I’ve been testing audio products for well over seven years now, full-time — first at our sister site What Hi-Fi? and now here at TechRadar. articles.title: Okta builds shared architecture for agent runtime security - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Okta builds shared architecture for agent runtime security
Agent runtime security requires controls across the technology stack as enterprises move AI agents into production.
This week, Okta turned its agent security framework into a multivendor reference architecture through the Blueprint Alliance. The effort is intended to help buyers navigate competing vendor claims, according to Eric Kelleher (pictured), president and chief operating officer of Okta.
“One of the challenges companies have in navigating this is [that] every technology vendor they talk to from every component of the stack is telling them that they’re the one-stop shop that’s going to fix everything,” he said. “So, the biggest challenge that we have in talking to our customers is helping them navigate the confusion of understanding how to think about the problem, how to secure AI in a way that’s simple.”
Kelleher spoke with theCUBE Research’s Krista Case and co-host Rebecca Knight at Okta’s Oktane event, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how the Blueprint Alliance brings identity and security signals together to monitor agent behavior and guide responses to risk. (* Disclosure below.)
Okta coordinates agent runtime security across vendors
The Blueprint Alliance architecture distills agent security into four questions: where agents are, what they can do, what they are doing and how to respond. Okta layers its identity signals atop endpoint and network telemetry, Kelleher explained.
“We’ll look at what agents are connecting to and we’ll compare that against the systems that it’s been authorized to connect to, to see if there’s a disparity,” he said. “That real-time data all flows back into a system to help us identify, ‘Does something look suspicious?'”
Okta can deactivate a flagged agent to block new sessions, and it plans to expand its kill switch capabilities at the Agent Gateway to revoke active tokens and sessions. The appropriate response will depend on the agent’s behavior and the risk it poses, Kelleher noted.
“There are going to be cases where agents, as they’re exploring their intended work, end up stepping over boundaries that were not intended, where you’ll want to redirect them and bound them back in,” he said.

articles.title: Virginia Tech lab 3D prints a liquid metal composite to guide heat, boost thermal conductivity 40x — the nozzle stretches gallium-indium droplets inside soft silicone, can also create self-healing traces
articles.text:
Virginia Tech lab 3D prints a liquid metal composite to guide heat, boost thermal conductivity 40x — the nozzle stretches gallium-indium droplets inside soft silicone, can also create self-healing traces
Heat follows the toolpath through a flexible part.
Virginia Tech graduate student Hugh Grennan mixed eutectic gallium-indium (EGaIn) into uncured polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) silicone in a “3D Printing LIQUID METAL!” video on the 3D Printing Nerd YouTube channel hosted by Joel Telling. He cast a slab of the mixture, pressed a line into it to light an LED, sliced that line with a razor blade to show it still conducted, and then printed the same material on a syringe-fed printer to guide heat rather than electricity.
The metal is eutectic gallium-indium, which Grennan described as “about three parts gallium, one part indium” that, once mixed, is “liquid at room temperature.” The lab’s website says the droplets give the composite “soft elasticity” and “extreme toughness,” along with “autonomously self-healing electrical circuits.”
The metal is mixed into the uncured PDMS, which breaks it into separate droplets, each wrapped in a thin gallium oxide skin. About an hour in an oven turns the silicone from a gel into a solid, but the droplets inside stay liquid. The droplets are “on the order of 10 to 100 microns in diameter,” Grennan said in the video. The video was filmed at VT MADE, the university’s “New Center for Advanced Manufacturing,” a group of labs that includes the Soft Materials and Structures Lab where Grennan works.
The printer is a syringe-fed machine built so the lab can load the composite and print straight from the syringe, Grennan said. Droplet shape is determined by a setting that controls the ratio of how fast the composite leaves the nozzle compared to how fast the print bed moves. The proper selection stretches the round droplets into long, thin ones. Stretching the droplets allows heat to travel along the long axis of each, “away from a heat source to a heat sink,” Grennan said. Asked about uses, he pointed to custom heat sinks and stretchable wearable devices.
A 2025 paper in Advanced Functional Materials, co-authored by Michael Bartlett, the associate professor of mechanical engineering who runs the lab, put the printed composite’s thermal conductivity along the droplets’ direction at 9.9 W/mK, about 40 times that of the unfilled silicone. A separate 2024 paper in Additive Manufacturing says that the oxide skin “is found to play a unique and critical role in the reconfiguration and retention of droplet shape.”
For the electrical demo, Grennan pressed a line into the cast slab with an indenter. The pressure forced the droplets to merge into a continuous conductive track, and a small LED lit up. Under a microscope, the track appeared as a solid line with metal squeezed to the surface. He then cut across it with a razor blade, pressed again near the cut, and the LED came back, faintly.
Asked whether cutting raised the resistance, he said “not necessarily,” since cutting or puncturing simply “[reforms] all those pathways and the liquid metal flows” through them. The droplets begin insulated from one another by the silicone and by their own oxide skins. A conductive path here is metal that has flowed together, with a cut, something the path can flow around.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The video is a demonstration of research by the lab going back multiple years. It shows how the technology works in an understandable way while pointing to multiple applications. “It’s really cool to have this like it’s just a tool in the toolkit,” Grennan said. Liquid metal is already used in some PC hardware as a thermal interface. Nvidia’s GeForce RTX 5090 Founders Edition uses a gallium alloy in place of thermal paste.
The wearables market Grennan pointed to keeps growing, too. Market analysis firm IDC puts worldwide shipments in the first quarter of 2026 at 145.7 million units, up 4.3% from a year earlier. The lab’s newest listed paper covers a stretchable liquid metal and polymer feedstock for 3D printing parts that conduct on their own. If the lab’s papers are a guide, we can expect improved heat spreaders and flexible device wires. Named applications include directed cooling for electric vehicles, robots, and electronics, and practical refinements for wearables.

articles.title: Why Kenya’s mobile money agents are under pressure
articles.text:
Mobile money shops were once among Kenya’s simplest small businesses, built around customers depositing, withdrawing, and sending cash. Now, the network is shrinking as more Kenyans transact directly from their phones.
Data released by Kenya’s tech regulator, the Communications Authority (CA), reveals a sharp structural shift in the mobile financial ecosystem. Between March and June, the country lost roughly 34,000 mobile money agents. The total number of registered agents dropped by 5.6%, falling from 602,470 to 568,463 in just three months.
The contraction in physical infrastructure does not signal a slowing market. During the exact same three-month window, total mobile money subscriptions grew by 1.2%, rising from 53.37 million to 54.01 million. Annually, subscriptions surged by 13.2%.
Phones over agents
The paradox of fewer agents serving significantly more users highlights a fundamental transformation. Kenyans are no longer using mobile money simply as a digital remittance service that requires converting paper bills into phone balances. Money is staying inside the digital loop. The widespread adoption of direct digital checkout channels has shifted transaction flows entirely away from cash counters.
Consumers now have more ways to spend money without visiting an agent. One option is Buy Goods tills, which are merchant numbers that let customers pay a shop directly from M-PESA or Airtel Money, so someone buying food at a supermarket or kiosk doesn’t need to withdraw cash.
Pochi la Biashara, an M-PESA business wallet for small traders, allows kiosk owners and other informal businesses to receive customer payments separately from their personal M-PESA wallets.
PayBill numbers, payment accounts corporations use to collect money from customers, let customers send money directly to organisations such as schools, insurers, and utility companies to settle bills.
Bank-to-wallet integrations have removed another trip to the agents by allowing customers to move money between bank accounts and mobile money wallets on their phones. The more payments that happen this way, the fewer customers need an agent to turn their digital money into cash.
Market concentration remains heavily skewed toward the dominant incumbent. Safaricom commands 88.8% of total mobile money subscriptions, alongside 69.8% of mobile voice subscriptions and 64.4% of mobile broadband connections. Airtel Money holds nearly the entire market, accounting for 11.1% of mobile money subscriptions.
While both networks historically depended on massive agent distribution channels to acquire customers and handle liquidity, the underlying unit economics for individual operators have broken down.
Agents’ core revenue driver has always been commissions on deposits and withdrawals. When a customer uses a till number to buy food or settles an account via PayBill, the physical agent earns nothing. As consumer habits shift toward merchant payments, the high-volume cash-in and cash-out transactions that once sustained agents’ livelihoods are disappearing.
Squeezed margins and regulatory pressure
Compounding the drop in top-line commission income is a dramatic rise in the cost of running a physical shop. Small agents across urban centres find themselves squeezed between falling foot traffic and soaring operational overheads.
“Cost of operation is high,” explained one agent in Kisii, a town 300 km west of Nairobi. “M-PESA shops generate from KES 11,000 ($85) to KES 30,000 ($230) in monthly commission. At KES 11,000 ($85), with rising rent costs, paying attendants, and still needing to justify your investment, it’s tricky. Business permits are up by 30%, too.”
Prior economic models no longer reflect current commercial realities.
“In the past, a commission of KES 22,000 ($170) meant you paid rent of KES 3,000 ($23) and the worker KES 5,000 ($38),” noted another operator in Ruaka, a satellite town 15 km northwest of the Nairobi Central Business District. “Now rent starts at KES 5,000 ($38), and attendants demand KES 7,500 ($58). There are additional expenses and fraud cases to deal with.”
An industry executive, who preferred anonymity, pointed to concerns about transaction costs and government scrutiny of mobile money accounts. Kenya Revenue Authority’s efforts to use transaction data for tax compliance have raised privacy concerns among some businesses and consumers, adding another source of pressure on a market already dealing with a decline in cash transactions.
The smartphone migration and fintech’s next phase
The double squeeze of declining transaction volumes, escalating fixed costs, and heightened regulatory scrutiny has forced thousands of operators to close shop.
The rapid spread of smartphones has accelerated the migration. Kenya recorded 52.26 million smartphone connections by June, up from 50.18 million in March. As basic feature phones fall out of favour, their numbers have dropped to 27.42 million, while more consumers gain access to app-based banking, QR code scanning, and direct merchant checkout. Mobile data usage has surged in parallel, reaching 64.26 million subscriptions, driven by faster 4G and 5G networks.
Mobile network operators like Safaricom and Airtel Kenya view the contraction of the agent network as both an opportunity and a strategic challenge. A fully digitised payment ecosystem drastically lowers cash-handling costs and capital expenditure required to maintain physical distribution networks.
Agents are important to telcos for onboarding non-digital users, managing liquidity and serving customers in rural areas. As cash transactions decline, operators will need to provide these shops with more ways to earn revenue beyond deposits and withdrawals.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks.

articles.title: How to Make a Cross-Country Move Feel Less Like a Logistics Nightmare - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Moving across the country sounds exciting right up until you start thinking about everything that has to happen in the correct order. Packing is only one part of it.
There are dates to coordinate, addresses to change, utilities to disconnect, travel plans to organise and belongings that somehow need to make it from one side of Australia to the other without disappearing into a black hole.
That’s why using experienced removalists for Perth to Sydney can take a lot of pressure out of the process. The value isn’t just in having someone move boxes. It’s in reducing the number of variables you personally have to manage while everything else in your life is already changing at once.
Work Backwards From the Arrival Date
A long-distance move becomes much easier when you stop thinking in terms of “moving week” and start thinking in terms of milestones. When do you need to be out of the old property? When can you access the new one? Will your belongings arrive before you do, after you do or roughly at the same time? Those dates shape almost everything else.
Once you know the end point, work backwards. Give yourself deadlines for decluttering, packing non-essentials, cancelling services and confirming transport. It’s far less stressful than trying to make every decision in the final few days, when the house is already full of boxes and everyone is tired.
Don’t Move Things Just Because You Own Them
Interstate moves are a very good time to become ruthless about what actually deserves to make the trip. Bulky, broken or rarely used items can cost time, space and money to move, especially when they’re things you could easily replace later.
Go room by room and ask a simple question: would I pay to move this if I didn’t already own it? If the answer is no, that’s a useful clue. Selling, donating or discarding items before the move can make packing easier and reduce the amount of stuff waiting for you at the other end.
Pack for the Journey, Not Just the House
Packing for an interstate move is different from packing for a move across town. Boxes may be handled more, spend longer in transit and need to survive a much bigger journey.
Use sturdy cartons, don’t overload them and make sure fragile items are properly wrapped. It also helps to label boxes with both the room and the contents, because “bedroom” is not very useful when you’re trying to find the one box containing chargers, medication or bedding.
Keep truly essential items with you rather than in the main shipment. Important documents, medications, a few changes of clothes, toiletries and basic electronics should travel separately so you’re not stranded if there’s any delay.
Expect the Timeline to Be Imperfect
Even with good planning, long-distance moves rarely line up perfectly. There may be a gap between leaving one home and getting access to the next, or your belongings may arrive later than expected. Planning for that possibility is far easier than being surprised by it.
Temporary accommodation, short-term storage or a small essentials kit can make that gap much more manageable. The important thing is not to assume every part of the move will happen on the same day, because interstate logistics often involve multiple stages.
Sort the Admin Before You’re Too Busy to Think
Address changes are easy to forget when you’re focused on boxes and travel. Banks, insurers, licence records, subscriptions, healthcare providers, schools, employers and government services may all need updating, and mail redirection can help catch anything you miss.
Utilities deserve the same attention. Confirm when electricity, gas and internet will be disconnected at the old property and when services can start at the new one. Arriving after a long journey to a home with no internet, no power or no hot water is the sort of inconvenience that feels much bigger when you’re already exhausted.
Keep Everyone on the Same Page
If more than one person is involved in the move, make sure responsibilities are clear. One person can handle utilities, another can manage travel, while someone else coordinates packing or pet arrangements. Shared lists can help prevent duplication and the classic problem where everyone assumes somebody else has already taken care of something.
Communication matters with the moving provider too. Confirm access details, parking restrictions, stairs, lifts and any unusually large or heavy items in advance. The more information everyone has, the fewer surprises there are on the day.
Make the First Night Easy
Your first evening in the new place should not depend on finding the correct box at the bottom of a stack. Pack a separate first-night kit with bedding, towels, chargers, basic kitchen items, toiletries and anything else you’re likely to need immediately.
It’s a small detail, but it makes a huge difference. After a cross-country move, the last thing anyone wants is to unpack twelve boxes just to find a clean mug and a phone charger.
A long-distance move will always involve some disruption, but it doesn’t have to feel chaotic. With clear timing, sensible packing and a bit of planning around the awkward gaps, the process becomes much more manageable and a lot less like a logistical nightmare.

articles.title: OpenAI annule la sortie du nouveau ChatGPT pour « garantir la sécurité » de ses IA
articles.text:
OpenAI appuie sur le frein. Le géant de l’IA a renoncé à lancer GPT-6.1 Astra, son prochain grand modèle, qui devait débarquer dans ChatGPT et Codex le mois prochain. Le modèle d’IA ne respectait tout simplement pas les exigences de sécurité de l’entreprise. L’intelligence artificielle « n’a pas tout à fait atteint le niveau » exigé, a expliqué Saachi Jain, responsable des systèmes de sécurité d’OpenAI, au Wall Street Journal. Par précaution, OpenAI a préféré temporiser et reporter la sortie de l’IA à une date ultérieure.
À lire aussi : Six ChatGPT hors de contrôle – OpenAI reconnaît plusieurs nouveaux dérapages « préoccupants »
Tromperie et excès de zèle
Tout d’abord, GPT-6.1 Astra se serait montré moins performant sur les tests d’alignement, c’est-à-dire sa capacité à suivre fidèlement les consignes. Surtout, le modèle d’IA s’est distingué par « des niveaux de tromperie plus élevés ». Concrètement, le modèle ne rapportait pas toujours honnêtement ce qu’il avait fait à ses interlocuteurs.
Ce n’est pas tout. L’IA pouvait aussi dépasser le cadre de la tâche demandée, sans l’autorisation de l’utilisateur, par exemple en faisant appel à des outils ou des services externes. OpenAI évoque par ailleurs des lacunes sur le respect du périmètre autorisé, mais aussi sur la façon de rendre compte du travail effectué. Bref, la start-up a jugé que le modèle d’IA était susceptible de n’en faire qu’à sa tête.
« Le modèle s’est avéré insuffisant en matière de respect du périmètre et des autorisations, ainsi que de communication avec l’utilisateur concernant le type de travail effectué », explique Saachi Jain.
En dépit de ses dérives, GPT-6.1 Astra a été jugé nettement plus capable que GPT-6. Il faisait notamment mieux pour mener seul des tâches complexes de bout en bout. Le modèle est aussi plus doué pour l’écriture. Comme l’explique OpenAI, il faut trouver la bonne limite entre le respect du périmètre, qui est fixé par l’utilisateur, et une certaine forme de « paresse » face aux obstacles. Autrement dit, une IA trop sage abandonne un peu trop vite, tandis qu’une IA trop zélée finit par sortir des clous pour répondre coûte que coûte à la demande de son interlocuteur.
« Nous voulons garantir la sécurité de nos modèles, tant pendant leur développement en interne que lors de leur mise à disposition des utilisateurs. Mais avant de les déployer, nous leur imposons des exigences particulièrement strictes en matière de sécurité et d’alignement », ajoute le responsable.
Une série de dérapages
C’est ce phénomène qui est à l’origine d’une grande partie des incidents récents. En juillet dernier, deux modèles d’OpenAI se sont échappés de leur environnement confiné, ont accédé à Internet et piraté la plateforme Hugging Face. Les IA cherchaient à répondre aux exigences d’un test de sécurité.
Plus récemment, le Premier ministre australien a révélé qu’un agent d’OpenAI a piraté un site du gouvernement et consulté des données privées sans la moindre autorisation. Là encore, l’IA cherchait simplement à récolter des données et à répondre à la mission qui lui était confiée. Le même week-end, on a appris que ChatGPT s’était attaqué à plusieurs reprises à un site de l’ONU, ainsi qu’à plusieurs entités du gouvernement américain, pour aspirer des informations.
Dans ce contexte, le débat sur le rythme de développement de l’IA s’est intensifié. Sam Altman d’OpenAI et Dario Amodei d’Anthropic ont appelé tout le secteur à lever le pied avant qu’il ne soit trop tard. OpenAI vient d’ailleurs de suspendre l’entraînement de ses derniers modèles, jusqu’à nouvel ordre, à la suite des différents incidents impliquant ses IA.

articles.title: Shopify ouvre son checkout aux agents IA dans le navigateur : une révolution pour l’e-commerce ?
articles.text:
Vous pouvez maintenant confier à un agent IA l’intégralité d’un achat sur une boutique Shopify, paiement compris. Ce lundi 28 septembre, la plateforme de commerce en ligne a ouvert son étape de paiement, Shop Pay inclus, aux assistants qui travaillent dans votre navigateur, alors qu’Amazon interdit sur son site les achats d’agents non autorisés.
Depuis le 10 septembre, les utilisateurs américains de Muse, l'agent IA personnel de Meta, peuvent lui confier des achats en ligne, à condition de valider eux-mêmes chaque commande. Moins de deux semaines plus tard, Amazon a bloqué cet usage sur sa boutique. Le géant de Seattle reproche à Meta de ne jamais l’avoir averti et soupçonne l’agent de stocker les identifiants de connexion de ses clients.
Dans la foulée, Shopify a pris la place et intégré Shop Pay à Muse sur l’ensemble des boutiques de ses marchands. La plateforme canadienne ouvre maintenant son paiement à tous les agents IA qui fonctionnent dans le navigateur. Elle pense que la phase d'achat sera ainsi plus rapide, mais laisse à chaque client la validation finale de sa commande.
Shopify adapte son paiement aux agents IA
Gil Greenberg est chef de produit chez Shopify chargé du commerce par agents IA. Dans un long message publié sur son compte X, explique qu'un achat confié à un agent de navigateur était souvent plus lent et moins fiable qu’un achat fait à la main. L’agent lit la page, repère un champ et le remplit. Il relit ensuite toute la page pour voir ce qui a changé et recommence pour chaque champ, avec parfois une erreur de saisie au passage. « Si votre agent opère dans le navigateur de l’acheteur, utilisez les outils WebMCP fournis sur la boutique en ligne et au moment du paiement pour finaliser efficacement la commande, au lieu de naviguer dans un HTML conçu pour les humains », a-t-il écrit à l’intention des concepteurs d’agents.
Shopify a construit ces outils sur l’Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP). Google a lancé en janvier ce protocole ouvert d’achat par IA, que Shopify a coécrit avec Etsy, Wayfair, Target et Walmart.
Pour chiffrer le gain, Shopify a mené un test sur deux boutiques de démonstration, avec le modèle GPT-6 Sol d’OpenAI. Il comportait dix tâches de paiement, dont un changement d’adresse et l’ajout d’un code promo. L'agent a mis en moyenne 10,3 secondes par tentative avec WebMCP, contre 27,4 secondes en navigation automatisée. La facture était aussi inférieure de 58 % au tarif public d'OpenAI. Enfin, l'agent a réussi ses 60 tentatives avec WebMCP, contre 56 sans.
Shopify laisse le dernier mot à l’acheteur
Avec WebMCP, l’agent IA agit toujours dans la session ouverte par l’acheteur et passe par les mêmes vérifications que lui. Si la banque demande une validation 3D Secure, ou si Shop Pay envoie un code de confirmation, l'agent rend la main à l’acheteur, a précisé Gil Greenberg. Les règles commerciales que chaque marchand a ajoutées à sa page de paiement sont aussi appliquées aux agents.
Amazon exige de son côté l’accord du marchand, en plus de celui de l’acheteur. « Il nous semble assez évident que les applications tierces qui proposent d’effectuer des achats pour le compte de clients auprès d’autres entreprises doivent agir en toute transparence et respecter la décision des prestataires de participer ou non », a expliqué un porte-parole d'Amazon.
La justice américaine a cependant annulé, le 4 août, l’injonction préliminaire qu’Amazon avait obtenue en mars contre Perplexity, dont l'agent IA passait lui aussi des commandes sur sa boutique. Pour la cour d’appel fédérale du neuvième circuit, c’est l’utilisateur, et non l’entreprise d’IA, qui accède au site au sens de la loi américaine contre le piratage informatique.
WebMCP est une proposition de standard web (discutée dans la sphère W3C) qui permet à un site d’exposer des “outils” directement actionnables par un agent IA. Au lieu de lire et manipuler l’interface HTML comme un humain (repérer les champs, cliquer, vérifier ce qui a changé), l’agent appelle des fonctions structurées prévues pour lui. Cette approche réduit les erreurs liées à la reconnaissance d’interface et accélère les étapes répétitives (formulaires, options de livraison, codes promo). Elle rapproche l’automatisation d’un modèle “API” tout en restant dans la session web de l’utilisateur.
Ce sont des opérations exposées comme outils, qui décrivent une séquence de paiement de manière explicite plutôt que via des clics dans une page. get_checkout sert à lire l’état de la commande (total, étapes restantes, informations manquantes) dans un format exploitable par une machine. update_checkout permet de modifier des éléments comme l’adresse, la livraison ou certains champs requis, avec des validations plus fiables qu’une saisie “à l’aveugle” dans le DOM. complete_checkout déclenche la finalisation, généralement après confirmation humaine, tout en laissant s’appliquer les contrôles de paiement (anti-fraude, disponibilité, règles du marchand).
3D Secure et les codes de confirmation Shop Pay sont des mécanismes d’authentification forte conçus pour prouver que le payeur est bien le titulaire du moyen de paiement ou du compte. Ils reposent sur un facteur que l’agent ne doit pas posséder (validation dans une app bancaire, SMS, push, biométrie), afin d’éviter qu’un automatisme puisse payer seul. Dans la pratique, l’agent peut préparer le panier et remplir les données, mais il doit rendre la main au moment où une preuve d’identité ou une autorisation explicite est exigée. Cette séparation réduit le risque de fraude et évite que l’agent ait à stocker des secrets sensibles (codes temporaires, accès bancaire) pour “terminer” le paiement.

articles.title: Gemini abandonne ses « Gems » et suit le grand mouvement des LLM épurés
articles.text:
Nos chatbots se simplifient au fil du temps, et Google ne veut pas rater le train.
À la mi-septembre, les utilisateurs de Claude ont vu disparaître la séparation entre l’onglet Chat, réservé à la conversation classique, et l’onglet Cowork, qui servait à confier des tâches plus longues à l’agent. L’objectif pour Anthropic ? Que tout se passe désormais au même endroit, et que l’assistant s’adapte à la demande
Google prend aujourd’hui le même chemin avec Gemini. Ce week-end, un bandeau est apparu dans le gestionnaire de Gems pour annoncer leur conversion automatique en Skills à partir du 17 novembre.
Des assistants qu’on n’ouvre plus
Inspirés des GPTs personnalisés lancés par OpenAI fin 2023, les Gems ont été conçus comme des assistants autonomes. Disponibles depuis août 2024, ils permettaient d’enregistrer des instructions pour une tâche précise, comme relire un texte ou préparer un voyage. Chaque Gem fonctionnait toutefois comme un chatbot à part, qu’il fallait aller chercher dans la barre latérale et qui ouvrait une nouvelle conversation, sans rien savoir de celle en cours.
Les Skills reprennent une autre logique, popularisée par Anthropic, qui a introduit ce format pour Claude en octobre 2025 avant d’en faire un standard ouvert. L’idée n’est plus d’avoir un chatbot par usage, mais un seul agent qui pioche la bonne compétence au bon moment. Concrètement, elles conservent le principe des instructions enregistrées, mais s’invitent dans n’importe quelle discussion. On les appelle en tapant « / » suivi de leur nom, on peut en combiner plusieurs dans une même demande, et Gemini peut aussi les activer de lui-même lorsqu’il les juge utiles.
La migration se fera sans intervention de l’utilisateur, même si Google conseille de télécharger au préalable les fichiers de connaissance associés aux Gems, faute de préciser lesquels seront conservés.
Gratuit, mais sous conditions
Jusqu’ici, les Skills étaient réservées aux abonnés Google AI Pro et Ultra, ce qui laissait craindre que les utilisateurs gratuits perdent leurs Gems sans solution de remplacement.
D’après des tests menés par Neowin, cette restriction a été levée et tous les comptes peuvent désormais créer leurs propres Skills, même si Google ne l’a pas annoncé officiellement.
L’accès reste cependant réservé aux plus de 18 ans et suppose d’activer la conservation de l’historique d’activité Gemini.

articles.title: IIM Kozhikode partners with Walmart Global Tech to nurture Indian deeptech startups
articles.text:
IIM Kozhikode partners with Walmart Global Tech to nurture Indian deeptech startups
IIM Kozhikode’s business incubator, IIMK LIVE, has tied up with Walmart Global Tech to launch DEEP LEAP, a Rs 2.89 Cr initiative supporting 50 high-potential early-stage tech ventures.
IIM Kozhikode’s business incubator, IIMK LIVE, has teamed up with Walmart Global Tech to launch DEEP LEAP, a new incubation programme designed to nurture promising deeptech ventures across the country.
This is Walmart Global Tech’s first formal institutional partnership in India dedicated to deep tech, bringing together academic incubation capabilities with the resources and reach of a global retail technology leader.
Supported by a total funding of Rs 2.89 Cr, which is part of Walmart’s CSR funds, Rs 1.5 crore will be set aside for equity investment or seed funding support for selected startups in this program.
DEEP LEAP will focus on early-stage startups that already have a prototype or minimum viable product. The programme is aimed at founders building in high-impact fields such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, quantum computing, robotics, autonomous systems, space technology, aerospace, semiconductors, and photonics.
From an initial pool of around 1,500 applicants nationwide, 50 startups will be chosen for a 12-month cohort. During the year-long programme, founders will receive strategic business support, go-to-market mentorship, product validation, investor readiness coaching, and a platform to present their tech on a dedicated Demo Day.
Speaking on the launch, Prof. Debashis Chatterjee, Director of IIM Kozhikode and Chairman of IIMK LIVE, noted that deeptech isn't just about crafting more advanced software or hardware—it is about addressing fundamental challenges to create meaningful impact. He emphasised that combining the strengths of academia, industry, and entrepreneurship through DEEP LEAP will help connect local founders with global opportunities.
Rahul Ghosh, Group Director of Data Science at Walmart Global Tech, shared a similar outlook on the initiative’s broader goals: "Walmart Global Tech is a people-led, tech-powered organisation and we believe in serving communities through the power of technology. Our partnership with IIM Kozhikode LIVE on supporting deep tech startups brings this vision to life. This unique collaboration at the intersection of academia and entrepreneurship is well-positioned to advance cutting-edge technology and make a meaningful, positive difference in the communities we serve. I am excited about the potential research and innovation impact that this partnership will create, not just for India but at a global scale."

articles.title: Hay un lugar en España donde no hay crisis de vivienda: alquileres a 20 euros en Marinaleda
articles.text:
Según los barómetros del Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), la vivienda se mantiene como el principal problema de España para los ciudadanos. Que se lo digan a los casi 5.000 desahucios que llevamos en 2026, las casi 30.000 personas sin hogar o los miles acampados en las plazas de España aupando el ya acuñado “Decreto Maricarmen”, frente a fondos buitre y rentismo desequilibrado.
En este contexto, si te digo que puedes tener una casa de dos plantas por 20 euros al mes, sin fecha de caducidad y sin nadie que pueda venderla, ¿te lo crees? No es un anuncio de los años 90: es lo que Marinaleda (Sevilla) ultima ahora con 24 viviendas municipales que se alquilarán por entre 15 y 20 euros. Allí el mercado no está roto, lo que está es regulado.
Una casa que no se puede vender. Un apartamento de un dormitorio se ofrece en España por 984 euros de media, casi 50 veces más. El alquiler de Maricarmen, la madrileña de 87 años, pasó de 500 a 2.650 euros. Este martes PSOE y Sumar cerraron el pacto para aprobar un decreto de vivienda. Pero este caso recuerda que existen más vías.
La de Marinaleda actualmente es sencilla: entras en una casa y no la vendes. Ahora hay dos promociones, de 10 y 14 casas de una o dos plantas. El alcalde, Sergio Gómez (Con Andalucía), asegura que los inquilinos podrán quedarse sin límite de tiempo, no venderlas. La propiedad seguirá siendo del Ayuntamiento y, cuando una familia se marche, la casa volverá a ser social. Para pedirlas hay que llevar dos años empadronado y se estudia cada situación personal.
Trabajar la casa en lugar de pagarla. Una empresa local (nunca una multinacional) levanta la obra y los futuros vecinos trabajan de peones: sus horas se descuentan del precio final. Como documentó elDiario, Pilar Prieto entró en su casa en 1993 con su marido y su hijo de cuatro años, sin haber tocado un ladrillo en su vida, y desde entonces paga menos de 20 euros al mes. Según el consistorio, más de 350 viviendas se han levantado así. El propio alcalde construyó la suya como peón y paga su alquiler al Ayuntamiento, como cualquier vecino.
El cabrero. José Domínguez, alias El Cabrero, fue un hombre que pasó de pastor en la sierra sevillana a convertirse en uno de los cantaores flamencos más ruidosos de la Transición. Cantaba de jornaleros, terratenientes, pobreza y libertad, y su compromiso con el movimiento libertario y las luchas del campo andaluz lo llevó a participar junto a los trabajadores de Marinaleda y a mantener una estrecha relación con el sindicalista Juan Manuel Sánchez Gordillo.
Y se transformó en tal símbolo de la ocupación y colectivización de tierras, cooperativas y trabajo comunitario, que nació un sistema de vivienda basado en su nombre. “El Cabrero” es un modelo de autoconstrucción financiado con fondos municipales, fondos del PER y trabajo voluntario de vecinos. Y ha permitido levantar cientos de viviendas públicas cuyo coste para los habitantes ronda eso, los 15 euros mensuales.
Casas indefinidas. Las 24 casas ya se estaban construyendo en octubre de 2024 y dependen de dinero autonómico. Según el alcalde, el Plan Estatal de Vivienda 2026-2030 asigna a Andalucía 718,2 millones estatales y 478,8 autonómicos, 1.197 en total. Andalucía ha recibido ya 136,8 millones de 2026, pero en Merinaleda la Junta no había abierto la convocatoria hasta ahora.
¿Y si te quieres quedar para siempre? El Sindicato de Inquilinas ha hecho de los contratos indefinidos su línea roja en el decreto Maricarmen. En Marinaleda lo tienen asumido desde hace décadas: Pilar paga una cuota que siempre puede afrontar. El borrador de Vivienda, en cambio, planteaba una prórroga de dos años y prohibir los desahucios solo hasta 2028.
Otras grietas. Como parte del colectivo, también conviene recordar la finca de El Humoso, el motor económico de Marinaleda. Los jornaleros lograron emancipar sus 1.200 hectáreas en 1991, tras años de conflicto, pero sigue pendiente de una solución firme sobre su futuro. Ya se tuvo que enfrentar a la amenaza del desalojo en plena crisis agraria, y aunque consiguió mantener la gestión pública, este pulmón económico no tiene la fuerza que tenía hace un lustro.
La aspiración de tener la casa en propiedad, algo que cada vez cuesta más a los jóvenes, choca de frente con la situación de Marinaleda, donde Pilar Prieto gestiona quedarse con la casa para dejársela a su hijo. A la vez, seguirán siendo inquilinos del Ayuntamiento. "No es un milagro, es gestión", resume el alcalde.
De gratis. Aquí, ni él ni ningún concejal cobran, ni siquiera por asistir a los plenos, y el Pleno votaría en contra de que una gran constructora levante casas. De hecho, las fuerzas policiales tampoco, porque no hay como tal. La vivienda está más cara que nunca y Marinaleda, en vez de apostar por el modelo de Madrid o Málaga, aboga por proteger a sus 2.562 vecinos (7 más que el año pasado) con un formato que requiere de compromiso colectivo. Cuando el suelo es público y el trabajo lo pone el vecino, la cuota deja de ser un problema y te permite vivir sin pensar en ello.

articles.title: Mon téléphone est-il compatible eSIM ? La liste 2026 des iPhone, Samsung, Google Pixel et Xiaomi
articles.text:
Mon téléphone est-il compatible eSIM ? La liste 2026 des iPhone, Samsung, Google Pixel et Xiaomi
Pour savoir si votre téléphone est compatible eSIM, ouvrez le clavier et composez *#06# : si un numéro EID de 32 chiffres s'affiche, votre modèle accepte les profils SIM virtuels. Même vérification possible dans les réglages, via l'option « Ajouter un forfait cellulaire » ou « Ajouter une eSIM ». Voici la liste 2026 des iPhone, Galaxy, Pixel et Xiaomi compatibles, puis les forfaits pour voyager sans roaming.
Compatibilité eSIM par marque en un coup d'œil
| Marque / Famille | Génération minimale compatible | Capacité multi-eSIM | Remarques / Exceptions régionales | Note de compatibilité (/5) | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Apple iPhone | iPhone XS/XR (2018) ; dès iPhone 11 sous iOS 26 | 8 profils minimum ; 2 lignes actives dès l'iPhone 13 | Sans tiroir aux États-Unis dès l'iPhone 14, et sur 12 marchés avec l'iPhone 17 ; Chine : 17e et Air seuls | 5/5 | 
| Samsung Galaxy | Galaxy S20, Fold et Flip d'origine (2019-2020) | 5 à 10 profils ; double eSIM active dès la série S24 | Chine, Hong Kong, Taïwan : aucune eSIM ; gamme A variable | 4/5 | 
| Google Pixel | Pixel 3 (2018) ; sans restriction dès le Pixel 4 | Jusqu'à 8 profils ; deux eSIM actives dès le Pixel 7 | Pixel 10 et 11 américains sans tiroir SIM | 5/5 | 
| Xiaomi / Redmi | Xiaomi 12T Pro (2022) | Deux lignes actives sur les versions internationales | Versions chinoises sans eSIM ; Redmi et Poco au cas par cas | 3/5 | 
Compatibilité détaillée, marque par marque
Apple iPhone : l'eSIM depuis 2018
Liste des modèles disponibles iPhone compatibles eSIM : XS, XS Max, XR, gamme 11 à 16, SE (2020, 2022), 16e, 17e, 17, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max et iPhone Air.
Une puce eUICC intégrée offre un espace de stockage pour au moins huit profils SIM virtuels, dont deux actifs en Dual SIM Dual Standby dès l'iPhone 13. L'iPhone Air (5,6 mm) n'a aucun tiroir : eSIM seule, partout. Les iPhone 17, 17 Pro et 17 Pro Max en font autant aux États-Unis, au Canada, au Japon, au Mexique et dans huit autres territoires ; l'Europe conserve la nano-SIM.
Points forts
•	Huit profils ou plus en mémoire.
•	Deux lignes actives dès l'iPhone 13.
•	Ajout d'une eSIM iPhone en quelques touches : QR code ou application opérateur.
•	Huit générations compatibles, de l'XS à la série 17.
•	Ligne perso, ligne pro et data voyage cohabitent.
Points d'attention / Limites
•	Aucune eSIM en Chine continentale, sauf iPhone 17e et Air.
•	Un iPhone eSIM-only américain n'a aucun tiroir pour SIM physique.
•	Hong Kong et Macao : liste de modèles restreinte.
•	Appareil verrouillé par l'opérateur : eSIM tierce parfois refusée.
•	XS, XS Max et XR absents du guide Apple sous iOS 26.
Samsung Galaxy : l'eSIM des S20 aux Fold8
Samsung Galaxy compatibles : S20 à S26 (Plus, Ultra, Edge, FE dès S23), Galaxy Fold d'origine, Z Fold2 à Fold8 (Ultra inclus), Galaxy Flip (Z Flip à Flip8), Galaxy Note 20 Ultra (hors États-Unis et Hong Kong), gamme A : A54, A55, A35, A56, A36.
Sur les Galaxy S26, Samsung autorise nano-SIM plus eSIM ou deux eSIM actives. Nouveauté 2026 : les Z Fold8 et Z Fold8 Ultra abandonnent le double tiroir nano-SIM des Z Fold3 à Z Fold7 ; comme le Z Flip8, ils n'ont qu'un emplacement physique, donc une seconde ligne passe par l'eSIM, avec deux profils actifs maximum.
Points forts
•	Double eSIM active possible dès la série S24.
•	L'eSIM Samsung s'ajoute via Connexions > Gestionnaire de cartes SIM.
•	Une nano-SIM et une eSIM cohabitent sans manipulation.
•	Cinq à dix profils mémorisés selon la génération.
•	Tablettes Galaxy Tab S9 à S11 : même compatibilité.
Points d'attention / Limites
•	Modèles Chine, Hong Kong et Taïwan : aucune eSIM.
•	S20, S21 et Note 20 Ultra américains exclus, tout comme le S20 FE.
•	Gamme A : A35 et A36 réservés à l'Europe, l'Amérique du Nord et la Corée.
•	Corée : la plupart des Galaxy achetés sur place n'ont pas d'eSIM.
•	Import : contrôlez le code modèle.
Google Pixel : l'eSIM sans restriction dès le Pixel 4
Liste des Google Pixel compatibles : Pixel 3 et 3a (avec exceptions), puis toute la gamme du Pixel 4 au Pixel 11, déclinaisons a, Pro, Pro XL et Fold comprises.
Chez Google, l'eSIM Pixel existe depuis le Pixel 3 (2018), et le Pixel 7 a inauguré la double eSIM active, sans SIM physique. En Europe, les Pixel récents combinent une nano-SIM et l'eSIM, avec deux profils actifs ; jusqu'à huit profils restent en mémoire.
Points forts
•	Deux eSIM actives simultanément dès le Pixel 7.
•	Aucune restriction régionale à partir du Pixel 4.
•	Ajout par QR code depuis Réseau et Internet.
•	Séries a abordables, du Pixel 7a au 10a, compatibles.
•	Pixel 10a : nano-SIM plus eSIM, ou double eSIM.
Points d'attention / Limites
•	Pixel 3 et 3a : exceptions en Australie, Taïwan, Japon et Asie du Sud-Est.
•	Pixel 2 : eSIM réservée à Google Fi aux États-Unis.
•	Pixel 10 et 11 américains : eSIM seule, sans tiroir.
•	Deux profils actifs maximum, même avec huit stockés.
•	Modèle acheté à crédit : déblocage opérateur nécessaire.
Xiaomi et Redmi : une eSIM au cas par cas
Liste des Xiaomi compatibles eSIM : 12T Pro, 13, 13 Pro, 13 Lite, 13T, 14, 14T, 15, 15 Ultra, 15T, 17 Ultra, puis Xiaomi Redmi Note 13 Pro à Redmi Note 15 Pro+ et Poco X7, F8 Pro, F8 Ultra.
Les versions internationales embarquent un tiroir nano-SIM et gèrent deux profils eSIM, avec deux lignes actives. Les variantes américaines sont eSIM seule, avec au moins quatre profils. Les modèles chinois restent en double nano-SIM, sans eSIM. Le 12T Pro fut l'un des premiers Xiaomi compatibles, en 2022.
Points forts
•	eSIM présente sur les Redmi Note 13 à 15, versions Pro.
•	Deux lignes actives sur les versions internationales.
•	Extension aux Poco X7, F8 Pro et F8 Ultra.
•	QR code d'activation standard, accepté par tous les fournisseurs.
•	Xiaomi 17 Ultra : l'eSIM arrive sur le dernier fleuron.
Points d'attention / Limites
•	Versions chinoises, souvent asiatiques : aucune eSIM.
•	Redmi d'entrée de gamme et Poco modestes : pas d'eSIM.
•	12T Pro : eSIM principalement sur le marché européen.
•	Certains Ultra, comme le 14 Ultra, livrés sans eSIM.
•	Réglage à vérifier dans HyperOS ou via *#06# avant l'achat.
Honor, Motorola, Oppo : les autres marques compatibles
Chez Honor, la gamme Magic reste compatible selon la région : Honor Magic7 Pro, Magic6 Pro, Magic V2 et V3. Motorola a introduit l'eSIM dès le Razr 2019, puis l'a étendue aux Razr 40 et 50 Ultra, aux Edge 50 et à plusieurs Moto G. Pour l'eSIM Oppo, retenez les Find X8, Find N5 et Find X9. Comme toujours, la région de vente et la version logicielle tranchent.
Choisir et activer un forfait eSIM : le rôle des fournisseurs
Une fois votre téléphone compatible eSIM identifié, gardez la SIM physique pour les appels et ajoutez un profil de données prépayé : le fournisseur envoie un QR code d'activation, ou passe par une application, et l'installation prend environ deux minutes. Trois acteurs se distinguent.
Ubigi couvre plus de 200 destinations avec des forfaits locaux, régionaux ou mondiaux, de 500 Mo à l'illimité, dès 2 €. Le forfait se recharge dans l'application et s'active automatiquement à l'arrivée grâce à Smart Start ; Ubigi promet jusqu'à 90 % d'économie face au roaming d'un opérateur classique.
Holafly mise sur la data illimitée, pour 1 à 90 jours, dès 3,79 € et dans plus de 160 destinations. Point de vigilance : data seule, sans numéro local, et un tarif supérieur aux offres à volume.
GoMoWorld affiche des prix identiques d'un pays à l'autre, en euros : 3,99 € pour 7 jours, puis 10,99 €, 19,99 € ou 29,99 € pour 30 jours, dans plus de 200 destinations. Tout se gère dans l'application, VPN européen inclus ; la connexion s'arrête quand la data est épuisée.
| Fournisseur | Type d'offre principal | Processus d'activation | Profil d'usage recommandé | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Ubigi | Forfaits data prépayés locaux, régionaux ou mondiaux, rechargeables | QR code reçu par e-mail ou application ; activation à l'arrivée | Voyages multi-pays, budget modulable, recharges en séjour | 
| Holafly | Data illimitée, durée de 1 à 90 jours | QR code ou application | Gros consommateurs, télétravail, partage de connexion | 
| GoMoWorld | Enveloppes de données fixes, quatre formules dès 3,99 € | Application uniquement | Petit budget, séjour court, usage modéré | 
Verdict : nos conseils avant l'achat ou le départ
Notre avis en quatre réflexes. Avant tout achat, composez #06# ou exigez l'identifiant EID : sans ce numéro, aucun téléphone compatible n'accepte d'eSIM. Contrôlez ensuite la région de vente : un iPhone, un Galaxy Ultra, un Pixel ou un Xiaomi Redmi Note importé des États-Unis ou d'Asie peut perdre son emplacement de SIM physique, voire toute compatibilité eSIM. Vérifiez aussi le blocage opérateur, puis comptez vos besoins : deux profils actifs suffisent presque toujours.
Pour les vacances, Ubigi convient aux séjours multi-pays, Holafly aux gros consommateurs et GoMoWorld aux petits budgets. Installez le QR code en Wi-Fi avant le départ, puis activez le profil à l'arrivée pour éviter le roaming.
Note finale : iPhone et Pixel (5/5) devancent Samsung (4/5), puis Xiaomi (3/5). Les amateurs de pliables regarderont aussi Honor Magic V, Motorola Razr ou Galaxy Flip, tous disponibles avec eSIM selon la région.
Avant de cliquer sur « acheter », prenez dix secondes pour composer *#06# : c'est le test le plus fiable.

articles.title: Kingston Retains No. 1 Position in Global DRAM Module Market
articles.text:
Monday, September 28th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Kingston Retains No. 1 Position in Global DRAM Module Market
Kingston Technology Company, Inc., a world leader in memory products and technology solutions, today announced it has been ranked the top third-party DRAM module supplier in the world, according to the latest rankings by revenue from analyst firm TrendForce. Kingston retains its number 1 position with an estimated 62% market share.
TrendForce reported that the global DRAM module market generated approximately $21.2 billion in revenue in 2025, representing a 59% YoY increase and a significant acceleration from the 7% growth recorded in 2024. The market's expansion was driven by rising DRAM prices and stronger shipment volumes during the second half of the year. According to the report, Kingston's revenue grew 48% YoY in 2025, reinforcing its leadership position in a market where the top five DRAM module suppliers accounted for 77% of total revenue. Kingston alone represented nearly two-thirds of the market.The DRAM market experienced a dramatic shift during 2025. Early in the year, DRAM module manufacturers increased DDR4 inventory levels in response to tariff concerns and DRAM suppliers' end-of-life plans for DDR4 products. Later in the year, growing demand from cloud service providers supporting agentic AI workloads significantly increased server DRAM consumption. This surge reduced DRAM availability for PC and consumer applications, contributing to higher memory prices and stronger module market performance.
Kingston's investments in supply allowed the company to strategically manage inventory throughout 2025 and as DRAM costs increased during the second half of 2025, Kingston was well positioned to support channel demand, helping drive its strong annual performance. TrendForce also noted that DRAM module manufacturers increasingly focused on industrial and enterprise server markets during 2025 while accelerating the transition to DDR5-based product portfolios. Kingston continues to expand its comprehensive memory offerings across consumer, enterprise, industrial, and data center applications, helping customers navigate evolving technology requirements and next-generation computing workloads.
Kristy Ernt, DRAM business manager, Kingston"Maintaining our leadership position in a dynamic and rapidly evolving memory market reflects Kingston's long-term strategy, strong supplier relationships, and commitment to serving customers worldwide. Our ability to anticipate market transitions, manage inventory effectively, and provide reliable memory solutions enabled us to support partners and customers throughout the year."
