articles.title: Como acessar a área de transferência no celular • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Como acessar a área de transferência no celular
O histórico de copiar e colar está disponível nos dispositivos Android, enquanto o iPhone armazena somente o último item copiado pelo usuário
A área de transferência é uma ferramenta bastante útil no dia a dia para reutilizar textos e links copiados no celular com agilidade. Esse recurso oculta e organiza informações temporárias na memória, facilitando o compartilhamento rápido de dados entre aplicativos.
No Android, dá para acessar a área de transferência abrindo um menu no teclado virtual e selecionando a opção de prancheta para ver o histórico completo. Já no iPhone, a Apple limita a função por segurança, permitindo colar apenas a última informação copiada e sem oferecer um histórico nativo.
A seguir, o Tecnoblog te mostra o passo a passo para ver o histórico de copiar e colar no celular Android.
A área de transferência no celular não é uma pasta específica ou aplicativo visível, mas sim um armazenamento temporário do sistema. Ela guarda conteúdos copiados na memória RAM para a pessoa reutilizá-los diretamente no teclado virtual ou ao colar em qualquer campo de texto.
Abra o Documentos, Bloco de Notas, WhatsApp ou qualquer outro aplicativo que permita digitar mensagens.
Toque na caixa de texto para exibir o teclado virtual do Android. Em seguida, toque no botão com quatro quadrados ou três pontos, nos cantos do teclado, para ver a configuração.
Toque na opção “Área de transferência” para ver o histórico do copiar e colar no celular Android.
Importante: nos aparelhos Samsung, um ícone de prancheta costuma ficar visível diretamente no teclado para acessar o conteúdo copiado para a área de transferência.
Sim, o iPhone possui área de transferência, mas o iOS armazena temporariamente apenas o último item copiado na memória. Para identificar a última cópia, basta pressionar um campo de texto e usar a ferramenta “Colar” do teclado virtual do telefone.
Não é possível ver o histórico da área de transferência do iPhone nativamente, pois o iOS armazena apenas o último item copiado na memória do sistema. Para visualizar ou gerenciar cópias anteriores, você precisará recorrer a aplicativos de terceiros.
No Android, você pode apagar o histórico da área de transferência pelo painel de gerenciamento do teclado, excluindo itens salvos ou selecionando a opção de limpar tudo. Essa ação remove definitivamente as informações do armazenamento temporário para proteger sua privacidade.
Já no iPhone, que não possui histórico nativo, você pode copiar um simples espaço em branco para substituir o texto copiado para a área de transferência. Esse truque simples limpa o dado sensível anterior da memória do iOS.
Sim, você pode acessar a área de transferência do Windows utilizando o atalho Windows + V no teclado. A partir do menu flutuante, dá para consultar o histórico recente, colar elementos ou apagar informações da memória temporária.
Já a área de transferência do macOS é acessada utilizando o atalho Command + Espaço. Depois, basta digitar Command + 4 para abrir o histórico do Spotlight, recurso disponível somente nas versões mais recentes do sistema operacional da Apple.

articles.title: Experts worry about Nvidia's AI chip sales in China and influence over Trump
articles.text:
On its face, the recent summit between Donald Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, didn’t change much in the world of AI regulation. Export controls were not discussed, with neither country seemingly interested in making concessions. An already tenuous trade truce was temporarily extended for just two months, and looming US controls that could drop soon could easily end that and trigger China to retaliate by cutting off exports of rare earths, analysts expect.
However, in the background of these shaky talks, Nvidia appeared to notch a big win, as China is currently mulling relaxing controls and allowing some of its biggest AI firms to import perhaps millions more of Nvidia’s banned chips over the next year.
Sources familiar with China’s talks told The Information that China’s tech oversight arm, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, asked Alibaba and ByteDance to share plans to buy Nvidia’s RTX Pro 5500 chips. Although these are gaming chips, China asked firms to detail how they plan to use them, with expectations that chips could be put into servers to help power the country’s most in-demand AI models.
Increasingly, Trump looks to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for advice on AI, but not everybody agrees that what’s good for Nvidia is good for the United States.
Already the world’s most valuable company, Nvidia would obviously profit enormously in a world where risks are downplayed, and both countries’ priorities remain powering rapid developments in frontier AI without pumping the brakes. Some critics worry that Nvidia’s profit motivations may be steering Trump’s thinking at a pivotal moment when it may matter how well a president actually understands the risks of a new technology.
Trump “completely aligned” with Nvidia
For Nvidia, a big goal since Trump took office was to open up more of China’s market so that Nvidia could start selling chips that were restricted during Joe Biden’s administration. Huang has blamed US export controls for cutting Nvidia’s share of China’s advanced AI chip market from about 95 percent to zero, The Information reported.
Trump was not an instant ally. Instead, he came into office asking “What the hell is Nvidia?” and rather than loosening Biden’s export controls, he initially tightened them further, most notably by banning exports of H200 chips to China. Trump was even thinking about breaking Nvidia up, expecting that stoking more competition among chipmakers domestically was crucial to America winning the so-called “AI race” with China.
But then he met Huang over dinner at Mar-a-Lago, where Trump said he “learned the facts of life” and understood that Nvidia as a firm is an “amazing” AI leader. Ignoring warnings from lawmakers and national security experts, Trump lifted the export controls on H200 chips, which China eventually allowed to be sold to some firms. Since then, Trump and Huang have appeared together in public repeatedly, and they regularly talk by phone, according to Stephen Witt, the author of The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, Nvidia, and the World’s Most Coveted Microchip.
In an interview discussing Huang’s influence over Trump, Witt told NPR that Trump’s recent claims—suggesting that it’s a “hoax” that AI might destroy humanity and that instead AI will be an economic boon—are “exactly Jensen’s talking points.”
“Jensen is now the president’s most influential adviser on technology issues,” Witt said. “The two have become quite close.”
Witt spent time with “tons” of people in the AI industry who share Huang’s views, he told NPR. And like Huang, they tended to downplay risks that software developers—including Nvidia’s biggest customers like Anthropic and OpenAI—are right now urging the White House to take seriously, he found.
“Most of the hardware people, most of the people who designed the networking equipment and the microchips, feel like Jensen does,” Witt said. “They tend to have a very low sense of risk regarding this technology. They just don’t see it.”
He said this debate has been going on between the two camps for the past 10 years, and “neither camp has moved at all.” With Huang growing closer to Trump, it seems likely the president will continue downplaying leading AI firms’ warnings and avoiding serious talks with China about their models’ risks. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed ahead of Trump’s talks with Xi that “the president is completely aligned with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia.”
Nvidia downplays risks
According to The Information, if China lifts export curbs on Nvidia’s gaming chips, it “would give Nvidia perhaps its best chance in more than a year to regain some momentum in China’s AI market.” If China gives the nod, ByteDance plans to order 1 million chips, which would automatically secure for Nvidia two quarters of projected sales.
That would certainly help improve Nvidia’s financial outlook in China, as China’s delayed approval of H200 sales meant sales were dismal, comprising less than 1 percent of Nvidia’s data center revenue in the most recent quarter.
Andrew Yoon, a researcher at an AI safety nonprofit called CivAI, told CNBC that in the AI industry, “Nvidia is the most aggressive in terms of, let’s just make money.”
“At every turn, they are really trying to just make sure whatever happens is good for Nvidia’s bottom line,” Yoon said.
If the US and China continue to loosen controls, some experts fear that too many chips may end up being diverted to China. Eventually, that could cause US data centers to lose a precious domestic chip supply that’s currently making it possible to stay ahead on frontier AI, the thinking goes.
Nvidia’s reporting suggests that as of now, the countries don’t compete for resources, though. In the first half of 2026, Nvidia reportedly took a $400 million hit due to vast quantities of unsold H200 chips. No American firms want those chips, since they can access Nvidia’s more advanced chips.
However, demand for chips made for China’s market could perhaps change, as more US data centers come online, policy experts believe.
Nvidia’s spokesperson told Ars that it China lifts curbs on “outdated” gaming chips “released nearly a half a decade ago,” it will only benefit US firms unfairly burdened by restrictions on chips that cannot be used to train AI. The statement recalls Huang’s remarks at a recent “All-In” summit hosted by Trump’s former AI czar, David Sacks. Huang publicly promised Trump: “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people.”
Yet, Witt joked that “Jensen is really the only one who wants to sell his equipment to China.”
Witt thinks that a responsible US president would set up a group like the National Transportation Safety Board to review mandatory reports of AI safety incidents. That could support the US-China safety alert system announced last week, which right now troublingly includes no tech experts. But that likely won’t happen, since “Jensen has convinced Trump that what’s good for Nvidia is good for America,” Witt said.
It remains unclear if China will approve the gaming chip sales, but sources told The Information that the government intends to allow at least some into the country. The pressure may be on to approve them, since “Chinese companies are rolling out AI products and services faster than they can find the chips to run them,” The Information noted. At least one buyer “plans to put eight RTX Pro 5500s in each server, a standard setup that lets the chips work together on larger AI models,” sources said. Supposedly, Nvidia is preparing to ship the first orders this December.
If Huang gets his way, Chinese firms will buy millions more of Nvidia’s chips in the coming years, helping the firm maintain global dominance over companies that are locked in on advancing AI.
Huang’s influence over Trump may be tested
During the most recent summit between Trump and Xi, Huang joined many US tech leaders at a state dinner, including Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Sam Altman, Mark Zuckerberg, and Satya Nadella. Noticeably, China invited none of its tech leaders.
Ro Khanna, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives’ select committee on China, told The Guardian that Trump could have used the tech leaders’ help to press Xi in their talks to set up technical working groups to monitor AI threats. But Trump seems to have “no interest in doing that,” Khanna said.
At the summit, Xi acknowledged that the US and China have the “responsibility to develop and manage AI for good” and “ensure that the development of AI is always under human control,” The Guardian reported. But neither country was willing to make “even a symbolic gesture” that an AI slowdown may be necessary if risks cannot be contained.
Jonathan Czin, a fellow in the China Center at the Brookings Institution, told The Guardian that he had “very low expectations going into this meeting for anything of substance, and the meeting managed to underwhelm even those low expectations.”
“Even going into this meeting, you’re dealing with a septuagenarian and octogenarian who may or may not have ever had first-hand contact with actually using AI, and what happens with this technology rests on their two shoulders,” Czin said. “The only thing they seemed to agree about is that neither of them wants to slow down with this technology, regardless of their actual understanding of it.”
Trump may soon have to reconcile the differences between some of Huang’s views on AI safety and his own law enforcement, however. While the FBI has accused six Chinese firms of aggressively copying US frontier models, Huang has sided with China, arguing that distillation of frontier AI models is “not robbery” but rather “competition,” CNBC reported.
“You’re allowed to test somebody else’s products all you want,” Huang said, suggesting that AI firms could disable services to block distillation if they wanted. He further noted that “Nvidia’s products are sometimes stripped ‘down to bones’ as companies tried to learn how they worked.”
“I’d really prefer they didn’t,” Huang said. “I’d really prefer that nobody learns from our products, and we have the benefit of just cruising along. But, you know, frankly, competition makes everything better.”
To Huang, getting Trump to agree with him might be easy, Witt suggested. As he explained:
When I interviewed Jensen years ago, he told me that every problem in the world is actually an engineering problem. Now, that’s true if it’s a personal problem or a business problem or a political problem. You study the inputs and then you modify the inputs to get the outputs that you want. In this case, I think Jensen has realized that the inputs for Trump are, like, flattery—like, public flattery, nonstop public flattery. And the outputs are, you know, lifting restrictions on sales of Nvidia equipment to China and zero regulation on AI.
Despite Bessent’s suggestion that Huang is pulling the strings, Trump took to Truth Social ahead of the “All-In” summit to make it clear that he expects to be trusted as the sole authority when it comes to AI safety.
“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

articles.title: Montage Technology Announces Mass Production of Gen 5 DDR5 Register Clock Driver
articles.text:
Monday, September 28th 2026
	
	
	
	
Montage Technology Announces Mass Production of Gen 5 DDR5 Register Clock Driver
Montage Technology today announced the mass production of its Gen 5 DDR5 Register Clock Driver (RCD05). Designed for high-performance DDR5 RDIMM memory modules, the RCD05 addresses the growing demand from data centers, AI servers, and other applications for memory systems with higher bandwidth and greater reliability.
Compliant with the JEDEC DDR5RCD05 specification, the RCD05 supports data rates of up to 8000 MT/s, an approximately 11% increase over the previous-generation RCD04, providing greater memory bandwidth for next-generation server platforms. The RCD05 integrates a high-performance, low-jitter PLL clock driver circuit and supports key features including continuous-time linear equalization (CTLE) and ZQ calibration, helping improve signal integrity and stability for high-speed signal transmission.
Mr. Stephen Tai, President of Montage Technology"The successful mass production of the RCD05 marks another important achievement in our continued efforts to advance DDR5 memory interface technologies. We will continue to work closely with our industry partners to deliver high-performance, highly reliable memory interface solutions that help next-generation server platforms achieve enhanced system performance."
In addition to the RCD05, Montage Technology offers a comprehensive portfolio of DDR5 RCD products supporting a range of data rates, along with memory interface and module companion chips for both server and client applications, including MRCD, MDB, CKD, SPD, PMIC, and TS. Together, these products enable Montage Technology to provide customers with a complete memory interface solution.

articles.title: Scammers used an AI voice clone and a fake WhatsApp message to move €95 million out of an Italian bank
articles.text:
AI Scammed: As AI models grow in complexity and capabilities, scammers are expanding their business opportunities as well. Social engineering techniques have fully translated into this new wild AI world, and high profile executives are losing their jobs as a consequence.
Sources familiar with the matter have unveiled yet another case involving an executive who lost his high-paying position due to an AI-based scam.
Paolo Molesini, chairman of private banking institution Fideuram, was targeted in a complex fraud scheme that began in February 2026. Molesini resigned from his position soon afterward, and the bank is still trying to recover the full amount extracted by cybercriminals.
Fideuram is the private banking arm of Intesa Sanpaolo, Italy's largest bank and one of Europe's biggest banking institutions. Like other private banks, the organization provides services to high-profile customers with significant financial assets. The sources said that Molesini first received a WhatsApp message that appeared to come from Intesa Sanpaolo CEO Carlo Messina.
Messina was apparently asking Molesini to help with a large overseas transaction. After the initial message, Fideuram's chairman received a phone call from a senior partner at a major law firm. However, there were no humans behind the call: The sources confirmed that cybercriminals used AI models to impersonate the lawyer's voice, convincing Molesini that the initial request for help had indeed come from his "boss," Messina, at Intesa Sanpaolo.
Fideuram was instructed to proceed with the transaction. The bank transferred a total of €95 million (around $108 million) to a series of accounts in foreign countries, including China and Hong Kong. However, Fideuram's team detected anomalies in the transactions and alerted the banks where the money had been transferred.
Thanks to local authorities and banking institutions in Italy, Portugal, and China, Fideuram was eventually able to recover €53 million from the fraudulent transactions. The remaining sum was apparently lost after passing through a complex network of overseas accounts, ultimately being converted into an undisclosed cryptocurrency.
Molesini resigned from his position in March without providing a specific explanation for his decision. The newly unveiled incident might explain why the executive left his high-paying position at Fideuram. As a private bank, the institution provides its affluent customers with a private broker to personally manage their financial needs.
The Fideuram incident highlights how AI models have become a significant security threat and a potential financial disaster in the making. Milan-based prosecutors are now trying to identify the alleged cybercriminals behind the AI-generated heist. One person living outside the European Union is reportedly under investigation for computer fraud.

articles.title: With Dazzle, Marissa Mayer bets your camera roll has more info on your life than your inbox | TechCrunch
articles.text:
When former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer earlier this month told me she was finally ready to unveil Dazzle, the personal AI assistant that raised an $8 million seed round last December, I couldn’t help but wonder if she’s playing copycat to Meta’s Muse, Instinct, and the wave of similar tools that have flooded the market over the past month.
But when Mayer finally gave me a demo, Dazzle proved it’s taking a different approach. Instead of building context about you from text-heavy apps like email, calendars and shopping histories, Dazzle’s AI assistant gets all its context from a single source: your camera roll.
“I think that photos are an underappreciated source of information,” Mayer said. “You’ll be surprised what we can learn about you and how good a job we can do with your photos.”
Mayer argues that if a photo is worth a thousand words, your camera roll is worth millions. By analyzing all the photos stored on your phone, Dazzle claims to understand your hobbies, interests, food and style preferences, how you like to spend their time, and with whom.
“We understand whether or not you like to ski, where your most recent trip was, what types of things your kids are into,” Mayer said.
It’s no surprise that Mayer has built an assistant centered around photos. Her previous startup, Sunshine, launched an AI-powered photo-sharing tool called Shine in 2024. While that product was widely criticized for its outdated design, failed to attract widespread usage, and eventually shut down, Mayer says it nevertheless built “interesting IP.”
I was eager to try Dazzle, which users can interact with through its app or via text. Dazzle splits its functionality into two core experiences. For immediate tasks, it can scan recent photos to pull details — like populating your calendar from an event flyer, or finding a repair-person after spotting a broken garage door in your camera roll.
Second, it mines your photo library to come up with personalized ideas for everything from holiday vacations to birthday gifts.
Given that plenty of tools can parse pictures — like looking up where to buy a product, or searching information on an interesting art piece — I was far more curious to test what Dazzle could learn from my photo history.
For instance, Mayer uses Dazzle to brainstorm family outings. By scanning her photos, she says, the assistant deduced that her family loves escape rooms, and subsequently suggested multiple SF Bay Area locations she’d never heard of.
When I tested Dazzle with a request for vacation recommendations, it suggested several Mediterranean spots, likely picking up on my past trips to Spain and Greece. But it also threw in Sicily, which surprised me since I was there four years ago. After some more tinkering, I noticed it has blind spots — it failed to remember my daughter already knows how to roller skate when I asked if I should buy her a pair for her next birthday.
Despite the hiccups, though, I appreciated Dazzle’s ideas for activities, like suggesting a local pottery studio, or a bioluminescent kayak tour in Tomales Bay.
I’m sure the product will improve with time, and while I’m undecided on whether I’ll keep using it, I like that its suggestions feel more personal than what you’d get from an AI assistant that only knows your calendar and email.
In the meantime, Mayer contends that given security concerns with products like Instinct and Muse, users may feel more comfortable handing over their photo libraries to an AI instead of granting it access to sensitive data like emails and messages.
She emphasized that Dazzle prioritizes privacy, and discards any personal information the AI flags as sensitive.
This flurry of new AI assistants is an exciting time for consumers. And while Dazzle isn’t as broadly useful as other offerings quite yet, it offers a glimpse of a future in which AI can do more than just execute tasks; it actually knows who you are.

articles.title: From payments to wealth: Where is India's fintech story headed next?
articles.text:
From payments to wealth: Where is India's fintech story headed next?
India’s fintech story is moving beyond payments and credit as rising incomes and longer lifespans create a growing need for personalised wealth advice. But access to independent, affordable financial guidance remains limited, leaving a gap that AI and digital infrastructure could help bridge.
If the last decade of Indian fintech belonged to payments, the next one could well belong to wealth. UPI made moving money instant and free. Digital lending turned access to credit into an afternoon on a phone. These solved the hardest, least glamorous work of inclusion. But the frontier has now shifted to the harder question that sits just after money lands in an account: what do you do with it? For most Indians, that question is still unanswered.
Why the demand for wealth is exploding now
Four forces are compounding at once, and together they turn wealth planning from a choice into a compulsion for the Indian middle class.
We are living longer, so savings must last decades more than our parents’ did. There is no government pension at the end of it. This is the first generation deciding that it won't depend on its children. And incomes are rising fast, leaving more people with surplus but no framework for it.
The result is a generation earning well and saving diligently, yet unsure if they are on the right track. Mutual fund Assets Under Management crossed Rs 87 lakh crore in August 2026. Tens of millions now invest with the discipline of a rent payment, but investing regularly and having a plan are not the same thing.
The structural gap
The uncomfortable truth is who Indians actually turn to for advice. Most of it comes from pseudo-advisors, mutual fund distributors and bank relationship managers whose income depends on the products they sell. However well-meaning, the incentive is structurally conflicted: they earn when you buy, not when you do well. And when people don't turn to them, they lean on family, friends or a WhatsApp group.
The genuinely fiduciary side, SEBI-registered advisers paid by the client and not the product, numbers only around 900 for the entire country, and most serve the HNI and UHNI segment where the economics work. A few newer players do good work, but only within a single asset class.
So, the salaried professional in the middle is left choosing between advice that's conflicted and advice that's out of reach and unaffordable. That gap, not access to investing, is the real unsolved problem of this decade.
Why it's finally possible now
What has changed is that three tailwinds have arrived together, and for the first time they make conflict-free advice both scalable and affordable for a 30-million-strong retail audience, not just the wealthy.
The RBI's Account Aggregator infrastructure can pull a person's full financial picture, bank balances, stocks, mutual funds, NPS and more, in minutes, with their consent.
On top of that, AI can read those cash flows, model goals against risk and inflation, flag what is leaking or off-track, and turn a once-a-year conversation into continuous, personal guidance, the kind of attention that once required a dedicated wealth manager. Crucially, it collapses the cost of that guidance, making it affordable for millions rather than a privilege of the few.
And the regulator itself is pushing in this direction. SEBI is working hard to ease RIA norms, because it sees what developed economies already have: a large middle class that needs access to fiduciary advice, not just products.
The open question, and the one new-age companies are all trying to answer, is how much of this should be pure AI versus AI with a human alongside. Will people be comfortable letting an algorithm suggest changes to their money, or will trust still need a human in the room? That answer has not been settled yet, and whoever gets it right will shape the category.
The way forward
Wealth is a slower, harder kind of trust to earn than payments. The outcome, a family that reaches its goals, only shows up years later. So the real question for a new-age player is this: can it compound trust along the way, through every workflow, every market dip, every review and nudge, so that it earns the right to be there when the outcome finally arrives?
That is the work of this decade. Not moving money faster, but becoming the advice Indians actually trust with what to do with their money — advice that's finally on their side.
(Rohit Tuteja is the co-founder and CEO of finny.club, a SEBI-registered fee-only investment adviser)
(Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of YourStory.)

articles.title: Ontario EV battery plant delayed by Volkswagen subsidiary
articles.text:
A subsidiary of German automaker Volkswagen is delaying its Ontario-based electric vehicle (EV) battery plant.
The company, called PowerCo Canada, announced last week that the St. Thomas, Ont., plant will start operations in 2029 instead of the original 2027 target. It said the delay would allow the plant to “accommodate next-generation battery technology.”
PowerCo spokeswoman Tegan Versolatto told the Globe and Mail that the company was using a “phase approach” in order to make sure the plant can meet future market needs and technology advances.
However, there were mixed reactions to the news about the delay and concerns over the impact on the possible 3,000 jobs it will offer, especially amid headwinds impacting the industry.
For one, there’s the anti-EV sentiment coming out of the U.S., with the federal government removing EV purchase incentives. Per the Globe, 5.8 per cent of U.S. new car sales were EVs in Q2 2026, indicating softer demand.
Canada, on the other hand, has more interest in EVs, but being a smaller market, it might not be enough to move the needle. Canadian data from Statistics Canada says 11 per cent of new sales in July were EVs. Canada’s new EV incentives are likely a factor, as is the Iran conflict, which is driving up gas prices and pushing people toward EVs and hybrids.
Another factor: several Canadian EV projects have already been canned, despite significant backing from taxpayers. Honda recently shelved a $15 billion EV plant, GM axed its EV delivery van manufacturing at its Ingersoll, Ont. plant, plans to build an EV battery plant in Quebec fell apart in 2025, just to name a few.
In light of all this, Ontario NDP Leader Marit Style expressed concern about the delay to the Globe, while Premier Doug Ford and ministers were optimistic about the plant. Similarly, St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston told the Globe that he’s still excited about the plant and drives by it every day.
Notably, PowerCo shared the delay alongside the news that Canadian construction company EllisDon would be the general contractor for the next construction phase.
Header image credit: PowerCo
Source: The Globe and Mail

articles.title: Meta is expanding its AI agent Muse to small businesses | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta announced on Tuesday that it’s expanding its AI agent Muse to small businesses and adding new integrations including Shopify, Dropbox, Slack, and more. The tech giant says the agent can help owners run their business and find new customers.
By plugging Muse into the software that small business owners are already using to manage sales, operations, and marketing, Meta is betting that an AI agent with context of a company’s whole operation will be more useful than a standalone chatbot, as it continues to compete against rivals like OpenAI and Google.
Muse can also link to Instagram professional account analytics, Facebook Pages, and Meta ad accounts. Meta says the AI agent also knows what a business sells, how a brand sounds, and what customers ask about most.
Additional integrations include Asana, Box, Canva, Figma, Granola, HighLevel, Intuit QuickBooks, Klaviyo, Lovable, Notion, Stripe, and Zoom.
Muse for Small Business is available for free with usage limits. Businesses that want more usage can purchase a subscription plan.
“Small businesses have been growing on our apps for nearly two decades,” Meta wrote in a blog post. “They told us they’re short on hours, not ideas. So we built Muse for Small Business to help get work done with the tools they already use.”
Meta has been focused on expanding its AI tools beyond the consumer and into the enterprise market. The launch of Muse for Small Business comes a day after Meta introduced “Meta Enterprise Platform,” a new initiative aimed at expanding the company’s AI offerings to businesses and corporate customers. The move could help Meta see a return on all the money it’s pouring into AI.
The tech giant hired Chirantan “CJ” Desai, the CEO of database software giant MongoDB, to lead the new initiative.
Meta says it will focus on bringing its full technology stack, including Muse, Meta Business Agent, Muse API, Muse Code, and more, to businesses and developers.
The rollout of Meta Enterprise Platform is built on the momentum of Muse, which launched earlier this month and topped the U.S. and Canada app charts ahead of ChatGPT.

articles.title: Après la French Week : 7 offres tech Amazon jusqu'à -22%, de la souris G305 au projecteur XGIMI
articles.text:
Les codes promo de la French Week ont expiré lundi 28 septembre au soir, et les Jours Flash Prime n'ouvriront que le 6 octobre. Dans cet intervalle, sept produits tech affichent des baisses chez Amazon, du PC portable Snapdragon X au vidéoprojecteur 4K triple laser.
Trois produits de cette sélection figuraient déjà dans nos bons plans de la French Week : le clavier Logitech G915 X TKL, la souris G Pro X Superlight 2 et le Redmi Note 17. Leur prix affiché n'a pas bougé depuis, seul le code réservé aux abonnés Prime a disparu.
La sélection penche vers le jeu vidéo, avec un clavier, deux souris et une manette, mais elle couvre aussi le travail et le salon avec un PC portable Lenovo et un vidéoprojecteur XGIMI. Les remises sont calculées par rapport au prix de référence sur 30 jours ; la souris G305, elle, est affichée à son prix le plus bas relevé. Les prix sont ceux constatés au moment de notre sélection et peuvent évoluer d'ici le 6 octobre.
Les 7 offres Amazon retenues avant les Jours Flash Prime
- Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3 15,3" Snapdragon X (8/512 Go) à 599,99 € au lieu de 749,99 €
- XGIMI Horizon 20 Max à 2 489,99 € au lieu de 2 990 €
- Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 6+256 Go à 253 € au lieu de 303 €
- Logitech G915 X TKL AZERTY à 139,99 € au lieu de 179,95 €
- Manette Xbox Carbon Black à 42,44 € au lieu de 51,90 €
- Logitech G305 noire à 24,99 €
- Logitech G Pro X Superlight 2 blanche à 89,99 € au lieu de 110,33 €
Pour qui chaque offre a du sens
La manette Xbox mise à part, chaque produit de la sélection est commenté ci-dessous, avec ce qui justifie l'achat et ce qui peut faire hésiter.
- Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3 : sa puce Snapdragon X et son écran de 15,3 pouces en font un PC de bureautique, de navigation et de visioconférence sous Windows 11. Avant de commander, notez que le chargeur n'est pas inclus selon la fiche Amazon et que le clavier n'est pas rétroéclairé. Les 8 Go de mémoire visent un usage courant plutôt que des logiciels lourds.
- XGIMI Horizon 20 Max : nous lui avions attribué 9/10 en janvier, pour une luminosité qui tient dans un salon partiellement éclairé et une image 4K issue d'une source triple laser. Google TV intègre Netflix en natif, et la prise en charge du VRR et de l'ALLM en fait un projecteur confortable pour jouer. À ce prix, mieux vaut prévoir une toile de projection dédiée pour en tirer le meilleur.
- Xiaomi Redmi Note 17 : il mise sur l'endurance, avec une batterie de 7 700 mAh et une charge à 45 W, et sur un grand écran de 6,99 pouces. C'est un choix pour qui veut tenir longtemps loin d'une prise sans viser le haut de gamme. Xiaomi vend à part une version 5G : vérifiez la connectivité sur la fiche si ce point compte pour vous.
- Logitech G915 X TKL : sans pavé numérique et épais de 22,6 mm, ce clavier libère de la place pour la souris. Il se connecte en Lightspeed 2,4 GHz, en Bluetooth ou en USB-C, et Logitech annonce environ 42 heures d'autonomie rétroéclairage au maximum. Ses switchs GL Clicky produisent un clic audible, à éviter dans une pièce partagée.
- Logitech G305 : capteur HERO de 12 000 ppp, connexion sans fil Lightspeed et alimentation par une pile AA : c'est une souris sans fil simple pour jouer avec un petit budget. À 24,99 €, elle est affichée à son prix le plus bas relevé.
- Logitech G Pro X Superlight 2 : 60 grammes, capteur HERO 2 et 95 heures d'autonomie annoncées. Dans notre test, nous avions salué sa légèreté et sa connexion Lightspeed fiable, mais jugé son prix de lancement de 169 € difficile à défendre. À 89,99 €, la réserve tombe en grande partie ; reste la mollesse des boutons latéraux, que nous avions aussi relevée.
Ces prix peuvent-ils encore baisser le 6 octobre ?
Les remises de la sélection restent mesurées, entre 16 et 22 %, la plus forte revenant au clavier G915 X TKL. Pendant la French Week, les codes réservés aux abonnés Prime faisaient mieux sur trois produits : nous avions relayé le G915 X TKL à 124,99 €, la Superlight 2 à 84,99 € et le Redmi Note 17 à 238 €. Si vous avez manqué ces codes, l'écart reste de 5 à 15 €.
Rien ne garantit que ces produits figureront parmi les offres des Jours Flash Prime, ni à quel niveau. Si vous êtes abonné Prime et que l'achat peut attendre une semaine, le 6 octobre mérite un coup d'œil ; si le besoin est immédiat, attendre un gain hypothétique a peu de sens. Pour situer la G305 et la Superlight 2 face à d'autres formats, ergonomiques ou pensés pour le MMO, notre comparatif des meilleures souris gamer passe en revue les modèles que nous recommandons.
Avant de commander : trois questions fréquentes
Faut-il être abonné Prime pour profiter des Jours Flash Prime ?
Oui. Les offres des 6 et 7 octobre 2026 sont réservées aux membres Prime, dont l'abonnement coûte 6,99 € par mois ou 69,90 € par an.
Le Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3 Snapdragon X fait-il tourner tous les logiciels Windows ?
La plupart, oui. Sa puce ARM fait tourner en émulation les logiciels conçus pour les processeurs x86, et certains y fonctionnent moins bien : vérifiez vos applications indispensables avant l'achat.
La manette Xbox Carbon Black fonctionne-t-elle sur PC et smartphone ?
Oui. Elle se connecte en Bluetooth à Windows 10 et 11, Android et iOS, et peut aussi s'utiliser en filaire via un câble USB-C. Elle fonctionne sur piles AA.

articles.title: SpaceX puts Starship into orbit for the first time, deploys 26 Starlink satellites - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
SpaceX puts Starship into orbit for the first time, deploys 26 Starlink satellites
Space Exploration Technologies Corp. put its Starship rocket into orbit for the first time today on the vehicle’s 14th test flight.
Liftoff came at 8:49 a.m. EDT from Starbase in South Texas. The upper stage was back down in the Pacific a little over three hours later, well ahead of schedule.
One of the six Raptor engines on the Starship upper stage shut down early during ascent. After reviewing the telemetry, SpaceX’s flight control team judged the ship otherwise healthy. About 25 minutes into the flight, one Raptor fired to put it into a circular orbit roughly 170 miles up. The Super Heavy booster, which SpaceX did not try to catch this time, lost at least one engine of its own before a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico.
Once in orbit, Starship released 26 third-generation Starlink satellites over about half an hour. Three of the satellites carried cameras to photograph the ship’s heat shield tiles, and SpaceX rates each new unit at about 1 terabit per second of added network capacity. “First orbital flight of Starship successful!” Chief Executive Elon Musk wrote on X.
The flight plan had called for almost 10 hours aloft and a splashdown off Chile, with a backup reentry zone north of Hawaii held in reserve. Mission managers switched to the backup once the satellites were deployed, according to Spaceflight Now. The ship made its deorbit burn at about 11 a.m. EDT and splashed down shortly before noon. The vehicle then tipped over and exploded as residual propellant ignited.
None of the 13 earlier flights, the first of which launched in April 2023, reached orbit. The current version of Starship, known as V3, debuted on Flight 12 in May with a liftoff from a new pad at Starbase. On Flight 13 in July, SpaceX deployed 20 production Starlink V3 satellites on a suborbital path and relit a Raptor engine in space. The ship flown today carried a reworked heat shield. Extra ablative material covers part of its aft section, according to NASASpaceFlight, and redesigned curved tiles are meant to cut heating in the gaps between them.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman called the flight a “gorgeous launch” in a post on X. A version of Starship is one of two landers his agency is counting on to put astronauts back on the moon. Artemis III is due next year, when four astronauts will fly an Orion capsule to meet prototypes from SpaceX and Blue Origin LLC in Earth orbit. The landing itself is set for Artemis IV in 2028. No Starship has refueled another in orbit yet, and each lander could need as many as 15 tanker launches before leaving for the moon.
When SpaceX reported its first quarterly results as a public company in August, the space segment that houses Starship showed a $542 million operating loss and $1.08 billion in research and development spending.
SpaceX expects to launch Starship from Florida for the first time late this year or early next, Spaceflight Now reported.

articles.title: Adani Family Office backs Nudge as startup pivots to rewards-led commerce
articles.text:
Adani Family Office backs Nudge as startup pivots to rewards-led commerce
Nudge, operated by iSocial Sports, is shifting from its earlier sports-led model towards receipt-based rewards, commerce and purchase intelligence for brands.
The Adani Family Office has backed Nudge, formerly known as BeBetta, in its shift towards rewards-led commerce and consumer intelligence.
The investor has backed the company across two consecutive rounds. Jhaveri Credits and Capital Limited, a listed Indian company with interests including securities and investments, has also backed the business, alongside other family offices, alternative investment funds and private investors from India and Dubai.
The company did not disclose the amount raised in its announcement.
The funding comes alongside a change in direction. BeBetta, which built a sports-led engagement and rewards business, has been rebranded as Nudge as it shifts towards rewards-led commerce and consumer intelligence.
The company claims it now has more than 3.3 million monthly active users, 400,000 daily active users, over 50,000 verified bills scanned each day, more than 200 brand partners and a presence across over 200 Indian cities.
Nudge allows consumers to scan purchase receipts from categories such as grocery, retail, dining and pharmacy to earn Nudge Coins, which can be redeemed with partner brands. On the enterprise side, it turns receipt information into structured, item-level data showing what consumers actually bought across online and offline channels. Such data can help brands move beyond measuring impressions or clicks towards tracking purchases.
“Receipts provide a direct and consented view of what people actually buy,” co-founder Meet Shah said, describing the company’s new focus as an effort to connect everyday purchases with rewards, commerce and actionable intelligence.
That proposition comes as Indian marketing becomes increasingly commerce-led. Advertising on e-retail platforms reached Rs 17,601 crore in 2025, up 55.9% year on year, according to the dentsu Digital Advertising Report 2026, with retail media accounting for 24.6% of digital media spending.
Meta and the Retailers Association of India have also highlighted the growing importance of omnichannel shopping, where consumers move between digital discovery and physical stores.
There is evidence of continued investor interest in adjacent consumer and rewards businesses. Consumer rewards platform Onpoint raised $600,000 in July from First Cheque and Whiteboard Capital, while women’s wellness brand Nua raised $50 million in September.
For Nudge, the next 12 to 24 months will centre on increasing the density of its purchase panel, launching paid brand-intelligence products and expanding its receipt-based model into MENA and Southeast Asia. The broader goal is a consumer-intelligence platform for the Global South, built from India.
Nudge said its consumer data is collected with explicit consent and used in aggregated and de-identified form.

articles.title: 26 000 € pour une limousine avec 755 km d’autonomie : Volkswagen frappe un grand coup avec l’aide de Xpeng
articles.text:
C’est possiblement la Phaeton des temps modernes. Les puristes s’étrangleront d’avance à la lecture de cette phrase. Pourtant, la nouvelle Volkswagen ID. Unyx 09 a tout d’un vaisseau amiral. Cette berline de 5,08 mètres de long et 1,98 mètre de large entre de plain-pied dans la catégorie des limousines. Son empattement XXL de 3,03 mètres respecte également les fondamentaux du segment pour offrir une superbe habitabilité.
Alors, pour quelle raison devrait-on perdre les pédales ? Si la Phaeton était un pur produit de l’ingénierie allemande, cette ID. Unyx 09 a en réalité été étroitement conçue avec le chinois Xpeng. C’est peut-être pour cette raison que l’auto affiche des tarifs aussi bas. Comptez ainsi 199 900 yuans pour l’entrée de gamme, soit environ 26 000 €. C’est le prix d’une ID. Polo, pour un modèle faisant un mètre de plus !
À lire aussi : Pour la première fois de son histoire, Volkswagen ferme une usine en Allemagne
755 km d’autonomie : le mirage du cycle chinois ou la vraie bonne affaire ?
Et ce qui continue à choquer est l’autonomie, autrement supérieure. Alors que l’ID. Polo bloque à 450 km, l’ID. Unyx 09 file sur un rayon d’action de 755 km grâce à sa batterie lithium fer phosphate de 92 kWh. Impressionnant pour le tarif, sauf qu’il s’agit d’une mesure sur le cycle CLTC. Vous connaissez la chanson… En WLTP, il faudra retrancher pour tomber possiblement autour des 600 km.
On est d’un coup moins jaloux, notre ID.7 faisant mieux en dépassant les 700 km en WLTP. C’est vrai, mais l’ID. Unyx 09 prend l’ascendant côté équipement avec des jantes de 21 pouces, des étriers de freins Brembo, des feux matriciels permettant de projeter des motifs sur la route, un affichage tête haute en réalité augmentée de 85 pouces et un grand écran tactile boosté à l’intelligence artificielle.
Freins Brembo, affichage géant et IA : la liste des équipements qui impressionne
Et grâce à Xpeng, le système de conduite autonome repose sur une puce Turing d’une puissance de calcul de 750 TOPS, ce qui est du jamais vu chez Volkswagen. De quoi prendre en charge la majorité des situations de conduite de A à Z comme le FSD de Tesla. Une suspension pneumatique à double chambre développée par Continental pourrait tout de même rappeler le moelleux de la Phaeton.
En outre, la technologie de recharge 5C héritée de chez Xpeng permettra théoriquement de recharger complètement la batterie en moins d’un quart d’heure. Deux versions seront proposées. Une propulsion avec 308 ch et 755 km d’autonomie et une quatre roues motrices avec deux électromoteurs développant 188 et 308 ch permettant 705 km d’autonomie. L’auto n’arrivera certainement pas chez nous vu comment Audi bataille déjà pour empêcher l’arrivée des AUDI chinoises en Europe…

articles.title: La deuda de los centros de datos de IA se encarece: el bono del Tesoro llegó a su nivel más alto en años
articles.text:
El rendimiento de los bonos del Tesoro estadounidense a diez años superó el 5,17%, su nivel más alto en años, y encareció el financiamiento del boom de centros de datos que sostiene a la industria de la inteligencia artificial (IA).
El banco JPMorgan proyectó que la industria emitirá hasta USD 4,1 billones en deuda relacionada con la IA hasta 2030 para pagar terrenos, electricidad, refrigeración y chips de los centros de datos.
PUBLICIDAD
Los diferenciales de los bonos vinculados a la IA ya rondan los 115 puntos básicos, frente a los 78 puntos básicos del mercado corporativo en general, de acuerdo con datos de Reuters. Esa brecha marca cuánto más deben pagar estas empresas para atraer inversores.
La construcción de un centro de datos exige desembolsos enormes antes de generar ingresos: terrenos, edificios, infraestructura eléctrica, sistemas de refrigeración, redes y chips gráficos avanzados. Durante gran parte del boom, el crédito barato aceleró esas obras.
Hasta hace poco, la principal limitación de la industria era conseguir suficientes chips, electricidad y espacio físico. Ahora se suma una restricción distinta: cuánto está dispuesto a prestar el mercado de bonos y a qué precio.
PUBLICIDAD
Cuál es la brecha entre gigantes y empresas pequeñas
Microsoft, Amazon, Google y Meta financian buena parte de su expansión con deuda, pero mantienen calificaciones crediticias de grado de inversión que les garantizan tasas más bajas y acceso casi ilimitado a los mercados de capital. El resto de la industria enfrenta un panorama muy distinto.
Las llamadas neoclouds, empresas más chicas que alquilan capacidad de cómputo a los grandes laboratorios de IA, dependen casi por completo de la deuda para construir sus centros de datos y tienen menos margen para absorber el encarecimiento del crédito.
“En lugar de una lista de 50 neoclouds, probablemente haya 20 en las que el mercado esté realmente interesado”, dijo Riley Thompson, vicepresidente de Mitsubishi HC Capital America, a CNBC.
PUBLICIDAD
Andrew Giudici, jefe global de financiamiento corporativo e infraestructura en la calificadora KBRA, agregó que en un contexto normal las empresas frenarían un poco ante tasas más altas, aunque no prevé un freno mayor en la demanda de los prestatarios.
CoreWeave, que salió a la bolsa el año pasado, advirtió en sus presentaciones ante el regulador bursátil que un aumento de 100 puntos básicos en las tasas podría sumarle unos USD 30 millones en gastos por intereses.
Por qué la demanda de cómputo no cede
Pese al encarecimiento, los inversores no le dieron la espalda a la deuda de la IA. La empresa CleanSpark, que pasó de minar criptomonedas a operar centros de datos, colocó bonos por USD 2.280 millones y recibió órdenes por cerca de USD 10.000 millones.
PUBLICIDAD
Esos bonos a cinco años ofrecieron un rendimiento inicial del 8,25%, muy por encima del costo habitual de financiamiento corporativo, lo que confirma que el apetito de los inversores sigue firme cuando el retorno ofrecido los compensa.
Bernie Margulies, director ejecutivo de American Compute, una firma que asesora sobre financiamiento de GPU, resumió la lógica de los prestatarios más grandes: “Si tenés un contrato con Anthropic, ¿realmente 50 puntos básicos te van a frenar?”, dijo a CNBC.
La firmeza de la demanda explica esa disposición a pagar más caro. OpenAI y Anthropic están valuadas cerca de USD 1 billón cada una en el mercado privado, y ambas firmaron compromisos de capacidad de cómputo con años de anticipación.
PUBLICIDAD
Los grandes proveedores de infraestructura también reflejan esa demanda. Meta lanzó en septiembre su asistente Muse, que sumó más de 2,5 millones de descargas en dos semanas y superó a ChatGPT en el ranking de la tienda de aplicaciones de Apple, según CNBC.
De qué forma el mercado se ajusta a la IA
Un inversor de crédito privado que pidió no ser identificado dijo a CNBC que, de ahora en más, cerrar acuerdos con neoclouds será más difícil porque estas compañías tienen menos colchón financiero para absorber costos más altos.
El resultado, según los analistas consultados, podría ser una consolidación: las empresas con balances sólidos y contratos de largo plazo ganarían terreno frente a los operadores que dependen casi por completo de financiamiento externo.
PUBLICIDAD
Los grandes proveedores de la nube ya comprometieron cientos de miles de millones de dólares en gastos de capital este año y anticipan un nuevo aumento en 2027, un ritmo que ahora deberá sostenerse con crédito más caro para buena parte del sector.
Reuters había reportado semanas pasadas que los compradores de bonos corporativos se volvieron más selectivos frente a la ola de emisiones de deuda ligada a la IA, una tendencia que el salto de los rendimientos del Tesoro terminó de confirmar.
El bono del Tesoro a diez años, que marca el piso para el costo del crédito en todo el mercado estadounidense, se ubicaba esta semana en su nivel más alto desde 2007.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Australians falling victim to a new scam and calling cybercriminals - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Australians have been advised over the years to not click on suspicious links or answer unknown numbers but cybercriminals have turned the tables with a new scam that gets people to call them.
It’s called the callback scam and it’s on the rise.
Telstra’s data shows it has grown from 29 per cent in 2025 to 45 per cent of reported email-based scams in 2026.
It usually starts with a person receiving an email about an unauthorised purchase, an unpaid invoice, a failed subscription payment, or unusual bank activity.
The message also contains a number to call if you want to respond immediately.
For many this seems like a step towards a solution and because it’s you who initiated the call it doesn’t feel unsolicited.
And then you are speaking directly with a cybercriminal who then moves to the next stage of the scam.
Now they can confirm your number is real and go through a script to try and obtain more information and other financial details.
The scam exploits typical human behaviour play the need to resolve an urgent unexpected change over the phone rather than going back and forth on email, text, or online chat.
Telstra’s research found that 69 per cent of Australians believe they couldn’t be tricked into contacting a scammer by phone, while 85 per cent say they prefer to resolve issues by picking up the phone.
This shift in tactics is encouraging victims to initiate the contact themselves.
Telstra has blocked more than a billion scam calls since 2020 but the callback scam gets around this.
Because you are calling back instead of receiving a call this also gets around the blocking.
Here are Telstra’s tips on avoiding becoming a victim of the callback scam:
– Find the number yourself
Don’t reply, click or call from the message. Always check the organisation’s official app or website for contact information.
– Check the source
Look for odd email addresses, unfamiliar mobile numbers or missing Sender IDs. If the source does not match the brand, do not trust the message.
– Check the claim before trying to fix it
Look at your bank account, subscription or order history before acting on the message.
– Keep security codes to yourself
One-time codes are designed to protect your account. A legitimate organisation should not ask you to provide one so it can “secure” or “cancel” something.
– Be wary of instructions to move money
A bank or other legitimate organisation will not ask you to transfer funds to a “safe account” or purchase gift cards or cryptocurrency.
– If in doubt, hang up
If someone discourages you from ending the call or checking independently, end the conversation.
– Report suspected scams
If you suspect a phishing scam, report it.

articles.title: Southwest and United don't want Boeing's newest 737 MAX software on their new planes
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Southwest Airlines and United Airlines have asked Boeing to deliver new 737 MAX jets with an earlier software version after the manufacturer identified a glitch involving an automated navigation function. Neither airline has aircraft flying with the affected software, according to company statements. However, both carriers have told Boeing they do not want it installed on incoming planes.
The problem can arise after a flight crew abandons a landing and changes the aircraft's planned route. Under certain conditions, an automated navigation feature may not work as intended. Pilots could then have to fly without some autopilot functions until they restore the system or continue using manual procedures.
That can add to the workload during a critical phase of flight. A missed approach typically requires a crew to climb away from the runway, follow a new route and manage the aircraft at a relatively low altitude. Weather or other operational issues may also be factors.
Boeing told 737 MAX operators about the issue in late August. The company said at the time that it did not consider the problem a safety risk. It has since started a formal safety review and shared the results with the Federal Aviation Administration.
The FAA is investigating. A senior agency official said the regulator will act if necessary.
Boeing said it had reminded operators of the existing procedures pilots can use to handle such situations safely. The company added that its engineers are developing a software update intended to permanently resolve the problem.
Boeing is also working with airlines on procedures that would allow pilots to re-enable the affected navigation function. Its August notice said more guidance was expected by November, with a software update planned for early 2028. Boeing said it is trying to move both dates forward.
GE Aerospace developed the software at issue. The company said it is working with Boeing and will support the FAA's review.
It is not yet known how many MAX aircraft have the software installed. Boeing said it is working to determine that number, but airlines are not required to tell the manufacturer when they update cockpit software. Aviation data firm Cirium lists 2,422 MAX 8 and MAX 9 aircraft in service worldwide.
Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest, and United all operate MAX jets. Those airlines said none of their active aircraft are using the software version at issue. Boeing has told carriers they can return to an earlier version.
The software issue could also affect Boeing's plans for its newest MAX variants. The FAA approved the smaller MAX 7 for passenger service last month with the newer software installed, according to a senior agency official. Boeing Chief Executive Kelly Ortberg has said he expects the MAX 10 to receive approval soon.
The FAA's findings could complicate that process. If the agency determines that the glitch is an unsafe condition that must be corrected, it could affect MAX 10 certification.
Southwest has a particular interest in the outcome. The carrier has been waiting years for the MAX 7 and plans to begin flying it next year. Federal rules generally require newly built aircraft to match the configuration approved during certification. It remains unclear whether new MAX 7s could be delivered with the earlier software Southwest has requested.
Delta Air Lines, United, American, and Alaska have MAX 10s on order.
Boeing said it first learned of the issue from a MAX operator in November 2024. The company initially concluded that the report did not meet its standard for a safety review. It reconsidered after speaking with airlines and receiving additional feedback.
The matter comes as Boeing continues to face close scrutiny of the MAX program. Crashes involving the aircraft in 2018 and 2019 killed 346 people. Those accidents involved the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System, or MCAS, which repeatedly pushed the planes' noses down. Boeing later changed the system and added safeguards before the MAX returned to service.

articles.title: SpaceX's Starship goes orbital, deploying first next-gen Starlinks
articles.text:
SpaceX's 14th Starship test flight began with a Monday morning liftoff from Starbase, Texas. The city of South Padre Island is visible in the background.
Credit:
SpaceX
SpaceX's 14th Starship test flight began with a Monday morning liftoff from Starbase, Texas. The city of South Padre Island is visible in the background.
Credit:
SpaceX
SpaceX’s Starship rocket thundered into the sky over South Texas early Monday. It was the 14th test flight of the world’s most powerful launch vehicle. This time, however, the rocket’s massive upper stage squeezed out some extra oomph from its Raptor engines and accelerated to orbital velocity.
On all of Starship’s previous flights, SpaceX intentionally dialed back the full capability of the rocket to fly a suborbital trajectory, slow enough for Earth’s gravity to pull the vehicle back into the atmosphere before it could complete a full lap around the planet. After several successful suborbital flights in a row, SpaceX officials decided this launch should go all the way to low-Earth orbit. And it did.
What’s more, SpaceX packed 26 of the company’s newest generation of Starlink broadband satellites into the rocket’s cargo bay. One by one, the flat-packed satellites—too large to fit inside SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 rocket—were released from Starship’s payload deployer using a system of pulleys and cables to eject the satellites overboard like a Pez dispenser spits out candy.
A dramatic morning
Starship Flight 14 began with a booming sendoff from Starbase, Texas, at 8:49 am EDT (7:49 am local time; 12:49 UTC) as 33 methane-fueled Raptor engines pushed the 407-foot-tall (124-meter) rocket off its launch pad. The engines generated up to 18 million pounds of thrust to propel the fuel-laden rocket into the sky over Starbase, SpaceX’s private spaceport just north of the US-Mexico border.
Heading east from South Texas, the rocket powered through the speed of sound and soared into the stratosphere before its Super Heavy booster stage detached from Starship’s upper stage. The booster executed a rapid high-altitude turnaround to begin thrusting back toward the Texas coast. Several minutes later, the Super Heavy first stage made a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico just off the coast of Starbase.
The upper stage continued its climb into space before shutting off its Raptor engines a little more than eight minutes into the fight. Up to this point, the rocket followed a similar trajectory as SpaceX’s previous Starship test flights.
The company’s flight control team had a few minutes to decide whether to proceed with the next phase of the flight: a restart of one of Starship’s Raptor engines to add the final bit of speed required to reach orbital velocity. For a brief period, it appeared as if SpaceX was going to forego the orbital flight and allow Starship to continue coasting toward a reentry over the Indian Ocean, as it had done many times before.
The question of what to do next centered on the performance of the rocket’s Raptor engines. One of the six Raptors on Starship shut down prematurely during its ascent burn, and the five others burned longer to compensate for the malfunction. Less of a worry for Starship’s orbital flight, but still a concern for future launches, was the apparent failure of two of the 33 Raptor engines on the Super Heavy booster—one during launch and another during the booster’s return maneuvers.
Dan Huot, a SpaceX commentator providing live updates on the company’s webcast of Monday’s flight, initially reported that mission managers were going to abort the orbit insertion burn. Officials ultimately decided to proceed. The failed Raptor engine was not the same one that needed to fire to place the rocket into low-Earth orbit and steer it toward reentry and splashdown at the end of the flight.
A view inside the engine bay of the Starship rocket, with three “sea level” Raptor engines in the middle and three “vacuum” Raptor engines in the outer ring. One of the steerable center engines was used for the orbit insertion and de-orbit burns.
Credit:
SpaceX
A view inside the engine bay of the Starship rocket, with three “sea level” Raptor engines in the middle and three “vacuum” Raptor engines in the outer ring. One of the steerable center engines was used for the orbit insertion and de-orbit burns.
Credit:
SpaceX
SpaceX engineers were being “extremely conservative” in their planning for Monday’s flight, Huot said. A worst-case scenario for the first orbital flight of Starship would have been a failure that stranded the 100-ton vehicle in orbit. That could have caused it to fall back to Earth in an uncontrolled manner, creating a potential risk to public safety.
“We were only going to go if we were very confident in the core systems that have to work to get you out of orbit once you’re up there,” Huot said. “We took some extra time, added some extra drama, but we were able to clear the… three center engines and do our first-ever orbital insertion burn. So that was a huge success.”
The Raptor engine selected for the insertion burn performed flawlessly, reigniting for 19 seconds to give Starship the nudge it needed to overcome the pull of Earth’s gravity. The maneuver added approximately 204 mph to Starship’s speed, a little more than 1 percent of the rocket’s overall velocity, to reach a stable orbit at an altitude of about 171 miles (276 kilometers).
Delivering for Starlink
Achieving orbit meant SpaceX could continue with the next phase of the mission. This involved the first deployment of commercial-grade Starlink V3 satellites for the company’s global broadband network. SpaceX launched a batch of Starlink V3s on the previous Starship flight in July, but that mission was suborbital, and the satellites quickly burned up as they fell back into the atmosphere.
The Starlink V3s will bring significant upgrades to the Starlink constellation. The satellites can only launch on Starship. They’re too large to fit inside the payload fairing of the Falcon 9 rocket, which SpaceX has used to deploy more than 12,000 Starlinks since 2019. The Starlink V3s, each weighing about 2 metric tons (4,400 pounds) at launch, are fitted with larger power-generating solar arrays and improved antennas.
The changes enable each Starlink V3 platform to add 1 Tbps of capacity to the Starlink network, 10 times more than the older satellites launching on Falcon 9, according to SpaceX. There were 26 Starlink satellites aboard Monday’s launch. Future Starships could deliver up to 60 Starlink V3s to orbit on a single flight. On its website, SpaceX wrote that Starlink V3s will “greatly expand the network’s capacity and user speeds.”
Upgraded Starlink satellites will also improve the network’s performance for direct-to-device connectivity. Future Starlink V3s could also be used for SpaceX’s Starshield service for the US military. SpaceX reported that its satellite team established contact with all 26 Starlink V3s after separating from Starship.
The satellites launched Monday were initially deployed into a low-inclination orbit, ranging about 30 degrees north and south of the equator, due to strict range safety rules restricting overflight of populated areas during launch. SpaceX is expected to launch Starship into higher-inclination orbits as it gains flight experience with Starship and debuts new launch pads in Florida and Louisiana.
One of SpaceX’s Starlink V3 satellites is seen exiting the rocket’s Pez deployer as the vehicle soared over South Africa.
Credit:
SpaceX
One of SpaceX’s Starlink V3 satellites is seen exiting the rocket’s Pez deployer as the vehicle soared over South Africa.
Credit:
SpaceX
SpaceX’s first Starlink V3s had to wait a while for a ride to space, but Monday’s flight showed Starship is up to the task. SpaceX started phasing out Starlink launches on the Falcon 9 earlier this year. There are no more Falcon 9 launches for Starlink on SpaceX’s schedule at Cape Canaveral, Florida. Falcon 9 launches to place older-generation Starlink satellites into polar orbit will continue from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, at least for a while longer.
Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space, expects SpaceX to work on integrating the new capabilities of Starlink V3s into the Starlink network in the coming months. More already-built Starlink V3s will likely be on most of SpaceX’s next series of Starship flights.
“They just sat at a warehouse in Texas, as I understand it, because the satellites were finished well ahead of the launch vehicle,” Henry said in a live broadcast of Monday’s Starship flight hosted by Spaceflight Now (the author of this story was also a guest).
SpaceX said before Monday’s flight that this group of Starlink V3 satellites will be integrated into the broader constellation. They should begin serving customers as soon as a few weeks after launch, according to SpaceX, but it will likely take many more launches for Starlink customers to notice a difference in their service.
“It’s great that they have the capacity onboard in orbit, but until there is a meaningful number of V3 satellites launched, they won’t be the spacecraft that defines the user experience just yet,” Henry said.
Calling it a day
Soon after completing the satellite deployment sequence, SpaceX officials decided to bring Starship home earlier than planned, giving up on a chance to test the vehicle’s long-duration endurance in orbit.
“Out of an abundance of caution given the engine issue experienced during ascent, the flight control team decided to limit the duration spent on orbit and proceeded with de-orbiting Starship to a splashdown location in the northern Pacific Ocean,” SpaceX wrote in a recap of Monday’s test flight. “This area was one of two pre-coordinated landing zones identified before launch that was cleared of sea and air traffic.”
The de-orbit burn went off without a hitch, and Starship plunged back into the atmosphere over the Pacific Ocean, guiding itself toward a splashdown north of Hawaii, one of multiple backup return sites mapped out in advance of Monday’s flight. The reentry was uneventful, and Starship’s heat shield appeared to hold up well against temperatures up to 2,600° Fahrenheit (1,430° Celsius) as the vehicle streaked over the remote Pacific.
A bird’s-eye view of Starship in orbit captured by a camera on one of the Starlink V3 satellites.
Credit:
SpaceX
A bird’s-eye view of Starship in orbit captured by a camera on one of the Starlink V3 satellites.
Credit:
SpaceX
Like its most recent flights, Starship dropped belly-first through scattered clouds before turning upright for a final landing burn. The splashdown was right on target, with the final moments of descent in view of a buoy prepositioned at the backup landing zone.
Splashdown occurred at 11:57 am EDT (15:57 UTC), a little more than three hours after liftoff, three times longer than Starship’s previous suborbital flights. The original flight plan called for a mission lasting nearly 10 hours.
As expected, the vehicle tipped over and broke apart in a fireball upon reaching the ocean and was unable to replicate the serendipitous intact splashdown on Starship’s last flight in July. SpaceX anticipates most of Starship’s water landings to have fiery endings, but the days of Starship splashdowns may be nearing their end.
“Most importantly, Starship made it to orbit,” Huot said after splashdown. “We did our first-ever orbital insertion burn. We kept the drama up a little bit as we were going through that coast time making sure everything was good. We were only going do all this stuff today if we were really, really sure that those sea level engines on Starship were going to perform because we needed to do that de-orbit burn.
“We were able to get there,” Huot said. “We got on orbit. Teams continued to look at it. We were going to get the data that we wanted, so we made the call due to this earlier reentry to [near] Hawaii.”
What’s next for Starship?
SpaceX has a steady stream of Starships and Super Heavy boosters in production and testing at Starbase, setting up for an increasing cadence of flights in the coming months. The company has not announced any official launch dates, but a schedule of “upcoming high-profile missions” released by the Federal Aviation Administration’s Air Traffic Control System Command Center this week indicated the next Starship flight could take off from Starbase in October.
Ground crews are moving into testing and activation of a new Starship launch pad at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, with an eye toward hosting a Starship launch there before the end of the year. A cavernous new Starship factory is also taking shape at Kennedy. SpaceX is expected to transport Super Heavy and Starship rockets to the Florida launch base from its factory in Texas until the new on-site production facility is complete.
The results from Monday’s test flight suggest that SpaceX still has work to do on the latest iteration of its Raptor engine. The Raptor 3 engine variant uses a lighter, streamlined design, combining a lower part count with higher thrust.
A family portrait of SpaceX’s Raptor engines.
Credit:
SpaceX
A family portrait of SpaceX’s Raptor engines.
Credit:
SpaceX
SpaceX has now encountered engine problems on each of the three Starship flights that have used Raptor 3s. During a May flight, one Raptor engine shut down prematurely on the Super Heavy booster, and another stopped running on Starship’s upper stage a few minutes later. Multiple Raptor engines failed to ignite on the launch pad for the next flight in July, prompting a last-second abort. SpaceX swapped out two of the engines before proceeding with a successful launch a week later.
Elon Musk, SpaceX’s founder and CEO, wrote on his social media platform X that the changes introduced with the Raptor 3 engine “greatly reduces mass and leak paths, but makes it harder to replace some parts.”
“While deleting parts sounds easy in theory, it is actually very difficult to figure out how to do so in practice and requires many iterations,” Musk continued. The inside of the Raptor 3 engine “has very complex geometry that can only be manufactured using highly modified 3D metal printing,” he wrote in another post.
Although the Raptor 3 is still a work in progress, the propulsion issues have not stopped SpaceX from making headway with Starship, and it’s unlikely the engine problems on Monday’s flight will delay the next Starship launch.
The FAA is also giving SpaceX the all-clear on Monday’s flight. The regulatory agency will not require SpaceX to conduct a formal mishap investigation. An FAA spokesperson told Ars: “All flight events for both the Starship vehicle and the Super Heavy booster occurred within the scope of planned and FAA authorized activities.”
Next on SpaceX’s to-do list will likely be an attempt to bring Starship back to Starbase for a catch by the launch pad’s giant mechanical arms, repeating a feat engineers have already accomplished with the Super Heavy booster. Returning Starship to the launch site will require a reentry over land, necessitating additional safety reviews to ensure no undue risk to populated areas as the vehicle approaches Starbase. Eventually, SpaceX aims to make these landings routine enough to enable full and rapid reuse of Super Heavy and Starship.
Other near-term objectives for Starship include longer-duration orbital flights and then the first demonstration of in-orbit refueling, a prerequisite for future missions to land astronauts on the Moon under the auspices of NASA’s Artemis program.
In the meantime, expect Starship to launch many more Starlink satellites. Commercial and government demand for Starlink services, along with SpaceX’s longer-term plans for orbital data centers, will keep Starship plenty busy as engineers bring the rocket’s more advanced capabilities online.
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

articles.title: A Ferrari will race an F-35B fighter on an aircraft runway
articles.text:
The Italian Navy is racing an F-35B fighter against a Ferrari in probably the coolest-sounding race ever
F-35B fighter Vs Ferrari SF90 — a clash of two titans
- An F-35B and Ferrari SF90 will race at Grottaglie Air Base
- Barone's tuned Ferrari hits 330 km/h across the 500-meter sprint
- The jet completes its takeoff exactly as the race course ends
The Italian Navy has organized an unusual matchup between one of its F-35B fighter jets and a Ferrari SF90 sports car.
Set for October 11 2026 at the Grottaglie air base in southern Italy, the event pits vertical takeoff aircraft against Formula-tuned horsepower.
Fabio Barone, who holds seven speed records in Ferrari vehicles, will drive the car during the contest.
A runway built for landing, not racing
The first race covers 500 meters along an aluminum runway typically reserved for F-35B landing approaches at the base.
At that distance, the jet will complete its takeoff just as the course ends. Barone said his Ferrari normally accelerates from zero to 100 km/h in 2.8 seconds under standard settings.
With specialized engine adjustments applied for the event, that time drops slightly to 2.6 seconds flat. Over the full 500-meter stretch, the car is expected to hit 330 km/h before finishing.
"With that acceleration, I will face 2.2g, meaning 140kg of pressure" said Barone, adding the jet will likely start more slowly but carries far greater raw power overall.

A longer second race stretches across 2.8 km, combining both asphalt and aluminum surfaces along the runway.
After the first 500 meters, the aircraft will take flight and finish the course airborne. It will fly roughly 20 meters above the ground for the remainder of that longer race.
The F-35B and FS90 will share a single runway only 35 meters wide, and driving at high speeds over the aluminum plates could destabilize the car's handling
Echoes of a Formula 1 stunt from 2003
Races between military jets and race cars are not without precedent in Italy, dating back over two decades.
In 2003, Formula 1 driver Michael Schumacher raced a Ferrari against an Italian Air Force Eurofighter jet at Grosseto air base (see main picture) in a contest which drew a crowd of roughly 50,000 spectators to watch the two machines go head-to-head.
The Eurofighter won two of those races, covering 900 and 1,200 meters, without ever leaving the ground.
Schumacher still won a shorter 600-meter sprint, reaching 294 km/h and finishing the course in 9.6 seconds, beating the jet by two tenths of a second, despite the aircraft's clear power advantage.
Barone has his own history staging similar stunts involving military hardware and Ferrari engineering, having previously driven a Ferrari along the flight deck of the Navy's Trieste carrier vessel, reaching 164 km/h across roughly 200 meters before braking hard to avoid going overboard.
Barone said the appeal of racing a fighter jet comes from doing something genuinely unusual in public view.
"Everyone can race against another car, and this is a chance to put on a show," he said, citing Schumacher's 2003 run as inspiration.
Public stunts pairing military aircraft against sports cars tend to favor spectacle over strict competitive fairness.
Whichever machine crosses the finish line first, the event mainly serves as a marketing moment for both the Navy and Ferrari.
Via DefenseNews
