articles.title: Africa's AI problem isn't talent
articles.text:
I first encountered the strategic importance of technology restrictions while working in semiconductor manufacturing at Intel. Export licensing was part of the environment.
The underlying logic was straightforward: some technologies were considered too strategically important to be freely transferred to geopolitical competitors, including China. That logic has followed technology into the AI era.
Advanced NVIDIA GPUs have become subject to export restrictions affecting China, because access to high-end compute is now recognised as a strategic advantage. Yet China’s experience also demonstrates something important. Despite significant constraints, Chinese companies have continued to develop impressive AI systems, including models from DeepSeek and Moonshot AI.
There is, however, an important distinction between China and Africa. China has enormous pools of engineers, researchers, capital, industrial capacity, and technology infrastructure. Its challenge is partly about restrictions on access to the most advanced compute. Africa faces something more basic. We do not have enough compute.
The missing layer in Africa’s AI ambition
For an African founder building an AI company, compute is not an abstract infrastructure issue. It can determine what gets built. A startup may have the engineering talent, the idea and the customers, yet still struggle to access the hardware required to train or run its models at a commercially useful scale.
Lelapa AI has described this problem from the perspective of an African AI company, including the experience of relying on overseas infrastructure, dealing with connectivity and time zone constraints, paying higher infrastructure costs, and having product development constrained by GPU availability. That last point deserves more attention.
When compute is abundant, founders can start with the problem they want to solve and work backwards to the required infrastructure. When compute is scarce, infrastructure begins to shape the problem itself. The founder begins to ask which model can be trained within budget, which experiments can be abandoned, how much fine-tuning is feasible, and whether the product can scale beyond its initial customers. The result is not simply a higher cost base. It can produce a more conservative startup ecosystem.
Compute is part of startup capital
We often talk about the African technology ecosystem in terms of venture capital, talent and market access. Compute belongs in that conversation.
For an AI company, GPUs are part of the capital stack. The relevant question is not merely whether a GPU exists somewhere in Africa. A developer needs to know whether it can be accessed when required, how much it costs, whether capacity can be reserved, how reliable the connection is and how easily data can move between the storage and compute environment.
Those details determine whether an AI company can experiment quickly or spend its time managing infrastructure constraints. This is why the emergence of companies such as Chassis and UduTech matters. They are working to address the lack of local compute infrastructure and make high-performance computing more accessible to African developers.
Other companies are approaching the problem from a different direction. Refiant AI, for example, is working on computational efficiency by reducing the compute required to run sophisticated models. Both approaches point to the same underlying reality: the African AI ecosystem cannot reach its full potential if compute remains scarce, expensive or difficult to access.
The GPU is only half the story
There is another issue that deserves more attention. Compute infrastructure is physical infrastructure. A serious AI facility needs electricity, cooling, connectivity, electrical and mechanical engineering, controls, commissioning and maintenance. It needs technicians who understand critical environments and construction professionals who can deliver them.
That means the AI infrastructure workforce is much larger than the community of machine-learning engineers. Africa has substantial technical talent. The challenge is organising that talent around the physical and digital infrastructure required to support the next generation of AI companies.
Nigeria’s National Digital Cloud Policy is therefore significant. Its ambition to attract private investment and to develop Nigeria as a regional digital-services hub is in the right direction. But the real test will be what developers experience.
If a Nigerian founder can access a high-end GPU locally, at a predictable price, with reliable power and connectivity, and without the friction of moving data halfway around the world, then infrastructure policy has begun to translate into ecosystem advantage. If local infrastructure exists but remains inaccessible, unreliable, or prohibitively expensive, the headline capacity will matter much less.
What availability really means
The industry should become more transparent about this. Saying that Africa has AI infrastructure is not enough. We need to know how much compute is actually available to developers and researchers, what type of accelerators are accessible, where they are located, and what they cost. The most useful metrics may be remarkably simple.
How long does it take a developer to get access to a GPU? What does an H100-hour cost? How much does it cost to train a representative model? How reliable is the service? How easily can a startup scale from 1 GPU to 100? Those are the questions that determine whether infrastructure is useful.
Africa does not need to reproduce Silicon Valley. It does not need to build the same companies or chase every frontier model. But African founders should have enough access to compute to decide what they want to build based on the opportunity, rather than first asking what their infrastructure budget will allow. That is the real strategic issue.
Compute scarcity does not only constrain what African startups can afford. It can constrain what they imagine is possible. And if Africa wants to participate meaningfully in the AI economy, that constraint is one we cannot afford to leave in place.
Oluwaseyi Ayodeji is an AI infrastructure Senior Program Leader with decades of experience in the technology industry, including a year as an auditor at PricewaterhouseCoopers. He is the founder of Regal Stack, a think tank focused on Africa’s sovereign participation in the global AI economy.

articles.title: Bose is bringing back wired earbuds as teens ditch Bluetooth
articles.text:
In a nutshell: Bose is going back to basics, and today's youth is largely to blame. The company is now accepting pre-orders for a new set of noise cancelling earbuds that trade in wireless Bluetooth connectivity for a wired listening experience. It's the company's first set of wired buds in more than a decade.
Bose said the new earbuds come at a time when wired listening is gaining popularity. Wireless Bluetooth connectivity has been all the rage in personal audio products over the last several years, but it's not foolproof. While most modern devices support Bluetooth, older audio gear often does not. What's more, Bluetooth connections aren't always the most reliable. Then there is the headache of having to manage charging and battery life, and dealing with audio lag.
With wired earbuds, you just plug in and press play.
The buds aren't fully retro, however, as Bose went with a USB-C connector instead of the tried and true 3.5mm jack. They feature an in-line remote with tactile physical buttons for volume control, playback, calls, and cycling of noise cancellation modes. They are also rated IPX4 for water resistance and include a zippered carrying case for storage and protection when not in use.
No app is needed, and the buds draw power from the phone, tablet, or computer they are plugged into. Playback output is fixed at 24bit/48kHz, we're told.
Wired headphones started gaining momentum in the second half of 2025, and entered 2026 on a high note. According to Circana, sales surged 10% between July and December of last year and were up 20% in the early portion of this year. This jives with recent CD and vinyl sales trends, both of which are experiencing a revival.
Bose noise cancelling wired earbuds are scheduled to launch on October 15 priced at $99. They are offered in white or black colorways, in addition to a limited edition mint color. Look for them online at Bose's website and in-store at select Best Buy retail locations.

articles.title: Kubernetes Teams Get a Safer Way to See Their Own GPU Metrics
articles.text:
Adobe engineers have described an open-source approach for giving teams self-service access to their own Prometheus metrics in multi-tenant Kubernetes environments, without exposing the shared metrics of other teams. The design is particularly aimed at GPU-heavy environments, where teams may need visibility into utilisation and power consumption to understand whether expensive accelerator capacity is actually being used.
The problem is straightforward but difficult to solve safely. A central Prometheus instance may contain metrics from thousands of namespaces, making it unsuitable for unrestricted tenant access. Giving every team query access could expose another team's data, while allowing large numbers of users to query the shared store can also create a performance and noisy-neighbour problem. Adobe's solution places a tenant-aware proxy between users and the central Prometheus and optionally gives each tenant its own smaller Prometheus instance.
The architecture uses existing Kubernetes and CNCF technologies rather than introducing another metrics platform. Requests pass through NGINX and kube-rbac-proxy for authentication and authorisation before reaching a multi-tenant Prometheus proxy. The proxy identifies the tenant, discovers available Prometheus backends, and restricts queries to that tenant's namespace.
A key component is prom-label-proxy, which modifies incoming PromQL queries to enforce a namespace constraint. This is important because simply asking developers to include the correct namespace in their queries would not provide a sufficient security boundary. The restriction is applied by the proxy before the query reaches Prometheus, preventing a tenant from deliberately constructing a query that accesses another namespace.
The platform also introduces a Kubernetes custom resource called MetricAccess, allowing teams to declare which metrics they require. Metric definitions can use exact metric names, regular expressions, or PromQL selectors. This provides a self-service mechanism while leaving the underlying collection and access controls with the platform team.
For teams requiring their own dashboards and alerts, the design can periodically remote-write a curated set of metrics into a tenant-specific Prometheus instance. With metricIsolation enabled, only the tenant's own series are collected, reducing the amount of data stored in the tenant's Prometheus as well as limiting what can be queried.
Adobe reports that one example configuration reduced a tenant's stored series from more than 10,000 to roughly 300. Apart from reducing storage and query requirements, this creates another isolation boundary: data that is never collected into the tenant's store cannot subsequently be exposed through that store.
This separation also changes the operational model. The central Prometheus continues to provide infrastructure-wide collection, while tenant-specific Prometheus instances handle the dashboards and queries that individual teams need. The shared system therefore does not have to serve every developer's routine observability queries.
The immediate use case is GPU visibility. Accelerator capacity can represent a significant infrastructure cost, but allocation alone does not indicate whether those GPUs are doing useful work. The authors describe finding a GPU that had remained at zero utilisation for 11 consecutive days despite being allocated and powered on.
With access to metrics such as GPU utilisation, framebuffer memory, power consumption and request rates, teams can build queries to identify idle GPUs, GPUs consuming power without corresponding application traffic, or workloads receiving traffic while their GPU capacity remains underutilised.
Although GPUs provide the most obvious example, the architecture is not GPU-specific. The underlying pattern is a tenant-aware observability layer built around authentication, query isolation, curated metric access, and optional per-tenant storage.
This is increasingly relevant as Kubernetes clusters become shared platforms for application teams, data workloads, and AI workloads. Platform teams need to provide sufficient observability for developers without turning a central telemetry system into either a security risk or a performance bottleneck.
There are several established approaches to the same underlying multi-tenancy problem. Grafana Mimir, for example, has multi-tenant isolation built into its architecture, using tenant identifiers to scope metric queries and requiring an authentication layer to establish the appropriate tenant context. Mimir also provides query-front-end capabilities for managing and scaling the read path. Cortex, the project on which several Prometheus-compatible managed services are based, uses a similar X-Scope-OrgID model to isolate metric data between tenants. The Adobe approach is somewhat different in that it keeps a shared Prometheus environment while adding Kubernetes-aware access controls and namespace-based filtering around it.

articles.title: Gov.br sofre falha e fica fora do ar nesta segunda-feira • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Gov.br sofre falha e fica fora do ar nesta segunda-feira
Plataforma de serviços governamentais passa por apagão.
A plataforma Gov.br está fora do ar para parcela dos usuários nesta segunda-feira (28/09), conforme testes feitos pelo Tecnoblog tanto no site oficial quanto no login de outros serviços governamentais. Ainda não se sabe o motivo da pane.
Centenas de queixas também se acumulam no DownDetector, mecanismo que monitora plataformas digitais. No site do Consumidor.gov, por exemplo, não é possível fazer a autenticação para conferir as respostas das empresas.
O Ministério da Gestão, que é responsável pelo Gov.br, confirmou ao Tecnoblog, em mensagem às 15h, que o serviço ”está passando por períodos de instabilidade” e que equipes da pasta e do Serpro “estão trabalhando para o restabelecimento”. A pasta não informou um prazo para que ele volte a funcionar.
Não custa lembrar: o Gov.br reúne centenas de serviços prestados por municípios, estados e pelo governo federal. Cerca de 180 milhões de usuários fazem parte da plataforma.

articles.title: TSMC to Scale 2 nm Production to 120,000 Wafers per Month by the End of 2026
articles.text:
Monday, September 28th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
TSMC to Scale 2 nm Production to 120,000 Wafers per Month by the End of 2026
TSMC has reportedly started expanding its manufacturing capacity as demand continues to outpace supply. According to a recent report from UDN, TSMC aims to increase its 2 nm manufacturing capacity at the N2 node, targeting an output of about 120,000 wafers per month by the end of 2026. This represents a 20% increase from the early August target of 100,000 wafers per month by the end of the year, indicating strong customer interest in the latest silicon technology. Even in the early stages, the company confirmed that the N2 node has four times the number of tape-outs compared to its previous leading-edge 3 nm N3 node. With the ramp-up of N2 production underway, the 20% increase suggests that customers are seeking more capacity, even as TSMC continues to scale production, indicating that demand isn't slowing down anytime soon.
At the end of the second quarter of 2026, the N2 node accounted for only 3% of TSMC's revenue, while the 3 nm node held 30%, and the 5 nm node secured the top spot at 33%. However, as we approach the end of Q3, we should see a significant shift in these figures, strongly favoring the N2 node. Until official data is released, we can't be certain of N2's exact revenue contribution, but it is expected to increase significantly based on several factors.Firstly, TSMC achieved about 20,000 wafers per month in late July. An increase to 120,000 N2 wafers by the end of 2026 suggests a corresponding revenue increase. Secondly, TSMC has been discussing price increases with customers, and the N2 node will likely see a significant price hike, as the latest nodes typically require more complex manufacturing processes. TSMC generated $16.26 billion in August, but September's revenue will be particularly interesting to observe as manufacturing scaling continues.

articles.title: Trump cuts fuel economy standards back to 2014 levels
articles.text:
The federal government’s war on fuel efficiency claimed another victim today. The Department of Transportation released a new rule for the country’s Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards, which, as expected, discourage the very idea of economical vehicles. Among the changes is a rollback to fuel economy numbers not seen in more than a decade, below even the low standards implemented in 2020, the last time President Trump was in power. The new goal is just 34.9 mpg by model year 2031.
This is nothing if not expected. When Sean Duffy was installed as Transportation secretary last January, he immediately announced that any fuel efficiency standards put in place under the Biden administration were dead and buried. Those rules had a slower ramp up than some might have liked but would have required automakers to sell many more electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids.
Now, we may have the possibility of some OEMs dropping their EVs and PHEVs entirely. The notice of final rulemaking criticizes the idea of emissions credits and blames them for automakers not investing in cleaner engine technology, and from model year 2028, such credits are a thing of the past. And plug-in vehicles will now no longer be included in an automaker’s fleet average; under previous rules an EV or PHEV could have a CAFE rating of hundreds of mpg.
Then again, since last year, Duffy’s department hasn’t exactly been proactive about enforcing the existing rules. In July last year it told automakers that it was not going to bother fining any of them for exceeding the CAFE limits, going back as far as 2022.

articles.title: Reco raises $55M as AI agent security startups crowd the market | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Terms like “AI sprawl” have become common fare on tech social media and in thought leadership as enterprises start deploying AI agents en masse. But CISOs worried about securing swarms of agents suddenly operating across networks are likely finding themselves dealing with a new kind of sprawl: vendors offering to help.
Just a quick glance at public Crunchbase and PitchBook profiles turns up at least two dozen companies selling some form of AI agent security. Some vendors vet the tools agents use, while others try to help companies control what data their agents can reach. Some others, like CrowdStrike, are building detection and response controls on the devices agents run, and still others are focused on finding and resolving unapproved AI usage.
The products differ, of course, but their promises to discover and govern agents sound quite similar, involving knowledge graphs, continuous monitoring, runtime security, tool access, MCP vetting, and the like.
Some are even updating their products to join the bandwagon. Until last year, AI security startup Reco was mostly selling software to map and secure SaaS and AI platforms. Now, it’s repositioned around a broader solution that uses a context graph to connect agents to apps, people, accounts, and permissions, giving security teams a way to see what an agent can reach and cut off access it doesn’t need.
According to Reco’s co-founder and CEO Ofer Klein, the biggest change over the past year that spurred the startup to broaden its scope was that companies are building and deploying AI agents faster than they can keep track of. At one of the startup’s Fortune 100 customers, he said, Reco’s platform found 21,000 agents the company didn’t know about. And at a large financial services customer, the startup claims it identified an agent set up by an ex-employee that could access Salesforce and share that data with a domain the company couldn’t see.
“The market demand right now for agent security is not only about the agent itself; it’s about the entire ecosystem end-to-end,” Klein told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview.
Klein’s not alone in stressing the urgency for companies to secure this sprawl. Security startup HiddenLayer‘s co-founder and CEO, Chris Sestito, earlier this month told me that when agents reach production, the scale of their costs and risk goes from theoretical to “full scale really quickly,” and that over 50 of his customers have AI agents in production touching critical systems and sensitive assets.
Cymphony, another AI startup, said at one U.S. public company, it found about 85,000 files that had become accessible to AI tools and agents.
There’s no doubt a ton of investors are interested in companies that can make a mint out of helping companies find and secure all these agents, and Reco has capitalized on that demand: The startup on Tuesday said it raised $55 million, building on a $30 million Series B in February. AT&T, a customer, invested in the extension via its venture arm, as did Forestay and Quadrille Capital.
Klein said the company’s valuation has “more than doubled” since the Series B was first announced in February, and vaguely estimated it in the “high hundreds of millions” though he wouldn’t share specifics. Annual recurring revenue right now is in the “double-digit millions of dollars,” he said, and he expects it to triple this year. The startup has more than 100 customers, and financial services companies account for about 40% of the business.
Reco’s bet, it appears, is that its existing coverage of SaaS apps, and the AI agents they are increasingly offering, will help it stand out from the crowd. The company currently integrates with more than 280 apps, and Klein says new integrations can be added within days. Klein said the platform uses browser and network signals to find agents outside apps it connects to directly within companies, and it has controls to inspect prompts and tool calls.
The startup will use the new funding for hiring, sales, partnerships, and customer support. The new funding brings Reco’s total capital raised to $140 million.

articles.title: Enterprise AI puts data readiness to the test - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
What to expect at the Dell AI Data Platform Event: Join theCUBE Oct. 6–7
The enterprise artificial intelligence conversation is moving past models and compute. As companies push projects into production, the harder problem is increasingly what sits underneath them: getting distributed, messy and often sensitive enterprise data ready for systems that need reliable context at speed.
“AI momentum is accelerating, but enterprises are discovering that moving from experimentation to production depends less on model selection and more on data readiness,” said Paul Nashawaty, practice lead and principal analyst — application development, modernization, cloud-native at theCUBE Research. “Our AppDev data shows that 86% of enterprises prioritize data unification over compute, while 64% of enterprise AI teams identify insufficient storage throughput as a leading training bottleneck.”
That challenge is at the center of Dell Technologies’ “AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale” virtual event, which will examine how enterprises and neocloud providers can bring data management, storage, security, sovereignty and governance together as AI workloads expand. The event features Dell Technologies’ Arthur Lewis, David Noy, Vrashank Jain and Gaurav Chawla, along with Nvidia’s Jason Hardy, Elastic’s Sri Desikan, IREN’s Kambiz Aghili, CTBC Bank’s Peter Chu, and Orbital Studios executives, among others.
Join theCUBE Oct. 6–7 for exclusive interviews and analysis as theCUBE Research analysts Dave Vellante and John Furrier speak with practitioners and industry executives about what it takes to move enterprise AI from experimentation into operational systems. We’ll be broadcasting Oct. 6 in the Americas and Oct. 7 in EMEA and APJ. (* Disclosure below.)
Enterprise AI puts data readiness to the test
Enterprises have spent heavily on models and accelerated computing, but the success of AI applications increasingly depends on whether those systems can reach the right data and use it effectively. Dell’s AI Data Platform addresses that challenge by bringing storage, data management and security together across environments where enterprise and neocloud AI workloads operate.
For developers, the issue goes beyond simply having access to more information. Nashawaty sees competitive advantage emerging from the ability to make trusted and governed data consistently available throughout the AI lifecycle.
“From an application development perspective, the competitive advantage is enabling developers to access trusted, governed data consistently across the AI lifecycle,” he said. “As enterprises move beyond pilots, the organizations that connect their data infrastructure to production-grade application delivery will be better positioned to turn AI investment into measurable business outcomes.”
The challenge becomes more complicated as agents reach beyond carefully maintained databases and warehouses. In a pre-event interview with theCUBE, Dell Technologies’ Vrashank Jain described agents as unpredictable in the data they may need, forcing enterprises to prepare far more information than they did for traditional applications.
“We’re shifting from a really predictable way to search things to a really unpredictable way of reasoning over loops,” Jain said.
As agents reach further into enterprise repositories, companies must prepare “a lot more data that they can cycle through,” he added.
That includes information stored across SharePoint, OneDrive, SaaS applications, legacy systems and other sources where data may lack structure, tagging or labeling. Jain argued that the longstanding problem of data preparation becomes much larger when agents require useful context from those previously difficult-to-use sources.
Context engineering moves into the architecture
Getting data ready is only part of the equation. Enterprises also have to determine which information an AI system needs at a particular moment without overwhelming models with unnecessary context or driving token costs higher. That is pushing context engineering into the enterprise data architecture.
Elastic’s Sri Desikan described an emerging approach in which context is prepared before an agent needs it, rather than requiring models to repeatedly search across multiple back-end systems.
“How can you pre-build this context in a way that minimizes token costs and maximizes accuracy?” Desikan said. “Any answer to a question should be accurate, factual and, to the extent possible, be consistent, from person to person.”
The implications extend beyond retrieval. Structured and unstructured information may need to be combined, ranked and verified as agents reason through multiple steps. Desikan pointed to vector search, hybrid search and re-ranking as technologies increasingly suited to agent workflows, where software rather than a human must determine which results have the appropriate context.
Furrier framed the emerging context layer as the “connective tissue” between models and enterprise data. He also drew a clear distinction between promising demonstrations and systems that can withstand real workloads.
“Production grade is different than giving a good demo,” Furrier said. “As it moves into production, you’ve got to have the discovery, low latency. You’ve got to feed the engines, feed the math, feed the GPUs and CPUs and XPUs.
Jain pointed to data preparation as one of the most visible differences between the two. Production systems have to process continually changing information, rather than relying on the carefully curated datasets often used in demonstrations.
“The other part that I think turns from a demo to production is, can this keep up when new documents are coming?” Jain said. “Because this isn’t a one and done situation.”
Agents change how data platforms are used
The rise of agentic systems is also changing who, or what, interacts with enterprise data infrastructure. Instead of a human writing a single query or conducting a search, agents can make repeated requests, call multiple tools and reason across several steps before reaching an answer.
Desikan said those multi-step interactions raise the stakes for search accuracy. An error made early in an agent workflow can compound as the system continues reasoning, eventually undermining trust in the result.
“Every agent is, at the end of the day, searching for something,” he said. “And that search has to have the right recall and precision so that the error doesn’t compound in production.”
The change is also increasing the volume of queries hitting enterprise systems. Agents may repeatedly query structured data, evaluate the response and then issue another query until they reach the desired result.
“We’re seeing SQL query demand actually skyrocket because of this,” Jain said. “Agents write a query, look at the answer, they write the query again, they get another answer. They keep writing this until they’re really happy about the answer, which means that they’re firing 10 times more queries than before.”
That shift is leading to a broader change in how enterprises think about data-platform users.
“We don’t have traditional users anymore,” Jain said. “The agents are the users.”
Security and resilience follow the data
More data access also increases the security stakes. AI workloads can span cloud, on-premises and edge environments while drawing on proprietary information that enterprises may not want copied, exposed or processed outside established governance boundaries.
“As AI moves into production, the security challenge expands beyond protecting models and infrastructure to protecting the data that gives AI systems context and value,” said Krista Case, principal analyst and practice lead for cyber resilience and security at theCUBE Research. “That data is distributed across clouds, data centers and edge environments, creating more places where sensitive information can be exposed, copied or governed inconsistently.”
Dell’s AI Data Platform reflects an architectural shift toward bringing AI closer to enterprise data while maintaining controls around security, governance and sovereignty. Those requirements become more important as agents interact with increasingly broad sets of structured and unstructured information.
For Case, cyber resilience ultimately comes back to visibility and control.
“For enterprises scaling AI, cyber resilience will depend on knowing where critical data lives, controlling how it is accessed and used, and ensuring it remains protected and recoverable throughout the AI lifecycle,” she said.
As companies move beyond pilots, the discussion is shifting from what models can demonstrate to whether the entire data foundation can deliver the accuracy, performance, governance and resilience required for everyday operations. The Dell AI Data Platform Event will put that transition under the microscope, with theCUBE examining how infrastructure, data architecture and agentic systems are coming together as enterprise deployments scale.
TheCUBE event livestream
Don’t miss theCUBE’s coverage of Dell’s AI Data Platform Event, Oct. 6 for the Americas and Oct. 7 for EMEA and APJ. Plus, you can access theCUBE’s exclusive content on demand after the event.
How to watch theCUBE interviews
We offer various ways for you to watch theCUBE’s coverage of Dell’s AI Data Platform Event, including theCUBE’s dedicated website and YouTube channel. You can also get all the coverage from this year’s events on SiliconANGLE.
TheCUBE podcasts
SiliconANGLE’s “theCUBE Pod” is available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube, which you can enjoy while on the go. During each podcast, SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante discuss the biggest trends in enterprise tech, including AI, cloud, cybersecurity and infrastructure, with context and analysis.
SiliconANGLE also produces our weekly “Breaking Analysis” program, where Vellante examines major developments in enterprise tech, combining insights from theCUBE with spending data from Enterprise Technology Research, available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.
Guests
At Dell’s AI Data Platform Event on Oct. 6–7, theCUBE will speak with Dell Technologies’ Arthur Lewis, David Noy, Vrashank Jain and Gaurav Chawla, along with Nvidia’s Jason Hardy, Elastic’s Sri Desikan, IREN’s Kambiz Aghili, CTBC Bank’s Peter Chu, and Orbital Studios executives.

articles.title: Demon's Souls reaches 40-50 FPS on private PS5 emulator with accurate graphics — KyTyPS5 surges from unplayable 1-2 FPS in just three weeks, new milestone comes only three weeks after the game barely booted
articles.text:
Demon's Souls reaches 40-50 FPS on private PS5 emulator with accurate graphics — KyTyPS5 surges from unplayable 1-2 FPS in just three weeks, new milestone comes only three weeks after the game barely booted
As one Reddit commenter put it, "hate-fueled progression."
Few projects in the software world have experienced such rapid evolution as PlayStation 5 emulation. A few hours ago, a video popped up of Demon's Souls Remake running at 40-50 FPS, seemingly with accurate graphics. Coincidentally or not, only scant months after Sony ditched physical releases of games — an announcement that landed as well as the Hindenburg — progress on KyTyPS5, SharpEmu, and AnyPS5 has gone into overdrive.
The video above is short and only shows a few sections of the game, but it's an impressive watch. Even acknowledging that the hardware specs displayed comprise an RTX 5090 and a Core i9-14900K, having a game working this well, at least graphically, only a month after "barely works" was a landmark is nothing short of staggering.
To wit, KyTyPS5 was running Demon's Souls Remake with 1-2 FPS on actual gameplay three weeks ago, and struggling to reach 30 FPS a fortnight past. The same emulator has been shown partially running GTA V before at 40-60 FPS, but that's an older title that presumably isn't as demanding as Demon's Souls.
The fact that the PlayStation 5's architecture is so similar to a standard PC apart from unified memory is a big reason why progress has been so speedy. As it stands, the major roadblocks aren't emulating a CPU or a GPU, but rather writing compatibility layers for the console's operating system and drivers, including but not limited to converting native graphics shaders to Vulkan's SPIR-V language.
Given the demo video's lack of stuttering, it's a reasonable assumption that the captured video was done after an initial run to avoid shader recompilation hitches. This particular aspect of emulation has always been a constant thorn in developers' side, as it's exceedingly difficult to predict which shaders a game will need before they're actually used.
The current best approach is to asynchronously compile and collect shaders from gamers' playthroughs and build a community database for preloading. This concept was popularized by RPCS3 around 2018, with a small team and limited to no budget.
Although Nvidia and AMD drivers have cached shaders in limited fashion for a long while, RPCS3's effort appeared seven years before Nvidia and Microsoft, with their gigantic piles of money, bothered to try and fix this issue properly with their Auto Shader Compilation and Advanced Shader Delivery, respectively.

What is NYT Connections?
NYT Connections is one of several increasingly popular word games made by the New York Times. It challenges you to find groups of four items that share something in common, and each group has a different difficulty level: green is easy, yellow a little harder, blue often quite tough and purple usually very difficult.
On the plus side, you don't technically need to solve the final one, as you'll be able to answer that one by a process of elimination. What's more, you can make up to four mistakes, which gives you a little bit of breathing room.
It's a little more involved than something like Wordle, however, and there are plenty of opportunities for the game to trip you up with tricks. For instance, watch out for homophones and other word games that could disguise the answers.

articles.title: El nuevo detalle de 'Avengers: Doomsday' en su último teaser que ha emocionado a los fans: "Como en los cómics"
articles.text:
Con el estreno de Avengers: Doomsday cada vez más cerca, Marvel sigue trabajando a contrarreloj para tener la película totalmente lista para su lanzamiento en cines. Y como mejor muestra, han publicado un teaser más en el que, si bien no se incluye ninguna escena nueva, sí que se aprecian detalles que antes no estaban ahí. Y uno de ellos ha sido especialmente comentado por los fans.
Concretamente, la escena es el momento en el que Thor se enfrenta al Doctor Doom. Un instante que ya habíamos visto antes pero que ahora cuenta con una notable mejora. y es que, cuando Doom desata su magia y dispara con su mano al Dios del Trueno, el rayo que sale de él ahora es bastante distinto. El equipo de Avengers: Doomsday ha añadido unas burbujas negras al haz de luz. Y cualquier lector de cómics sabe lo que es.
Estas burbujas negras son los conocidos como Kirby Krackle o Kirby Dots ("craquelado de Kirby" o "puntos de Kirby"). Este recurso creado por el artista de cómics Jack Kirby consiste en añadir puntos negros a explosiones, rayos de energía, disparos etc. para representar el espacio negativo a su alrededor. Concretamente, la magia del Doctor Doom suele aparecer dibujada con el Kirby Krackle alrededor de su haz de luz verde.
Y ahora, en Avengers: Doomsday, el temible villano también contará con este reconocible efecto. Un detalle que no ha pasado desapercibido entre los fans. Si hasta ahora se había criticado bastante el aspecto visual de la película, con este añadido la compañía se ha anotado un importante punto a favor. Las redes sociales ya están llenas de comentarios celebrando la creativa decisión de hacer este homenaje a las viñetas.
El multiverso colapsa en Avengers: Doomsday
En el reestreno de Avengers Endgame: Encore, Marvel incluyó varias escenas nuevas que conectan con Avengers: Doomsday. Y una de ellas tiene lugar en la Agencia de Variación Temporal, donde descubrimos definitivamente que el multiverso está colapsando. Miles de universos están chocando entre sí, provocando incursiones y la inevitable desaparición de algunos de ellos.
"Es lo más trascendental que le ha pasado jamás al UCM. Se percibe como el fin de los tiempos. La AVT se creó precisamente para proteger las líneas temporales del colapso, y ahora se encuentran en medio de un colapso catastrófico. Por eso, diría que esa escena tiene, efectivamente, una gran importancia. No diría que sea más importante que otra escena, pero sin duda es fundamental para la narrativa de Doomsday", explica Joe Russo en una entrevista concedida a Empire.
"Es el principio unificador que aúna el universo de los X-Men, el de los Vengadores y el de los 4 Fantásticos. Eso es lo que constituye el núcleo de la colisión entre estos universos", se une Anthony Russo. Avengers: Doomsday se estrena en cines el 18 de diciembre.

articles.title: Ohne Akku, mit ANC: Bose setzt bei neuen In-Ears wieder aufs Kabel
articles.text:
Ohne Akku, mit Geräuschunterdrückung: Bose bringt neue kabelgebundene In-Ears
Der Audiospezialist Bose bringt mit den Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds wieder kabelgebundene Ohrhörer auf den Markt – die ersten seit über zehn Jahren. Sie kosten 99,95 Euro, lassen sich ab sofort über die Bose-Webseite vorbestellen und sollen ab dem 15. Oktober ausgeliefert werden. Erhältlich sind sie in Schwarz, Rauchweiß und einer limitierten Farbe namens „Tautropfen-Minze“.
Strom aus dem Smartphone
Der große Vorteil am Kabel: Die Ohrstöpsel brauchen weder eine App noch eine Bluetooth-Kopplung. Einen eingebauten Akku gibt es ebenfalls nicht: Den Strom ziehen die Geräte wie früher aus dem Zuspielgerät, also etwa aus Smartphone, Notebook oder Musikplayer. Einen klassischen 3,5-Millimeter-Klinkenstecker haben sie allerdings nicht, stattdessen setzt Bose auf USB-C. Damit passen sie an die meisten aktuellen Geräte, auch an neuere iPhones.
Steuern lassen sich die Earbuds über eine Fernbedienung mit physischen Tasten, die im 1,30 Meter langen Kabel steckt. Darüber regeln Nutzer:innen Lautstärke, Wiedergabe und Anrufe und wechseln zwischen den Noise-Cancelling-Modi. Insgesamt gibt es drei Varianten: Der „Quiet-Modus“ blendet Störgeräusche aus, der „Aware-Modus“ lässt die Umgebung durch, und im „ANC-Off-Modus“ hören Nutzer:innen ohne aktive Geräuschunterdrückung. Auf der Rückseite der Fernbedienung sitzt ein Mikrofon für Telefonate. Diese Position soll laut Bose die Stimme klarer erfassen und zugleich Störgeräusche verringern, die entstehen, wenn das Kabel an Kleidung reibt.
Klang und Latenz
Bose verbaut seine eigene digitale Signalverarbeitung, die für einen ordentlichen Klang sorgen soll. Über das Protokoll USB Audio Class 2 verarbeiten die Ohrhörer Eingangssignale mit beliebiger Abtastrate und Bittiefe, ausgegeben wird mit 24 Bit und 48 Kilohertz.
Als Vorteil der Kabelverbindung nennt der Hersteller die geringe Latenz: Beim Videoschauen, Gaming oder Produzieren von Inhalten bleibe der Ton stets synchron. Gegen Spritzwasser sind die Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds nach Schutzart IPX4 geschützt – Regen oder Schweiß sollten ihnen also nichts anhaben.

articles.title: WEH Ventures marks first close of Rs 250 Cr Fund III
articles.text:
WEH Ventures marks first close of Rs 250 Cr Fund III
The Fund III of WEH Ventures aims to invest in 20-25 Indian startups cutting across sectors.
WEH Ventures, a seed-stage venture capital firm has announced the first close of Fund III with a target corpus Rs 250 crore. Though it did not disclose the quantum of funds raised in the first close.
A statement from WEH Ventures said the first close has attracted participation from a mix of family offices, exited founders and senior corporate and technology executives. Early backers include Play Capital, a Nordic Fund of Fund (FoF); family offices such as Eraya, Twin & Bull Investments and Heritage Investments; exited founders from companies including Oziva and GS Labs; senior executives and CEOs from companies such as Thermax, Haleon, Lenovo and PNB MetLife; as well as senior Silicon Valley executives associated with companies including Arlo and Intuitive Surgical.
The fund III aims to invest in 20-25 early stage Indian startups across a broad set of sectors including advanced manufacturing, agriculture, energy transition, artificial intelligence and healthcare, alongside consumer and fintech.
WEH Ventures said it has already begun deploying capital from Fund III and has committed to eight investments across advanced agriculture, robotics, healthcare diagnostics, retail and edtech.
WEH Ventures General Partner Deepak Gupta said, “Fund III builds on the strategy we have followed over the years: backing strong founders early when they are solving compelling problems and helping them build enduring businesses. What is changing is the breadth of opportunities we are seeing in the market. Fund III allows us to participate in this broader opportunity while staying disciplined about the stage and kind of founders we want to back.”
This VC firm claimed that it has shown strong performance since its Fund I in 2017 and Fund II launched in 2020. Fund I has returned material capital (1.4x), and Fund 2 has already returned capital with one exit and is tracking to well above top-quartile performance. It has invested in 30 startups till now.
Among the portfolio of startups in WEH Ventures’ include the likes of Smallcase, Jar, Pratilipi, Animall, MasterChow, AppsforBharat, Unbox Robotics and Mitigata.

articles.title: Le Rafale, fleuron de l'armée française, dégradé à deux reprises dans son usine : ce que soupçonnent les gendarmes
articles.text:
Un Rafale en construction a été dégradé à deux reprises dans l’usine Dassault Aviation de Cergy, dans le Val-d’Oise, et un salarié a été interpellé à la mi-septembre. Révélée vendredi par Le Parisien, l’affaire orienterait les gendarmes vers un conflit interne à l’entreprise plutôt que vers une ingérence étrangère. Elle s’ajoute à d’autres incidents sur des sites sensibles, au moment où Emmanuel Macron demande de mieux les protéger.
Deux dégradations sur une chaîne de montage
Dassault avait déposé plainte fin 2025, après avoir constaté la dégradation d’un Rafale en cours de construction. Les faits se sont répétés en juin 2026, sur la chaîne de montage d’un avion de chasse en fabrication. Les gendarmes de la section de recherches de la gendarmerie de l’armement, spécialisée dans les atteintes au secret-défense, ont interpellé un salarié mi-septembre. Franceinfo dit avoir obtenu confirmation de l’information.
« Dassault Aviation confirme avoir porté plainte pour actes de dégradation commis dans l’usine de Cergy par un collaborateur », a réagi l’entreprise, qui précise que la justice suit son cours. Le parquet de Paris n’a pas commenté. Les sources ne détaillent pas la nature exacte des dégradations.
Le mot « sabotage » va plus loin que l’enquête
Les enquêteurs ont d’abord craint une opération de déstabilisation visant un fleuron de la défense française. Après plusieurs mois de recherches puis la garde à vue du salarié, ils ont finalement privilégié un conflit interne à l’entreprise, selon Le Parisien. Le terme de sabotage circule dans plusieurs titres, mais rien n’indique à ce stade une commande venue de l’étranger.
Du hafnium volé chez Framatome
Il ne s’agit pas du Rafale, mais Le Parisien rapproche cette affaire d’une autre. Fin juillet, l’usine Framatome de Jarrie, en Isère, a constaté la disparition de plusieurs dizaines de fûts de cristaux d’hafnium, un métal notamment utilisé dans la propulsion des sous-marins nucléaires, des avions de chasse ou de certains missiles. Un salarié d’une quarantaine d’années a été placé en garde à vue le 19 août. Les gendarmes ont retrouvé chez lui plus de 150 kg de ce métal, d’une valeur estimée à plus de 1,5 million d’euros, ainsi que plus de 500 000 euros en liquide et une arme de poing.
Il a été mis en examen et incarcéré, sa compagne placée sous contrôle judiciaire. La DGSI a été avisée, mais aucune ingérence étrangère n’a été établie. Une source proche du dossier évoque plutôt un salarié qui a voulu « arrondir très largement ses fins de mois ».
Des drones près de sites sensibles à Toulouse
Le Parisien cite aussi deux affaires toulousaines. En juin, un Biélorusse de 48 ans a été interpellé alors qu’il filmait un prototype de drone de l’entreprise Delair. Il aurait envoyé la vidéo à un interlocuteur en Russie, ce qu’il conteste. Il a été mis en examen et incarcéré. Peu après, deux ressortissantes chinoises ont été interpellées en faisant voler un drone au-dessus de la zone aéroportuaire de Blagnac. L’analyse du drone n’a pas étayé les soupçons et elles ont regagné leur pays. Le procureur de Toulouse précise qu’« aucune ingérence étrangère n’est démontrée ».
À lire aussi : Des drones aux sous-marins, Airbus va protéger les communications secrètes de l’armée française
Macron demande un plan de protection
Le 18 septembre, le président a demandé au gouvernement de préparer un plan de protection des infrastructures critiques et des sites les plus sensibles de la base industrielle de défense, en évoquant le risque d’« attaques hybrides » russes. Jeudi soir, lors d’une intervention télévisée, il a répété : « Nous devons nous préparer ». Franceinfo précise qu’à chaque incident, la DGSI est alertée pour déterminer s’il s’agit d’un acte isolé ou d’une opération pilotée depuis l’étranger.

articles.title: Reco Raises $55 Million for Agentic Security
articles.text:
Agentic cybersecurity firm Reco today announced raising $55 million in a strategic funding round that brings the total raised by the company to $140 million.
The investment round was led by AT&T Ventures, with additional support from new investors Forestay and Quadrille Capital.
Founded in 2020, New York-based Reco provides organizations with an overview of the agents that are active in their environments and the risks they pose.
The company shows security teams which identities the AI agents use, their permissions, what data and which systems they reach, and the workflows they can initiate.
Using the Reco Graph, it maps the relationships between agents and accounts, API connections, sessions, MCP tools, workflows, and employee applications to identify unnecessary exposure, revoke excessive permissions and outdated access, disable risky integrations, and enforce policies.
Reco’s solution integrates with multiple AI providers and enterprise applications, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft’s Copilot, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Workday.
The company plans to use the fresh investment to hire new talent across its sales, partnerships, channels, and customer support teams.
“As both an investor and customer, AT&T recognizes the growing importance of helping organizations understand and manage how AI agents interact with business applications and data,” said AT&T Ventures head Vikram Taneja.
“Reco’s approach to visibility and governance aligns with the needs we are seeing across enterprises as agent adoption continues to evolve,” Taneja added.

articles.title: Kalshi loses again as judges rule prediction markets must obey gambling laws
articles.text:
Another federal appeals court has ruled that states can enforce their gambling laws against the prediction market Kalshi, which asserts that it can only be regulated by the US government. On Friday, a three-judge panel in the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ruled unanimously against Kalshi and in favor of Ohio and Tennessee.
While the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission has exclusive jurisdiction over “swaps,” the judges found that sports wagers offered on Kalshi do not meet the legal definition of swaps. Moreover, the court found that even if Kalshi wagers were swaps, the regulatory scheme created by Congress would not prohibit states from enforcing gambling laws on prediction markets.
“We hold that Kalshi has not shown that its sports-event contracts satisfy the statutory definition of a ‘swap’ so as to fall within the scope of the CFTC’s ‘exclusive jurisdiction,’” said the ruling written by Judge Julia Smith Gibbons, a George W. Bush appointee. “And, even assuming that Kalshi’s sports-event contracts are swaps, we alternatively hold that the CEA [Commodity Exchange Act] neither expressly nor impliedly preempts Ohio’s or Tennessee’s gambling laws.”
Kalshi sued Ohio and Tennessee after gambling regulators in each state indicated they would bring enforcement actions against the prediction market. The appeals court ruling on Friday upheld an Ohio district court decision against Kalshi and vacated a Tennessee district court order that went in favor of Kalshi.
Many states are trying to stop or restrict gambling on Kalshi, which offers sports betting throughout the US despite not obtaining state gambling licenses or paying state gambling taxes. Kalshi offers sports bets in some states where gambling on sports is entirely illegal and in other states where the law has restrictions on betting that Kalshi does not follow.

articles.title: Kiteworks patches critical flaw, brings customer systems online
articles.text:
American tech company Kiteworks has lifted a precautionary advisory asking customers to shut down systems after patching a critical vulnerability.
Formerly known as Accellion, it operates a Private Content Network (PCN) that integrates enterprise email, file sharing, Managed File Transfer (MFT), APIs, and web forms into a single platform.
Kiteworks provides services to thousands of global corporations and government agencies, and its Private Data Network has over 100 million end-users.
The secure file-sharing software company urged customers worldwide on Saturday to temporarily shut down their servers after receiving a warning of a potentially imminent cyberattack from federal intelligence authorities.
On Monday, the company brought all hosted customer systems back online after finding no evidence of compromise and no suspicious activity.
"Continuous monitoring throughout the period showed no abnormal activity, and the company has no indication that any Kiteworks or customer system was compromised," Kiteworks said.
"As of September 27th, the shutdown recommendation is now lifted for all customers. If you have not already restarted, you may bring your Kiteworks system back online," the company added in an update to the original advisory.
Kiteworks has also patched a critical vulnerability in an unnamed feature used by less than 1% of all customers and advised those with self-hosted Kiteworks Advanced Forms to contact support for further assistance.
"Kiteworks developed and deployed a fix during the window, applied an additional protective layer across all environments, and has no indication the vulnerability was ever exploited. All other Kiteworks products were unaffected," it noted.
The company has yet to share additional details on the fixed vulnerability and has not yet assigned a CVE ID for easy tracking.
Threat watchdog Shadowserver has spotted nearly 400 Kiteworks instances accessible over the Internet, most of them (234) from the United States, but provides no information on how many are honeypots or have already been patched.
Because they store sensitive documents, cybercrime gangs often target vulnerable file-sharing platforms in data-theft extortion attacks.
For instance, the Clop extortion gang, which has a long history of exploiting vulnerabilities in enterprise file-sharing platforms, also targeted a legacy Kiteworks File Transfer Appliance (FTA) software in zero-day attacks when the company was still known as Accellion.
Accellion said at the time that 300 customers used the 20-year-old legacy FTA software, with fewer than 100 of them breached and fewer than two dozen victims appeared "to have suffered significant data theft."
That Clop hacking campaign led to a stream of data breaches impacting many high-profile entities that used the Accellion FTA software to transfer sensitive files, including cybersecurity firm Qualys, energy giant Shell, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, supermarket giant Kroger, Singtel, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), the Office of the Washington State Auditor, and multiple universities.
Five Eyes members also issued a joint security advisory in February 2021 about these attacks and subsequent extortion attempts, warning Accellion customers to block Internet access to vulnerable servers and update them to block the attacks.

articles.title: OpenAI cancela el lanzamiento de GPT-6.1 Astra: su propio equipo de seguridad ha visto que el modelo no era fiable
articles.text:
OpenAI ha dejado en suspenso GPT-6.1 Astra, el modelo que planeaba lanzar en octubre, después de que sus propios investigadores descubrieran que el sistema no se comportaba de forma suficientemente fiable durante las pruebas internas. La empresa confirmó la decisión este lunes, tras un artículo publicado por el The Wall Street Journal.
Pausa. Este fin de semana varios medios se hacían eco de que OpenAI había pausado el entrenamiento de uno de sus modelos más potentes, sin especificar aún de cuál se trataba, tras el intento de hackeo de sus agentes de IA a varias webs del Gobierno de Estados Unidos y otros episodios erráticos.
Antes de eso, durante el verano, varios de sus agentes de IA experimentales que nunca estuvieron destinados a publicarse, accedieron a sitios web y sistemas sin autorización. Astra, que llegó recientemente a ChatGPT y Codex, se diseñó para completar tareas complejas con poca supervisión humana, que es precisamente el tipo de autonomía que ha estado causando problemas.
En detalle. Saachi Jain, responsable de sistemas de seguridad de OpenAI, declaraba al WSJ que el modelo había empeorado en dos áreas en comparación con GPT-6 Astra, lanzado en septiembre. Por un lado en honestidad, pues Jain asegura que el nuevo modelo engañaba más a los investigadores en las pruebas de alineación, pruebas que miden si un modelo hace lo que las personas pretenden. Y es que según OpenAI, a veces no informaba con precisión sobre todo lo que había o no hecho.
Además, según Jain, el modelo avanzaba muchas veces con ciertas tareas sin pedir permiso y, en ocasiones, recurría a herramientas o servicios externos incluso cuando eso podía ser inseguro.
El modelo sí mejoró en otras áreas, como lo que OpenAI denomina “pereza”, es decir, rendirse cuando una tarea se vuelve difícil. Pero Jain afirma que “no alcanzó el listón” para el lanzamiento.
Problemas. Los agentes de IA de OpenAI llevan ya una larga lista de problemas de seguridad que han suscitado las dudas de organismos, expertos y usuarios en todo el mundo, entre ellos el incidente de ciberseguridad de Hugging Face, acceso no autorizado a sitios web del gobierno australiano, o el reciente intento de extraer datos confidenciales en las webs del Departamento de Educación y Comercio y la SEC de Estados Unidos.
Ayer mismamente contábamos cómo OpenAI pausó el entrenamiento de sus modelos más avanzados después de todo el jaleo montado. El WSJ cuenta que el nuevo sistema de supervisión de la empresa detectó los últimos incidentes en un plazo de 15 minutos. Astra es un caso aparte, según afirma la empresa.
Por otro lado, la gestión de estos incidentes por parte de OpenAI ha suscitado algunas críticas. El Primer Ministro de Australia, Anthony Albanese, calificaba la brecha de junio en los sistemas gubernamentales como “inaceptable” y criticó a OpenAI por notificarlo a su Gobierno a través de una dirección de correo electrónico genérica, según comparten desde la BBC. Desde entonces, OpenAI se ha disculpado y ha declarado que “debería haber gestionado mejor su respuesta”. Sam Altman también ha reconocido en redes sociales que la empresa había sido más lenta de lo que deseaba a la hora de revelar los incidentes.
Y ahora qué. Las aguas están bien revueltas en materia de IA. Y es que todo ha ocurrido precisamente en un contexto en el que los principales laboratorios de IA piden echar el freno en el desarrollo por cuestiones de seguridad. Pero claro, esto es una carrera por la supremacía de la IA más potente entre Estados Unidos y China, por lo que ambos gobiernos han dado señales contradictorias sobre lo de tomarse las cosas con más calma.
Por otro lado, no son precisamente pocos los que piensan que, el alardear de una “IA peligrosa” es la maniobra de marketing perfecta para demostrar las capacidades tecnológicas soberbias de estos modelos. Aunque esto nunca lo sabremos. Lo que sí sabemos es que OpenAI afirma que seguirá utilizando el modelo subyacente de Astra para continuar con el entrenamiento y asegura que investigará las causas fundamentales de los problemas.

articles.title: Comienzan los Días Naranja de PcComponentes: Apple Watch Ultra con un 37% de descuento y unas gafas tipo Ray Ban Meta por menos de 50 euros
articles.text:
Hay algunas citas marcadas en rojo en el calendario, sobre todo las que tienen que ver con grandes ofertas comerciales. Cuando hablamos de tecnología, una de las fechas más importantes es, sin duda, los Días Naranja de PcComponentes. Este año, comenzaron el pasado domingo 27 de septiembre y finalizan el próximo domingo, 11 de noviembre. Dos semanas donde cualquier persona puede encontrar lo que esté buscando en el mundo tecnológico, desde teléfonos a televisores y pasando también por pequeños electrodomésticos. Todo ello con descuentos que llegan incluso al 40%.
Es sin duda la mejor ocasión para renovar cualquier equipo que tengamos por casa o hacer de una vez por todas esa compra pendiente que tenemos desde hace tiempo. Además de las ofertas que habrá durante todo el periodo, debes estar atento para las ofertas flash que duran sólo 24 o 48 horas. Los Días Naranja de PcComponentes vienen más calientes que nunca.
Teléfonos: Apple Samsung o Xiaomi
Seguramente una de las categorías que más interesa a la gente. Durante estos días puedes llevarte un iPhone 17 Pro Max con un diez por ciento de descuento, un Samsung Galaxy A56 por menos de 370 euros o un REDMI Note 15 Pro por menos de 250 euros.
Pero hay muchas más ofertas por lo que si estás buscando otro modelo, entra en la sección de teléfonos, pon los criterios de búsqueda y encuentra el modelo perfecto.
Televisores propios de PcComponentes y cualquier marca
Ahora mismo, para poder disfrutar en casa de la mejor calidad de imagen y sonido, no necesitas gastarte mucho dinero. PcComponentes ha lanzado una marca propia de televisores que está súper bien: resolución 4K, sistema operativo WebOS y tamaños que parten de las 50 pulgadas. Todo por un precio que ronda los 250 euros.
Pero si buscas otras marcas, quizá te interese este televisor Philips QLED de 75 pulgadas, con tecnología Quantum Dot y Dolby Atmos que tiene un descuento superior al 40% y se queda en menos de 600 euros. Una pasada.
Para terminar, te recomendamos un proyector que tiene un precio de tan sólo 39 euros. El típico capricho al que le acabas sacando mucho partido.
Dos smartwatches perfectos para todo tipo de personas
Si quieres entrar en el mundo de los smartwatches, tienes dos opciones: irte al top, al mejor de Apple, el Apple Watch Ultra 2, o cogerte uno mucho más sencillo, compatible con todo el sistema operativo Android y con una relación calidad precio magnífica. El primero, el Apple Watch Ultra 2, tiene un descuento del 37% y el segundo, el Amazfit Balance 2, cuesta tan sólo 249 euros.
El gadget de moda; unas gafas inteligentes por menos de cincuenta euros
Seguramente las hayas visto por ahí ya: unas gafas Ray Ban con cámara integrada que puede hacer fotos o grabar vídeos sin tener que depender de tu teléfono. Lo que pasa es que es un producto muy caro que todavía mantiene alejado a mucha parte de la población. Por eso, PcComponentes ha lanzado una versión bajo su marca propia Owlotech y que sólo cuestan 49,99 euros aprovechando la oferta de los Días Naranja.
Unas gafas con una estética bonita que además pueden recibir llamadas, sirven como auriculares para escuchar música y permiten la traducción en tiempo real. Son la tendencia del momento y seguro que dentro de pocos años todo el mundo lleva unas.

articles.title: J'ai testé le casque Nothing Headphones (1) Pro : trois transducteurs, et ça s’entend — Frandroid
articles.text:
Depuis ses débuts, Nothing cherche à se démarquer autant par le design de ses produits que par leur technologie. Fondée en 2020 par Carl Pei, l’un des cofondateurs de OnePlus, la marque s’est notamment fait remarquer avec ses écouteurs, régulièrement salués ici pour leur qualité audio et leurs performances acoustiques ou leur réduction de bruit active, tout en restant relativement accessibles. C’est bien simple, pour les écouteurs et désormais les casques, Nothing est devenue une marque qui compte, quasi incontournable pour qui souhaite le meilleur à prix convenable.
    Pour aller plus loin
            Quels sont les meilleurs casques audio Bluetooth de 2026 ? Notre sélection
            
Le Headphone (1), lancé en 2025, avait marqué un tournant net vers la haute-fidélité, avec un partenariat avec le fabricant d’enceintes britannique KEF. Certes, les partenariats avec des marques prestigieuses, il en existe de (trop) nombreux qui ne convainquent pas, mais le Headphone (1) sonnait vraiment comme un casque hi-fi filaire premium. On ne va pas pour autant donner le bon Dieu sans confession à ce Headphone (1) Pro, mais son passage au banc de test relève pour moi de la bonne nouvelle.
La grande nouveauté tient à l’emploi de trois transducteurs par oreillette, comme dans les enceintes hi-fi, là où la quasi-totalité des casques se contentent d’un unique transducteur large bande. On vous explique un peu plus loin pourquoi c’est une bonne idée, pourquoi ça n’a pas que des avantages et, surtout, si ça marche vraiment bien (sinon trois fois mieux).
|  | Headphone (1) | Headphone (1) Pro | 
|---|---|---|
| Architecture | 1 × 40 mm dynamique | 3 transducteurs | 
| Graves | 40 mm | 40 mm dynamique dédié | 
| Médiums | 40 mm | 13 × 8 mm dynamique | 
| Aigus | 40 mm | xMEMS dédié | 
| Audio spatial | Oui | Oui, avec suivi dynamique de la tête | 
| ANC | Jusqu’à 42 dB | Jusqu’à 46 dB | 
| Bluetooth | 5.3 | 6.1 | 
| Jack | Oui | Oui | 
| Poids | 329 g | 327 g | 
| Autonomie avec ANC | 35 h | 30 h | 
Nothing Headphone (1) ProSpécifications techniques
| Modèle | Nothing Headphone (1) Pro | 
|---|---|
| Typologie | casque circum-aural | 
| Réduction de bruit active | Oui | 
| Diamètre des transducteurs | 40 mm | 
| Autonomie annoncée avec fonction ANC activée | 30 heures | 
| Poids du casque | 327 g | 
|  | Fiche produit | 
Ce test a été réalisé avec un casque prêté par Nothing.
Nothing Headphone (1) ProUn look toujours aussi atypique
Nothing ne change pas sa formule. Le Headphone (1) Pro reprend l’esthétique années 80-90 immédiatement identifiable de son prédécesseur, avec ses coques carrées, son verre transparent et sa mécanique apparente. Le Pro pousse plus loin cette logique, avec une finition qui paraît sensiblement plus luxueuse.
La première chose qui saute aux yeux, c’est évidemment cette grande surface en verre qui laisse entrevoir un peu les vraies entrailles de la bête. Comme le verre est fumé, on ne voit en réalité pas grand-chose, mais c’est l’occasion de s’amuser un peu à essayer de deviner ce qui se cache. En pratique, rien d’exceptionnel, la partie arrière des transducteurs importe moins que leur membrane orientée vers l’oreille, qu’on ne voit pas, elle.
Le verre est un Panda Glass 9H présenté par Nothing comme résistant aux rayures et aux chocs.
Nothing annonce au passage une réduction de 45 % du poids des bras par rapport au Headphone (1). Pour autant, le casque ne s’est pas transformé en poids plume : 327 grammes, contre 329 grammes pour le Headphone (1). Le progrès se joue donc sur la répartition de la masse, et il est net. On peut secouer la tête et le casque bouge à peine, l’inertie est négligeable.
Nothing a élargi l’arceau de 10 % et épaissi son rembourrage de 12 %, tandis que les coussinets sont 50 % plus souples que ceux du Headphone (1). Les oreillettes peuvent en outre pivoter de 20 degrés afin de mieux épouser les différentes morphologies. Il est confortable ? Oui.
Des commandes bien différenciées
On retrouve aussi les commandes physiques du Headphone (1), qui restent l’un des points forts du casque. La molette, façon chaîne hi-fi vintage, permet de régler le volume d’une simple rotation (avec un cliquetis pour marquer les paliers) et de lancer ou mettre en pause la lecture d’une pression.
Un appui prolongé permet également de basculer entre les différents modes de réduction de bruit et la transparence. La palette, elle, sert à naviguer dans les morceaux : une poussée vers la droite passe au titre suivant, vers la gauche revient au précédent. Elle sert aussi à prendre ou refuser un appel.
Le troisième bouton permet par défaut d’invoquer l’assistant vocal, mais peut être personnalisé dans l’app Nothing X pour déclencher d’autres fonctions, notamment l’app ChatGPT ou de prendre une photo sur les smartphones compatibles. Cela permet par exemple de déclencher à distance l’appareil photo du smartphone.
Un petit interrupteur Flat EQ permet de forcer le profil d’égalisation par défaut, au cas où l’on aurait trop joué avec l’égaliseur de l’app (on y revient) et qu’on voudrait retrouver le son d’origine en un geste.
L’étui de transport est atypique puisqu’il utilise l’arceau comme poignée. Un peu à la manière de celui qui est proposé avec l’Apple AirPods Max 2 (en polyuréthane souple), il englobe les deux écouteurs du casque Nothing. Il est en plastique extrêmement rigide et particulièrement lourd.
On se dit alors que c’est parce qu’il intègre une batterie ou de composants électroniques mais en fait, pas du tout. C’est une simple pièce de plastique qui vient donc protéger et alourdir l’ensemble. Il pèse plus que le casque lui-même sur la balance, ce qui me fait m’interroger de la réelle pertinence de l’emporter avec soi, notamment lors des vols en avion où le poids peut être compté.
Une connectique analogique et Hi-Res Audio
Le Headphone (1) Pro dispose du Bluetooth 6.1, avec prise en charge des codecs AAC, SBC et LDAC, ainsi que de la connexion simultanée à deux appareils. Le casque peut donc passer d’un smartphone à un ordinateur sans avoir à refaire l’appairage à chaque fois. Un mode faible latence permet par ailleurs de descendre sous les 120 ms, principalement pour améliorer la synchronisation dans les jeux, avec toutefois un léger retard du son sur l’image. En lecture vidéo, la synchro est parfaite.
L’entrée mini-jack 3,5 mm (numérisée d’office) permet une écoute Hi-Res jusqu’en 24 bits/96 kHz, tandis que l’USB-C peut servir directement de liaison audio numérique et monter jusqu’en 24 bits/192 kHz sans compression.
Nothing Headphone (1) ProUne partie logicielle très complète
L’app Nothing X est ultra-complète et blindée de tutoriels pour utiliser le casque. On peut ajuster le fonctionnement de la réduction de bruit active, procéder à un test d’audition pour corriger la balance tonale selon ses capacités auditives ou bien activer l’audio spatial. Ou ne pas l’activer, tant les résultats ne sont pas mirobolants. Le son est immédiatement dénaturé et la scène sonore corrompue. Dans certains cas, cela peut améliorer des prises de son médiocres, mais avec des productions de qualité, le bénéfice de l’audio spatial est très limité.
Le très gros atout de l’app, c’est son égaliseur hybride. Des profils ont été développés avec Metropolis Studios pour offrir immédiatement une signature sonore différente de celle par défaut. Si vous n’y trouvez pas votre bonheur, l’égaliseur paramétrique s’impose. Il permet de choisir une tranche de fréquences très étroite ou large (cela s’ajuste via le réglage facteur Q) et de régler le gain au dixième de décibel près. Pour aller plus loin, on peut même ajuster la réponse en fréquence du transducteur principal et de celui des sons moyens.
Est-ce que ça vaut le coup d’y toucher ? Oui, si l’on est curieux, non si le son par défaut plaît naturellement.
Côté Bluetooth, le Headphone (1) Pro prend en charge les codecs SBC, AAC et LDAC pour la musique, ce dernier permettant une écoute sans fil en haute résolution. Nothing ajoute également le LC3, mais uniquement pour la fonction de diffusion audio Auracast.
Nothing Headphone (1) ProUne ANC toujours aussi efficace
Nothing muscle son système de réduction de bruit active avec dix microphones, contre six sur le Headphone (1), et annonce jusqu’à 46 dB d’atténuation, contre 42 dB pour le Headphone (1). Il s’agit d’un maximum théorique mesuré dans le laboratoire de Nothing, qui prévient que l’atténuation réelle varie selon l’environnement. L’ANC est adaptative, avec quatre niveaux : bas, moyen, haut et adaptatif. En pratique, la différence s’entend surtout dans les environnements complexes (transports, avec bruits stridents et conversations par exemple). Globalement, cette ANC se situe au niveau des meilleures, seulement dépassée par celle des rois de la catégorie que sont les Apple AirPods Max 2 et le Bose Quietcomfort Ultra Headphones 2e Gen.
L’isolation passive progresse aussi grâce à des coussinets utilisant une mousse 50 % plus souple, censée mieux épouser les contours de l’oreille et limiter les fuites sonores.
Quant au mode transparence, il ne fait pas oublier qu’on a un casque sur les oreilles, mais on entend très bien autour de soi. Pour tenir une conversation ou rester conscient de son environnement dans la rue, le Headphone (1) Pro remplit sa mission.
Nothing Headphone (1) ProUne expérience auditive surprenante
Le Nothing Headphone (1) Pro est équipé de trois transducteurs, deux dynamiques et un xMEMS, et c’est tout son intérêt. C’est le principe de l’enceinte acoustique, on utilise un transducteur par registre de fréquence (grave, médium, aigu) afin de mieux les restituer. Par mieux, il faut comprendre avec moins de distorsion et plus de réactivité. Sur une enceinte, le woofer est gros et lourd et lui demander de jouer aussi dans l’aigu aboutirait à énormément de distorsion. Pour cette raison, on utilise un tweeter, un transducteur petit et léger, incapable de faire du grave, conçu pour l’aigu qui vibre très précisément.
Nothing a décidé d’appliquer la même recette, afin d’affiner le son du Headphone (1) Pro. Le transducteur des basses fréquences est un dôme en plastique de 40 mm recouvert de métal et de céramique (pour moins se déformer). Celui des fréquences médium, un transducteur dynamique de 13 x 8 mm, est bien plus petit pour vibrer plus finement, tandis que celui des hautes fréquences est un modèle xMEMS encore plus petit, avec une membrane ultra-légère.
Par ailleurs, chaque transducteur dispose de sa propre amplification, ce qui améliore encore le son.
La signature tonale n’est pas très différente de celle du Headphone (1) ni même du Headphone (a), mais la réactivité globale est nettement meilleure. Pied de batterie, voix, cordes, tout est plus net et audible, avec des notes qui semblent mieux tenues, s’éteignent plus tard. Le son apparaît exceptionnellement riche et dense.
Courbe de réponse en fréquence
Un coup d’œil à la réponse en fréquence montre une courbe en W, avec des pics marqués dans le haut-grave, le médium et l’extrême aigu.
Entendons-nous bien, cette courbe est entièrement ajustable et si l’envie vous prend de renforcer un peu l’infra-grave, d’apaiser la bosse à 1 kHz si vous jugez le niveau de détail éprouvant, c’est parfaitement possible, et c’est toute la magie de ce casque. On fait ce qu’on veut avec la courbe et grâce aux trois transducteurs, les modifications à l’égaliseur dans l’app sont très efficaces (plus qu’avec l’unique transducteur du Headphone (1)).
Comportement dynamique et scène sonore
La réactivité exemplaire des trois transducteurs a pour conséquence une dynamique exceptionnelle. On la ressent dans les instruments, mais aussi beaucoup dans les voix, avec des inflexions plus marquées, des vibrations ou des respirations mieux perçues. C’est du très bon boulot.
Généralement, pour ne pas dire presque toujours, lorsque la dynamique est bonne, la scène sonore l’est aussi. Petite nuance avec le Headphone (1) Pro. La scène n’est pas aussi précise qu’on pourrait l’attendre. C’est très bon, mais les plans sonores manquent tout de même de l’aération entre eux qui sied aux casques d’exception.
C’est le revers de la médaille du système à trois transducteurs, ils se recouvrent sur certaines fréquences et ne les diffusent pas aussi vite ou pas tout à fait avec le même sens (phase). Ce n’est pas l’anarchie, simplement la précision de la scène, sa profondeur dans l’axe frontal notamment, restent un en deça d’un Sony The Collexion ou de l’exceptionnel casque Apple AirPods Max 2, ce qui est cohérent avec le prix demandé pour ce Nothing.
Une sensibilité à la source
Aussi étonnant que cela puisse paraître, le Headphone (1) Pro se comporte assez différemment d’une source à l’autre, essentiellement en termes de dynamique et de restitution des sons moyens (voix, percussions…). Un iPhone produit un son clairement plus doux (mais très dynamique au demeurant) qu’un smartphone Android avec le codec LDAC. C’est encore plus vrai en liaison filaire USB-C où le casque monte d’un cran en puissance, que ce soit sur des titres compressés ou lossless 24 bits.
Nothing Headphone (1) ProUne bonne qualité d’appels
Les quatre microphones dédiés aux appels sont associés à un système de réduction du bruit ambiant entraîné par IA. Cette technique permet d’isoler plus finement la voix de l’utilisateur. Nothing indique avoir entraîné son système sur 30 millions d’échantillons audio provenant notamment de rues, restaurants et environnements venteux. En pratique, cela fonctionne très bien, avec les limites que l’on connaît : si le bruit environnant est trop complexe et comporte des voix humaines proches, l’interlocuteur peut entendre un léger effet de pompage. Idem pour le vent, dont le Headphone (1) Pro n’est pas totalement protégé.
En bord de mer, il faut parfois se tourner. Reste que globalement, on peut compter sur ce casque pour passer des appels réguliers dans de très bonnes conditions.
Nothing Headphone (1) ProUne autonomie confortable
Nothing annonce jusqu’à 30 heures d’écoute avec l’ANC activée (28 heures en LDAC), et jusqu’à 68 heures sans l’ANC (53 heures en LDAC). La recharge rapide permet de récupérer deux heures d’écoute avec l’ANC (quatre heures sans) en cinq minutes, avec une charge complète en environ deux heures via USB-C.
L’autonomie est donc confortable pour un usage quotidien, même si elle est en léger retrait par rapport au Headphone (1), annoncé à 35 heures avec l’ANC. Trois transducteurs sont plus énergivores qu’un seul, c’est logique.
Nothing Headphone (1) ProPrix et concurrence
Vendu 349 euros en noir ou en blanc, le Nothing Headphone (1) Pro entre dans une zone tarifaire très disputée.
Face à lui, le Sennheiser Momentum 5 Wireless, vendu 399 euros, mise sur une approche plus classique : un unique transducteur de 42 mm, une restitution très neutre et organique, une scène sonore particulièrement large et une excellente maîtrise des transitoires.
Le Sony WH-1000XM6, lancé à 449 euros mais couramment trouvable à moins de 380 euros, constitue lui aussi un concurrent direct, avec une signature assez neutre également et une ANC tout aussi convaincante.
Enfin, le Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2e génération), à 449 euros, joue davantage la carte du confort et de la réduction de bruit, tout en proposant une restitution plus flatteuse, graves et aigus en avant.
Le Nothing Headphone (1), lancé à 299 euros et désormais trouvable à 199 euros, est son concurrent le plus direct.
