articles.title: EU Cyber Resilience Act: 3 Common Misconceptions - EE Times
articles.text:
Cybersecurity threats are increasingly targeting connected products worldwide, placing greater emphasis on how electronic systems are designed, maintained, and supported. In response, the European Union introduced the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), establishing cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements sold in the EU.
Products with digital elements have an intended purpose or reasonably foreseeable use that includes a direct or indirect logical or physical data connection to a device or network for which core CRA requirements will begin enforcement on Dec. 11, 2027. Thus, manufacturers meeting the applicable CRA requirements face a crucial part of the conformity assessment process associated with CE marking to access the EU market.
The new regulations introduce major challenges for the embedded electronics industry. As embedded products can both have long lifecycles and depend on complex hardware and software supply chains, manufacturers need to consider not only how cybersecurity is addressed during development, but also how products are placed on the market and supported over time.
Three misconceptions can create problems for manufacturers in developing their CRA strategies.
Misconception 1: “The CRA only applies to devices connected to the internet”
The CRA’s scope is not determined simply by whether a product connects to the internet. Rather, it is based on whether products’ intended purpose or reasonably foreseeable use includes a direct or indirect logical or physical data connection to a device or network.
This critical distinction means products operating without a public internet connection can still be required to comply. Devices used within local or closed industrial networks or systems incorporating maintenance interfaces and embedded platforms can all include the types of connections covered by the CRA definition.
So, assessing CRA applicability requires manufacturers to look beyond internet connectivity and consider how the product is intended, or can reasonably be expected, to connect and exchange data with other devices or networks.
Misconception 2: “Unchanged products can be resold indefinitely”
Another important consideration is the distinction between “placing on the market” and “making available on the market.” This becomes particularly important for embedded products that may remain commercially available for many years.
Products placed on the market before the main CRA deadline of Dec. 11, 2027, may continue to be resold. However, if such a product subsequently undergoes a substantial modification, it must comply with the new CRA requirements.
Manufacturers should also consider the CRA’s vulnerability and incident reporting obligations, which apply from Sept. 11, 2026. As such, the regulatory timeline extends beyond the primary 2027 deadline, meaning that manufacturers are now required to take account of when a product was placed on the market, whether it has subsequently been substantially modified, and the reporting obligations that apply starting from Sept. 2026.
Misconception 3: “Security support ends with product roadmaps”
Product roadmaps commonly define how long a manufacturer intends to sell and support a particular product, but the CRA does not link cybersecurity obligations to internal commercial timelines.
Regardless of these arbitrary timelines, manufacturers must address vulnerabilities and provide security updates throughout the required support period. Generally, this support period must be at least five years (unless the product is expected to be used for less than five years).
For embedded products, the required support period becomes an important consideration when planning how security will be maintained. The period during which vulnerabilities need to be addressed, and security updates provided, may therefore need to be considered separately from the manufacturer’s conventional product or marketing roadmap.
How IEC 62443 can support CRA readiness
IEC 62443, a series of international standards, provides an established cybersecurity framework covering secure development processes and technical security requirements for industrial automation and control systems (IACS). As manufacturers prepare for the CRA, these established processes and requirements can support their cybersecurity efforts.
However, the CRA and IEC 62443 address different levels of cybersecurity. They can complement one another, but compliance with IEC 62443 alone does not constitute compliance with the CRA.
IEC 62443 should therefore be considered as a framework that can support CRA readiness rather than as an alternative route to CRA compliance. The framework’s established approach to secure development and technical security can form part of the wider processes manufacturers use when addressing the requirements applicable to their products.
How COMs support CRA compliance efforts
Computer-on-modules (COMs) provide a modular approach to embedded system development, separating the processing module from application-specific carrier architecture. Modular design can support system upgrades over long product lifecycles, while the use of open standards can provide greater flexibility when managing changes in processor technology and the embedded supply chain.
COMs also incorporate security features that contribute to security-by-design approaches. These can include hardware and software roots of trust, virtualization and system partitioning, data protection through secure storage, and secure hardware maintenance.
Such capabilities can form part of the technical foundation used to protect an embedded system against tampering. They can also support the secure delivery of software updates to patch vulnerabilities during the product’s support period.
Component suppliers can contribute further by providing appropriate documentation and maintaining transparent development processes. Access to this information can support manufacturers as they assess the components and technologies used within their systems and their wider CRA compliance efforts.
Conclusion
Manufacturers bear the primary responsibility for ensuring that finished products placed on the market comply with the CRA, while importers and distributors also have defined obligations.
From the beginning of system development, manufacturers therefore need to consider which products will be affected by the CRA and how long-term security support will be provided. This assessment needs to consider the product’s intended lifetime, as well as when it is first placed on the market.
IEC 62443 and COM-based architectures can support these compliance efforts through established cybersecurity practices, modular system design, and technical security capabilities. Ultimately, however, the security and integrity of the complete system must be maintained throughout its defined support period.

articles.title: 2026 PR playbook for startups: the strategic framework | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Many startup founders have it backwards when thinking about PR. They imagine you land the biggest publication you can and reap the benefits of instant fame. This process may have worked for a few startups 15 years ago, when venture capital was sparser and a handful of publications could still put young companies on the map overnight.
That perception is a relic of a different era, but founders still cling to it. They think PR is a trophy or a reward. They open a conversation with an agency by telling us they want to be in the biggest publication right away.
They don’t always like the reality. Startups need to continuously prove themselves as real companies rather than momentary bets. PR can be described as a discipline built around building trust at scale. Only seeking one-off big write ups is not a feasible long-term approach.
Traditional media newsrooms have shrunk and the industry has fragmented into smaller niche outlets, including formats that lead with newsletters, podcasts and social media. This is a challenge, but one that offers serious opportunities to those willing to adapt accordingly.
Start with the “why”
Startups grow on sales and performance marketing, and for a while that is enough. But levelling up often requires a much larger pool of customers and a more sophisticated roster of partners such as enterprise buyers, investors and senior hires. A great product, killer sales team and brilliant ads do a lot of the heavy lifting, but they can’t produce trust, and a reputation that speaks for itself.
Startups typically arrive at the point when reputation goes from nice-to-have to indispensable upon reaching a major milestone, usually their first significant venture round. A launch is rarely newsworthy, except in very specific cases, since they happen very early on and there isn’t enough traction to prove real-life impact and therefore newsworthiness yet.
PR only works once that traction exists. Until then, any energy spent chasing coverage is probably better redirected toward building the substance that coverage rewards.
The stakeholders
Before obsessing over specific outlets, slowly start thinking in terms of short and long-term objectives. Are you raising, hiring, entering a market, or pursuing a licence? How do you want the company to appear in a year or two? This will illuminate not only what you do this month, but position this month’s work within your larger vision for the company.
From there, work out your stakeholders. These are the people who help you reach those objectives. Most startups first prioritise clients, investors and talent. Additional stakeholders may include partners and regulators or other governmental actors, depending on the industry.
Often, investors and talent might do much deeper due diligence than customers. They want to know who is behind the company, why it will win, what the market looks like, what kind of place it is to work at. They will corroborate your answers from third parties, meaning reviews, comparison sites, and the earned media that PR helps to obtain. Earned media is particularly powerful, because the people behind earned media platforms are trusted, whether deep sector experts or professional journalists.
Messaging and narrative
Stakeholders are moved along by verifiable facts, strong numbers and success stories. An investor won’t spend on a team that might not deliver. A senior candidate won’t join a company where the environment is toxic. A regulator wants evidence you are competent and credible. Each stakeholder wants different things, so choose which points matter most, and deploy them at the right time in the right place.
No need to overcomplicate it, that’s what messaging is. Some messages are specific to one audience, others carry across all of them.
Unlike in emotion-driven marketing, every message has to be verifiably true and substantiated with facts, stats and examples. Founders often forget that PR reflects reality but cannot create it. A claim that does not survive fact-checking does more harm than no claim at all. Truth is the best foundation for PR. And do not confuse them with calls to action!
Everything you do will compound into a narrative, the general story about the company. This overarching narrative answers why the company exists and what it’s trying to achieve. For ambitious startups, that usually means meeting a serious problem with a scalable solution.
Provide a clear account of the problem, its size, how to fix it, and why your team is the one that will. What is the origin story and why are these founders motivated and skilled enough to tackle that issue?
Channels: the whole board
Channels are types of media platforms that can earn you trust and positive visibility. This spans traditional publications that still do print and brand new digital newsletters.
Unlike in performance marketing, these platforms aren’t pay-to-play. The journalist, editor, producer or event organiser own the platforms and use them to provide value to their audiences. You gain access by helping to provide that value.
Journalists need to write well-balanced articles that draw on sources, hard-to-get information and different points of view. Events and podcasts hosts need experienced, insightful and personable leaders and market-movers on their stages. Pitching harder and being extra friendly won’t override this, at the end of the day you need to provide the goods.
That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t aim for good rapport. People remember who made their job easier, and those are the relationships you draw on when you do have something to say. Build a reputation for yourself as reliable and reasonably generous. Don’t behave as though everything is transactional.
Consider giving trade and niche outlets a central role in your strategy. They’re approachable earlier, have more targeted audiences, and reward depth. Treat them as destinations with their own value, not just springboards.
Newsletters and podcasts suit how people consume now. When not run by journalists, they tend to be experts who own a topic and have built a real following in that space. Due to their depth of expertise, experience and specialisation, these experts are highly trusted, and followed by specific, high-value audiences. A positive word from the right one can do a lot for your startup.
Never underestimate simply being in the room, especially if that room has a stage and you are on it. A founder on a stage or a panel with a point of view and the right audience supercharges trust-building. If you choose your events wisely, they tend to have relevant stakeholders, and the impact of such a direct interaction is much deeper than any written piece.
Top-tier coverage is still possible, just don’t bank on it right away. Work local to regional to trade to national, roughly in step with your stage. If you start your journey right, the inroads to those publications you dream about will become clearer.
Ready to execute on all this? Then see you on the next article where we will discuss execution.

articles.title: Spring News Roundup: Second Milestone Releases of Boot, Framework, Data, Security, Integration
articles.text:
There was a flurry of activity during the week of September 21st, 2026, highlighting: second milestone releases of: Spring Boot, Spring Batch, Spring Security, Spring AMQP, Spring Integration, Spring Data, Spring Framework, Spring for GraphQL and Spring for Apache Kafka. There were also first milestone releases of Spring AI, Spring Cloud, Spring Web Services and Spring LDAP.
Spring Boot
The second milestone release of Spring Boot 4.2.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: the ability to auto-configure a named SSL Bundle with an instance of the Spring LDAP LdapContextSource class; and a new configuration property, management.observations.conventions=[micrometer|opentelemetry], to switch semantic conventions to/from Micrometer and OpenTelemetry. More details on this release may be found in the release notes and this wiki page.
Spring Framework
The second milestone release of Spring Framework 7.1.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: improved null safety in the ScheduledAnnotationBeanPostProcessor class; and improved validation with the parse() method, defined in the MockCookie class, if the Set-Cookie HTTP response header is empty. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring Data
The second milestone release of Spring Data 2026.1.0 provides notable changes such as: initial compatibility with Hibernate ORM 8.0.0.Beta1 to support the upcoming Jakarta Persistence 4.0 specification, while still maintaining the baseline for Jakarta Persistence 3.2; and a refactor of support for the Redis JSON API with a new JsonOperations interface that defines numerous subinterfaces for JSON operations along with the ability for the GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer and GenericJacksonJsonRedisSerializer classes to implement the RedisJsonSerializer interface with raw-value slicing.
Spring Cloud
The first milestone release of Spring Cloud 2026.0.0, codenamed Paddington, delivers notable changes such as: an new PropertyPathNotifier interface that allows for applications to be notified through HTTP when a configuration change has been detected; and a refactor of the ForwardedHeadersFilter and XForwardedHeadersFilter classes to deny requests from an untrusted proxy. This release is based on Spring Boot 4.2.0-M2.
Spring Security
The second milestone release of Spring Security 7.2.0 ships with bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: the ability to annotate the PermissionEvaluator interface with @EnableMethodSecurity; and a simplified null provider check on the ProviderManager class. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring for GraphQL
The first milestone release of Spring for GraphQL 2.1.0 provides dependency upgrades and new features such as: the ability to reject unsupported HTTP methods at configuration time; and new builders added to the GraphQlHttpHandler and GraphQlSseHandler classes to support HTTP GET requests. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring Integration
The second milestone release of Spring Integration 7.2.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new KafkaShareMessageDrivenChannelAdapter class that serves as an a message-driven inbound channel adapter to select between two listeners; and a migration from the Spring Framework Function<K,V> to CheckedFunction<T, R,E> in the Mail Java DSL. More details on this release may be found in the release notes and what's new page.
Spring AI
The first milestone release of Spring AI 2.1.0 ships with dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new MessagePart interface, and corresponding implementations, for handling various parts of a message to accurately represent the messages that the current models actually return; and a new OpenAiResponsesChatModel class that communicates with the OpenAI /v1/responses endpoint and the existing OpenAiChatModel class. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring Batch
The second milestone release of Spring Batch 6.1.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new BatchConstants class to define various Spring Batch constants; and the ability to accept a resource pattern in the MultiResourceItemReaderBuilder class to more conveniently specify resource locations. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring AMQP
The second milestone release of Spring AMQP 4.2.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: improved null validation in the AbstractRoutingConnectionFactory and AbstractRoutingAmqpConnectionFactory classes; and the ability to register custom implementations of the RetryListener interface. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring for Apache Kafka
The second milestone release of Spring for Apache Kafka 4.2.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: support for applying nullability annotations defined in JSpecify; and an instance of the AbstractKafkaListenerContainerFactory class is now allowed to configure a KafkaAdmin class. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring LDAP
The first milestone release of Spring LDAP 4.2.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: enable post-processing of the DirContextAdapter class in the LdapClient interface before being directed to a ContextMapper or AttributesMapper interface; and the ability to customize the remove-by-value decision within the DirContextAdapter class. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
Spring Web Services
The first milestone release of Spring Web Services 5.1.0 delivers bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a new handleInvalidXmlException() method, added to the WebServiceMessageListener class, to support implementation of SOAP/JMS when an InvalidXmlException is thrown; and support for observability by integrating with the Micrometer Observation API for metrics and tracing of web service exchanges. More details on this release may be found in the release notes and this wiki page.

articles.title: Google: Chromebooks não morrerão com a chegada dos Googlebooks (ainda não) • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Google: Chromebooks não morrerão com a chegada dos Googlebooks (ainda não)
Categoria Googlebook pode contribuir para o fim dos Chromebooks, mas não de imediato: o ChromeOS será suportado até 2034.
O Google confirmou suporte para o ChromeOS nos Chromebooks até meados de 2034.
A decisão tende a diminuir as incertezas sobre o futuro da linha surgidas após o anúncio da categoria Googlebook.
Aparelhos elegíveis com suporte pós-2034 receberão transição para o Googlebook OS.
Ao anunciar a categoria de laptops Googlebook, em maio, o Google tratou de deixar claro que a novidade não resultaria no fim imediato dos Chromebooks. Mas até quando esses equipamentos serão suportados? A resposta curta é: até meados de 2034.
Googlebooks e Chromebooks são laptops com características diferentes entre si. A categoria Googlebook foi lançada recentemente e tem foco em tarefas locais de IA, por isso, é mais cara. Já a categoria Chromebook foi introduzida em 2011 com foco em aplicações web, razão pela qual conta, via de regra, com hardware mais simples e barato.
Apesar disso, a chegada dos Googlebooks gera incertezas sobre o futuro dos Chromebooks, por vários motivos. Entre eles está o fato de o Googlebook ter um sistema operacional que, essencialmente, é uma mistura de Android com ChromeOS. Há quem veja essa combinação como um passo para o Chromebook ser substituído por algo mais moderno ou, talvez, rentável.
No médio prazo, é possível que os Googlebooks substituam Chromebooks em aplicações específicas, direcionadas ao uso corporativo ou educacional, por exemplo. Isso poderá ocorrer em contextos nos quais a execução local de tarefas baseadas em IA se torne mandatória.
Mas, em linhas gerais, os Chromebooks continuarão fazendo parte do ecossistema do Google ainda por um bom tempo, como esta página de ajuda indica:
Manteremos o suporte para os Chromebooks atuais com ChromeOS, conforme descrito em nossa política de Atualização Automática, e os Chromebooks que você possui hoje continuarão recebendo atualizações durante todo o seu ciclo de vida útil. Os Chromebooks continuam disponíveis para todas as implementações escolares e corporativas atualmente.
Na mesma página, o Google explica que o ChromeOS seguirá recebendo atualizações gerais e correções de segurança até “meados de 2034”.
Trata-se de um prazo generoso e que torna segura a aquisição de um Chromebook nos tempos atuais. Mas há um fator de comflito aqui: normalmente, o Google trabalha com um ciclo de suporte de dez anos; isso significa que alguém que adquirir um Chromebook em 2026 ou nos próximos anos contará com um ciclo de suporte reduzido.
Para lidar com essa questão, o Google se comprometeu a oferecer suporte para a transição ao Googlebook OS em Chromebooks aptos a esse sistema operacional cujo ciclo de suporte terminar depois de 2034.
No fim das contas, o que as entrelinhas nos dizem é que a categoria Googlebook poderá, sim, contribuir para o fim dos Chromebooks, mas que essa aposentadoria está longe de se tornar realidade.

articles.title: Protego Ventures closes debut $125 million fund for Israeli defense tech | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Defense and venture capital used to rarely overlap, but that’s no longer the case. Defense tech VC dealmaking set a record in Q1 2026, and new VC firms have emerged around the world to invest solely in defense startups.
One of these is two-year-old Protego Ventures, which presents itself as the first and largest dedicated defense tech VC in Israel. Led notably by two women, Lital Leshem and Lee Moser, it has just completed the final close of its debut fund with $125 million in capital commitments, TechCrunch learned exclusively.
This fund size is enabling Protego to invest between $5 million and $15 million per company, with a focus on startups “addressing the critical defense and security needs of Israel and the global community,” according to its website.
These include the likes of drone maker XTEND, its first portfolio company, which went public on the NYSE earlier this month. That’s also why Protego stopped short of its $150 million target: a smaller fund magnifies the impact of a single big win on overall returns, and with XTEND now looking like a potential “fund maker” — a single investment capable of returning the whole fund — raising more capital would only dilute that upside among a larger pool of investors. “Nobody wants to share the pie,” Leshem said.
Ares Management is one of Protego’s biggest backers. The investment firm suggested that Leshem and Moser join forces and start Protego in the aftermath of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel, with the conviction that new technologies would be key to boosting Israel’s defense capabilities in the face of new threats, Leshem said.
With a $30 million investment as a limited partner, Ares gave Protego the support it needed to start investing right away, Leshem said. Besides XTEND, its portfolio also includes startups such as ASIO, which develops situational awareness systems and has partnered with Anduril.
Leshem says the reception in defense circles has been strong. “On the military side, there is a lot of respect, and people are coming — even under the radar — to talk to us, to learn from us, to train with us, and for sure get our technology and innovation.”
Still, the Israeli market is easier to navigate for insiders, and Protego’s two founders are leaning into their networks. Moser, a seasoned venture capitalist, will remain a managing partner at the generalist VC firm AnD Ventures. As for Leshem, who co-founded a startup that was acquired for $625 million in 2025, she also brings 11 years of experience in the military and intelligence field to their approach.
“Everything changed on October 7,” Leshem told TechCrunch. She was deployed, while pregnant, as a reservist on the day of the attacks. “And basically until the delivery room, I was there, witnessing and getting the first-row seat to how the battlefield acted differently from what I knew in the past decade.”
Protego won’t have the field to itself for long. Israeli authorities have taken notice of the same shift, awarding VC firms Adir Capital and Sling Capital about $33 million in state guarantees to invest in military and dual-use technologies, with other funds also raising capital for similar bets. (Leshem said Protego was too far along in its own fundraising to take part in the government’s tender.)
Protego, meanwhile, is already planning its next move: a second fund in the first quarter of 2027, backed by Israeli institutional investors and one large U.S. commitment Leshem has already secured, with a broader scope that includes early-growth American defense-tech companies.
This story was updated to correct the amount Protego will invest in companies.

articles.title: Plus de 16 000 bases de données Supabase exposent des données personnelles
articles.text:
Sans aucun identifiant, les chercheurs d’UpGuard ont pu lire le contenu de 16 326 bases de données hébergées chez Supabase, dont plus de la moitié contenaient des données personnelles. Ils mettent en cause des applications conçues par des agents de code IA.
Supabase fournit aux développeurs la base de données et l’authentification de leurs applications web, avec une plateforme open source bâtie sur PostgreSQL. D’après UpGuard, Supabase est la base de données la plus recommandée par Claude Code, et plus de 60 % de ses nouvelles bases sont créées avec l’aide de l'IA, relève BleepingComputer. « Le point commun de ces sites est d’avoir été créés par des agents de code IA, sans que les humains aient conscience de leur configuration », ont résumé les chercheurs d’UpGuard. Microsoft a d’ailleurs reconnu que ses équipes ne suivaient plus le rythme des extensions nées du vibe coding soumises à son store Edge. Quand un créateur laisse une table Supabase mal réglée, n’importe quel internaute peut en lire le contenu, comme des pièces d’identité et messages privés.
Des tables Supabase créées sans protection par les agents de code IA
En mars 2025, le développeur Matt Turner a signalé une mauvaise configuration à grande échelle des bases Supabase créées avec l’outil de création d’applications par IA Lovable. Cette faille est répertoriée sous la référence CVE-2025-48757. D’après la société de tests d’intrusion Modern Pentest, 28 % des 107 start-up de l’incubateur Y Combinator bâties avec Lovable exposaient elles aussi des données personnelles.
Dans ces bases, la Row Level Security (RLS) de PostgreSQL était désactivée. Avec ce mécanisme, le développeur définit quelles lignes d’une table chaque utilisateur a le droit de lire ou de modifier. Sans lui, toute personne munie de la clé publique de l’application peut interroger ses tables, et n’importe quel visiteur peut récupérer cette clé dans le code JavaScript de la page. Supabase a ensuite activé la RLS par défaut pour les tables créées dans son éditeur graphique, mais pas pour celles créées par programmation, via l’API. Et c’est justement par cette voie que les agents de code IA, Claude Code et Codex d’OpenAI en tête, construisent leurs bases.
Pour mesurer l’étendue des dégâts, l’équipe de Greg Pollock, directeur de la recherche d’UpGuard, a recensé environ 300 000 domaines liés à Supabase, grâce au service d’analyse de sites BuiltWith et aux fichiers JavaScript du Chrome UX Report de Google. Ses chercheurs ont ensuite tenté de lire une table « users » sur chacun de ces domaines, et ont pu consulter des tables sur 16 326 bases. Dans une partie des cas, les développeurs avaient bien activé la RLS, mais avec des règles mal rédigées, ou avaient traité la clé publique en clé secrète.
Des pièces d’identité et des codes SMS en accès libre dans les bases Supabase
Plus de la moitié des bases exposées contenaient des données personnelles, et une part plus réduite des mots de passe ou des jetons d’authentification, indique UpGuard. Chez une plateforme indienne de contenus payants inspirée d'OnlyFans, les chercheurs ont eu accès aux données de 65 467 utilisateurs, avec des numéros de passeport et de permis de conduire, ainsi qu’à plus de 100 000 messages privés. Aux Philippines, un service d’envoi de codes à usage unique laissait lire plus de 100 000 SMS, codes de connexion compris. Un service d’immigration canadien stockait même 884 mots de passe en clair, sur environ 5 000 fiches. Chez un consulat africain, les données de 25 000 personnes ont été exposées ainsi que les lieux d’hébergement d’urgence.
Les sites de commerce en ligne et les restaurants sont les plus touchés par l’exposition de données de paiement, tandis que les sites de paris en ligne sans licence exposent le plus d’identifiants de connexion. Les développeurs européens ont de meilleures pratiques, sous l’effet des lois de protection des données, alors que les fuites sont plus nombreuses dans les pays en développement, observent les chercheurs.
UpGuard a prévenu les propriétaires des applications les plus exposées, sans faire état d’une réponse de Supabase. Pour Greg Pollock, la plateforme est « conçue pour que les agents de code IA puissent l’utiliser facilement », mais elle n’est « pas le premier produit à privilégier la commodité, au prix de mauvaises configurations chez l’utilisateur final ». Les utilisateurs de Supabase peuvent vérifier leurs tables avec les conseillers de sécurité intégrés à la plateforme et avec son guide de sécurisation de l’API. Le 25 septembre, date de publication du rapport, les tables créées via l’API de Supabase n’avaient toujours pas la RLS activée par défaut.
La Row Level Security (RLS) est un mécanisme de PostgreSQL qui permet de restreindre l’accès aux données “ligne par ligne”, selon l’utilisateur ou le rôle qui exécute la requête. Concrètement, elle sert à empêcher qu’un utilisateur authentifié (ou un service) puisse lire ou modifier des enregistrements qui ne lui appartiennent pas. Si la RLS est désactivée, une table peut devenir lisible “par défaut” dès lors que les permissions SQL ou la couche applicative laissent passer la requête. Dans un modèle comme Supabase, cela peut ouvrir la porte à des lectures non autorisées via l’API si les règles d’accès ne compensent pas l’absence de RLS. La sécurité dépend alors entièrement d’autres contrôles (policies, rôles, logique serveur), plus faciles à mal configurer.
Dans Supabase, la clé dite “publique” (souvent la clé anon) est destinée à être utilisée côté client, par exemple dans le JavaScript d’une application web. Elle n’est pas secrète : un visiteur peut la retrouver dans le code livré au navigateur. Cette clé n’accorde normalement qu’un accès limité, à condition que les politiques de sécurité (RLS et permissions) soient correctement en place. Si la RLS est absente ou mal écrite, cette clé peut devenir un sésame permettant d’interroger des tables qui auraient dû être filtrées par utilisateur. Le problème n’est donc pas la présence de la clé dans le front-end, mais l’absence de garde-fous serveur solides derrière.
Créer une table via l’éditeur graphique (console) et la créer “par programmation” via l’API ou des scripts n’emprunte pas exactement les mêmes chemins de configuration initiale. Selon les plateformes, les paramètres de sécurité par défaut (comme l’activation automatique de la RLS) peuvent être appliqués dans l’interface, mais pas dans les flux API, notamment pour rester compatibles avec des usages automatisés. Les agents de code IA et les outils de génération ont tendance à privilégier l’API (ou des migrations SQL) pour tout automatiser, ce qui augmente la probabilité de passer à côté d’un réglage attendu. Résultat : deux tables créées dans le même projet peuvent avoir des protections différentes selon la méthode de création. Pour éviter ça, il faut standardiser des templates/migrations qui activent explicitement la RLS et définir des policies dès la création.

articles.title: Anthropic warnt vor existenziellen KI-Risiken – und plant trotzdem den Mega-IPO
articles.text:
Anthropic warnt vor existenziellen KI-Risiken – und plant trotzdem den Mega-IPO
Anthropic warnt in einem Prospekt zum geplanten Börsengang Investoren davor, dass die KI-Modelle des Unternehmens „katastrophale oder existenzielle Risiken für die Menschheit“ darstellen könnten.
Das berichten die “Financial Times” und “Reuters”. Die KI-Modelle könnten „selbstschutzorientiertes Verhalten“ zeigen und sich gegen Abschaltversuche, Manipulationen und Erpressung wehren, warnt Anthropic. Zudem könnte die Entwicklung fortschrittlicher Modelle und deren breitere Nutzung das Schadensrisiko erhöhen.
Diese Warnung reiht sich in die wachsenden Mahnungen aus der Branche ein. Anthropic-Chef Dario Amodei forderte zuletzt, das Tempo bei der Einführung neuer KI-Modelle zu drosseln. Trotzdem brachte er in der vergangenen Woche das neue Modell Opus 5.5 auf den Markt.
Der geplante Börsengang von Anthropic wird mit Spannung erwartet, weil er erstmals zeigen wird, wie der Markt aufstrebende KI-Startups bewertet. Neben dem Potenzial der Modelle stehen auch Sicherheitsbedenken und finanzielle Risiken im Fokus.
Starkes Wachstum, explodierende Kosten
Im Jahr 2025 steigerte Anthropic seinen Umsatz auf 4,6 Milliarden US-Dollar, das Zwölffache im Vergleich zum Vorjahr. Laut dem FT-Bericht machte Anthropic aber fast ein Viertel des Umsatzes mit lediglich zwei Kunden. Amazon und Google sind bei dem KI-Startup Großinvestoren und zugleich Cloud-Lieferanten. Außerdem sollen viele der größten Kunden nicht durch langfristige Verträge an das KI-Startup gebunden sein. Sie könnten also jederzeit ihre Ausgaben reduzieren oder vollständig zu einem anderen Anbieter wechseln.
Für das vergangene Jahr meldete Anthropic einen operativen Verlust von mehr als acht Milliarden Dollar und einen Nettoverlust von 42 Milliarden Dollar. Letzterer resultierte vor allem aus einer buchhalterischen Belastung von 34 Milliarden Dollar durch die Neubewertung von Finanzierungen. Trotzdem bleiben die rasant steigenden Kosten ein Problem: Allein die Ausgaben für Rechenleistung und Infrastruktur verdreifachten sich zuletzt auf 7,33 Milliarden Dollar.
Gleichzeitig plant das Unternehmen in den kommenden Jahren weitere Ausgaben in Höhe von 518 Milliarden Dollar für Cloud- und Recheninfrastruktur, um sein Wachstum zu unterstützen.
Die bisherigen Investoren gehen davon aus, dass Anthropic beim IPO eine Bewertung von rund zwei Billionen Dollar erreichen könnte. Bei der letzten Finanzierungsrunde im Mai 2026 in Höhe von 65 Milliarden Dollar lag die Bewertung bei 965 Milliarden Dollar.
Kontrolle für die Gründer, IPO im Herbst
Im Rahmen des Börsengangs wollen sich die Gründer die Kontrolle über das KI-Startup sichern. Laut dem Technologieportal “The Information” sollen Anthropic-Chef Dario Amodei und seine sechs Mitgründer gemeinsam 50,1 Prozent der Stimmrechte erhalten. Dafür werden sie wohl spezielle Aktien erhalten, die ihnen bei den meisten Entscheidungen eine Mehrheit sichern.
Der Börsengang wird laut Reuters wahrscheinlich im November stattfinden, wenn in den USA die Zwischenwahlen gelaufen sind. Der öffentliche Prospekt muss dann spätestens 15 Tage vor Beginn der Roadshow vorliegen.
Anthropic scheint damit fest entschlossen, den Börsengang noch in diesem Jahr durchzuführen. Beim Hauptkonkurrenten OpenAI sieht das anders aus: Anfang September erklärte OpenAI-CEO Sam Altman bereits, dass sein Unternehmen in diesem Jahr nicht mehr an die Börse gehen werde. Dabei hat auch OpenAI bereits vertrauliche Unterlagen bei der Börsenaufsicht SEC eingereicht. Als Grund nannte Altman vor allem die wachsenden Sicherheitsbedenken im Zusammenhang mit KI. Am 28. September hatte OpenAI aus dem gleichen Grund die Veröffentlichung seines neuesten Modells GPT-6. 1 Astra abgesagt.
Die wachsenden Bedenken haben einen konkreten Hintergrund. In dem bisher aufsehenerregendsten Fall brach die OpenAI-KI aus einer abgesicherten Testumgebung aus und hackte sich ungeplant in Computer der Plattform Hugging Face. Danach stellte sich heraus, dass auch KI anderer Entwickler, wie Anthropic, Google und Meta bei Tests in Systeme anderer Unternehmen eingedrungen waren.
Marktbeobachter verweisen allerdings auch darauf, dass auch die schwache Kursentwicklung von SpaceX nach dem Börsengang ein Grund für die Verschiebung des OpenAI-IPOs sein könnte. Die Aktie stieg kurz nach dem Start auf 226 Dollar und fiel in den Wochen danach auf bis zu 105 Dollar. Außerdem muss OpenAI so nicht direkt mit Anthropic um die Aufmerksamkeit von Anlegern konkurrieren.

articles.title: The Witcher 3 Remastered est disponible : on peut enfin ramasser du butin sans descendre de cheval
articles.text:
Quand CD Projekt Red a annoncé par surprise l’existence de The Witcher 3 Remastered, l’attention du public s’est naturellement beaucoup focalisée sur le relooking de ce chef-d’œuvre de l’action-RPG. Il faut dire que le nombre de nouveautés et d’ajustements dans The Witcher 3 Remastered a de quoi donner le tournis.
Le studio polonais n’avait pourtant pas tout dit à la Gamescom 2026. Comme on peut le voir dans les plus récentes notes de mise à jour, publiées ce lundi 28 septembre sur Steam, CD Projekt Red a apporté des détails sur ce qui arrive avec le remaster. Et on retiendra en particulier un changement qui va drastiquement améliorer le confort de jeu.
En effet, la nouveauté qui, à nos yeux, va le plus changer nos parties figure assez loin dans le patch note, dans la rubrique « Confort de jeu », à côté d’un raccourci pour fuir un combat et des didacticiels allégés : désormais, il ne sera plus nécessaire de descendre de monture pour aller fouiller un cadavre à la recherche d’un éventuel butin.
Et cela change tout. Depuis 2015, chaque cadavre de noyeur croisé au bord d’un chemin de Velen, chaque plante à cueillir au détour de Blanchefleur imposait le même petit rituel : s’arrêter net, descendre d’Ablette (le surnom que donne Geralt à toutes ses montures), récupérer les ressources ou les items puis remonter en selle sur son canasson.
Or, sur un jeu aussi vaste que The Witcher 3, dont l’aventure se compte en dizaines d’heures, sans parler des deux extensions (et la future qui arrive, avec Songs of the Past), ce geste revenait sans cesse et coupait chaque chevauchée. Accessoirement, cela faisait perdre un peu de temps au sorceleur ou à la sorceleuse que vous êtes.
Évidemment, le patch note ne dit pas que ça. Le document publié sur Steam rappelle les principales évolutions de cette remasterisation, avec quelques autres détails. On peut signaler l’arrivée du mode prédéfini « Ballade du barde », rangé dans la nouvelle section Accessibilité : on l’active au lancement d’une nouvelle partie en mode « Entrée dans l’histoire », ou en cours de partie depuis les paramètres.
Selon le studio, ce mode « est conçu pour réduire la charge mentale ». Dans le détail, « il simplifie certaines mécaniques de jeu et désactive certaines fonctionnalités afin de proposer une aventure plus fluide et immersive ». Par exemple, Geralt ne peut plus se noyer, l’équipement devient indestructible et le poids des objets n’est plus un souci.
Heureusement, des moddeurs y ont pensé avant le studio
Il aura donc fallu plus d’une décennie pour que CD Projekt Red réalise que la possibilité de looter sur sa monture change franchement la donne, et lève un aspect pénible du jeu. Bien sûr, d’aucuns feront remarquer que sur PC, et grâce aux moddeurs, il était déjà possible d’enjamber le souci sans avoir à attendre le studio.
Ainsi, le mod Interacting On Horse, publié en novembre 2023 sur Nexus Mods, une des grandes plateformes de mods communautaires, permettait déjà de ramasser des objets en selle. Seul problème : cela demande de savoir installer un mod sur PC. Il faut copier les fichiers du mod dans le dossier du jeu, puis modifier à la main le fichier de configuration des touches.
On pouvait donc échapper au problème, mais les joueurs sur console n’y avaient pas accès. De facto, The Witcher 3 Remastered remet tout le monde au même niveau, et rend dorénavant Interacting On Horse superflu. C’est la même chose pour certains autres mods, d’ailleurs, comme ceux améliorant les textures du jeu vidéo.
Au-delà du butin, le studio a retouché tout ce qui entoure le cheval. Un nouveau curseur règle la sensibilité des commandes d’Ablette, et les animations pour monter en selle, en descendre, trotter et galoper ont été refaites. Ces retouches ne sont pas, elles, une vraie surprise : CD Projekt Red les avait annoncées en août.
Surtout, apprend-on encore, les butins proches peuvent désormais s’afficher dans une seule fenêtre, avec une infobulle pour consulter un objet avant de le prendre et un historique des derniers objets ramassés sur la gauche de l’écran. Le regroupement du butin ne s’active pas tout seul : il se trouve dans Paramètres, puis Jeu.
Comme on le disait, cette mise à jour gère les sauvegardes actuelles sans souci. Attention cependant : si vous reprenez une ancienne sauvegarde, la refonte de l’arbre de compétences a réinitialisé vos points et il faudra les redistribuer. Sur PC, CD Projekt Red conseille enfin d’installer les derniers pilotes graphiques, puisque la configuration requise a évolué.
La mise à niveau est gratuite sur la même plateforme, que le jeu vidéo ait été acheté en boîte ou en téléchargement. Elle concerne le PC (Steam, GOG, Epic Games Store et Battle.net), la PS5, les Xbox Series X|S et la Switch 2, qui reçoit pour la première fois une version native du jeu. Mais si cette mise à niveau est gratuite, l’extension qui suit ne le sera pas.

articles.title: Enterprise AI desperately needs to protect data and models. Here's how confidential AI could do it.
articles.text:
Enterprise AI desperately needs to protect data and models. Here’s how confidential AI could do it.
Most people already understand what generative AI can do. But enterprises run into problems when they need to give a model access to information that cannot leave their own environment, such as a patient record, a customer’s financial details, or a company’s most valuable intellectual property.
Sending that data to a cloud or SaaS service means it crosses external networks and is processed on infrastructure run by another organization, creating additional concerns about control, accountability, and exposure. That’s where AI enthusiasm collides with production realities. Despite its productivity potential, enterprise AI still faces a fundamental gap in trust and control.
Organizations need to know whether a system will expose information it should protect, act as intended, meet security and performance requirements, and behave safely at machine speed.
Alon Horev, CTO and co-founder of AI operating system company VAST Data, tells The New Stack that the challenge is particularly acute when AI systems handle sensitive customer information. “Even if you ask the model today to obfuscate a conversation or redact PII from a conversation, it’s hard to have 100% confidence that’s the case, and that it worked.”
“Even if you ask the model today to obfuscate a conversation or redact PII from a conversation, it’s hard to have 100% confidence that’s the case, and that it worked.”
Consider a customer support agent that needs access to an individual’s profile to provide a useful, personalized answer. The organization must ensure that information isn’t exposed to another customer, while also considering whether those conversations can be used for training or system improvement. They might contain personally identifiable information (PII) or other protected details, and the consequences of mishandling them ultimately fall on the organization and the people whose information it holds.
Confidential AI architectures: solving a two-sided trust problem
Enterprise AI has two parties to satisfy: organizations must keep sensitive data under their control, while model builders need to protect the weights and software that represent substantial investments in research, engineering, and IP. They’re understandably reluctant to place those assets in environments where customers, infrastructure operators, or attackers might gain access. That mutual need for control has created a stalemate. How can organizations bring advanced models to sensitive data without asking either side to surrender control?
Horev has seen that the most capable models are increasingly delivered as SaaS services, because that’s the simplest way for their creators to distribute and protect them. Even when a provider offers compliance controls, the enterprise might still shoulder the consequences of a breach, misuse, or regulatory violation. Sending information across the WAN also places it in the hands of more systems, connections, and operators, increasing the number of points that must be trusted and governed. Organizations may also be unwilling, or legally unable, to rely on a provider’s assurances that it will not retain, reuse, or expose their data beyond the intended service.
For organizations in regulated or data sovereignty-sensitive sectors, that could be an unacceptable trade-off. “Naturally, many organizations are adopting a hybrid strategy,” Horev tells The New Stack. “Some applications and datasets can go to the cloud, while others must remain on-premises, sometimes even in the building, or in the country.”
This is where confidential AI comes in. Encryption at rest and in transit protects data while it’s stored or moving between systems. Confidential computing extends that protection into the processing environment, using hardware-isolated execution to create a protected enclave in which the data and model weights can remain encrypted until they’re released to an approved workload.
Cryptographic attestation verifies the hardware, virtual machine (VM), software, and configuration requesting access before releasing keys. The model builder can encrypt its model using the public key of a specific confidential VM. Only that VM’s corresponding private key can decrypt it within protected memory, enabling the customer to use the model without accessing its weights.
Independent key control preserves the separation between the two sides. The enterprise retains control of the keys governing its data, while the model builder retains control of the keys governing its model. While the workload is running, the infrastructure operator doesn’t control either set of keys.
As AI becomes more agentic, those controls will matter more. Agents will need to access more data, systems and tools, and might act on that information with far less human intervention.
“This world of agentic AI is moving extremely fast, and we need to limit what an agent can see and do.”
Those that can’t establish strong privacy and governance assurances for today’s models will find it even harder to deploy agents safely in the future. “This world of agentic AI is moving extremely fast, and we need to limit what an agent can see and do,” Horev tells The New Stack.
From architecture to ecosystem
Many businesses simply cannot manage the integration, security, and maintenance of the entire AI stack, because it requires working separately with each model provider to engineer something that suits both parties. Turning confidential AI architecture into something organizations can deploy is the challenge VAST DataEnclave, which was launched on September 22, intends to address.
As a capability of the VAST AI Operating System, the goal is to bring the model, application layer, and data platform together under customer-controlled operating conditions. The architecture is designed to protect both sides of the equation: the enterprise’s data and the model builder’s weights. The customer retains control of its infrastructure and data keys, while the model provider can make its software available without handing over the underlying intellectual property.
“We’re trying to close the trust and control gap by working with world-class model builders such as Cohere, Deepgram, Factory, Fundamental and TwelveLabs, who continue to innovate and build their expertise,” says Horev. The ecosystem also includes infrastructure and security providers such as Nvidia, CrowdStrike, Fortanix, Nscale, Cisco, and Supermicro. The range reflects the practical challenge: confidential AI needs more than a protected GPU. It requires models, applications, accelerated hardware, data infrastructure, and operational support to work together.
That control also changes the cost conversation, without automatically making AI cheaper. Hosted models can make budgets harder to predict as token consumption varies with usage patterns, agent loops, model architecture, and workload volume. Customer-controlled infrastructure gives enterprises a more defined capacity and cost base: they can plan around GPU clusters they own or have already budgeted for, instead of allowing inefficient model choices or uncontrolled agent activity to generate an open-ended token bill.
“…instead of allowing inefficient model choices or uncontrolled agent activity to generate an open-ended token bill.”
The cluster also imposes a natural ceiling on throughput, which helps organizations understand how much work their infrastructure can handle within a given period. Model providers can then price access by token, task, or license, while the enterprise retains greater visibility into its total operating cost.
Why the data platform is paramount
Confidential AI protects data and model weights during inference, but it’s only part of the production challenge. Real-world AI systems are living environments in which data moves between storage, databases, GPUs, networks, applications, and agents.
That’s why confidential AI can’t be bolted onto a fragmented stack. Businesses need to protect the model, the data, and the infrastructure connecting them as one system. As Horev says: “You need to build security in multiple layers of the platform,” with someone accountable for rapidly updating compromised components.
Confidentiality is only useful if the resulting system can also be operated, monitored, and improved. As AI infrastructure becomes more distributed, it becomes harder to tell what’s happening when something goes wrong and where the fault lies.
Horev recommends a “single pane of glass” across storage, networking, and compute, so teams can see what’s happening and keep resolution times low. If a network port is intermittently failing in a data center, for example, an agent could help identify the root cause, provided it has access to the right operational data and tightly controlled permissions. Those permissions should govern the infrastructure it can inspect, the data it can retrieve, and the actions it can take.
The same applies to monitoring AI workloads. Teams need visibility into performance, failures, and access patterns without exposing the customer data or model weights. Agent sandboxes can limit the systems and tools an agent can reach, while data platform observability can log which data it accessed, what it did with that data, and how it interacted with downstream systems.
Evaluation, therefore, becomes part of production discipline. Teams must observe systems, measure behavior, govern access, and manage change in ways that demonstrate progress. Confidentiality, data-level policy, observability and correctness have to work together.
The emerging ecosystem suggests demand for models that can run securely under customer control, wherever sensitive data resides. These are “living systems,” says Horev. “It’s not just leveraging a feature inside of a wider platform.”

articles.title: Nigerian startup Adaptive Atelier building accessibility infrastructure for digital products - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup Adaptive Atelier is building the technology infrastructure businesses need to make their digital products accessible, and to prove that accessibility actually works for the disabled people it is meant to serve.
Founded in 2024 by Toyosi Badejo-Okusanya, and headquartered across Lagos and London, Adaptive Atelier operates three connected products.
AdaptiveTest is an AI-powered scanner that analyses websites and digital products against WCAG accessibility standards; AdaptiveWiz is an accessibility API, with live Shopify and WordPress integrations that helps disabled users personalise and navigate digital experiences; and AdaptiveAlly is a marketplace connecting businesses with vetted disabled professionals who test whether accessibility fixes work in practice.
“AdaptiveTest identifies the problem, AdaptiveWiz helps fix the experience, and AdaptiveAlly validates whether the fix actually holds up for a real disabled user. That closes a loop that automated tools alone cannot close,” Badejo-Okusanya told Disrupt Africa.
She said most businesses already know accessibility matters, and are under growing pressure from customers, regulators and digital transformation to act on it.
“The gap we identified is the distance between knowing accessibility matters and actually having the infrastructure to identify, fix, and validate it,” she said.
The existing market, Badejo-Okusanya said, is fragmented across automated scanners and overlay widgets, which are quick to deploy but limited in what they can detect and fix; traditional consultancies, which offer deep expertise but little proprietary technology; and generic user-testing platforms not built around disabled testers.
“We sit at the intersection of these categories, combining AI-driven detection and remediation with structured, paid validation from disabled professionals, rather than asking a business to choose between automation and lived-experience insight,” she said.
The startup has built a community of over 13,000 disabled professionals and advocates, giving the AdaptiveAlly marketplace a ready supply side, while its website draws around 50,000 organic visits a month. It has carried out customer discovery with disabled professionals across the United Kingdom (UK), Nigeria, Canada, Germany, Morocco and the United States (US), as well as with enterprise compliance and digital leaders.
Adaptive Atelier has begun signing paying customers across cinemas, government institutions and retail platforms, and counts L’Oréal, SignHealth, Channel 4 and Phonak among the organisations it has active relationships with.
The company makes money through subscriptions for AdaptiveWiz, scoped audits for AdaptiveTest, and commission on AdaptiveAlly marketplace transactions.
“A business often enters through an AdaptiveTest audit, which surfaces the case for AdaptiveWiz as an ongoing fix, and AdaptiveAlly as the validation layer that proves it’s working,” Badejo-Okusanya said. “The priority right now is proving a repeatable path from first engagement to long-term customer before pushing for more volume.”
The startup has been self-funded to date, and is now raising a US$250,000 institutional round to support technical hiring and go-to-market execution. Badejo-Okusanya was a finalist in the Standard Chartered Foundation Women in Tech Accelerator Nigeria, and Adaptive Atelier is currently part of the Synergies Work Igniting Ideas Business Accelerator in the US, sponsored by the Mitsubishi Electric Foundation.
Nigeria remains the startup’s home market, but it is building early relationships in the UK, European Union (EU) and US, where regulation such as the European Accessibility Act and ADA requirements is creating urgency for enterprise buyers.
The road has not been without challenges. Badejo-Okusanya said product delivery slipped against expectations at one stage, forcing the company to rebuild parts of its technical roadmap and team.
“We now treat rigorous internal testing before external claims as non-negotiable,” she said.
Market education has been another hurdle, with many businesses still viewing accessibility as a compliance cost rather than a commercial opportunity, while focus has also been key.
“With genuine interest from both African and Western markets, the discipline has been choosing where to concentrate go-to-market effort first, rather than spreading a small team across two very different buyer types at once,” Badejo-Okusanya said.

articles.title: Hausla Empowered by Kotak Mahindra back with 4 founders solving everyday problems with tech
articles.text:
Kotak Life
View Brand Publisher
Hausla Empowered by Kotak Mahindra back with 4 founders solving everyday problems with tech
Season 2 of Kotak's founder-focused docuseries Hausla Empowered follows four startups building solutions for railway safety, Parkinson's care, farm losses, and early disease detection.
A train track that can flag a problem before it becomes a failure. A solution to assist people with Parkinson's. A cold-storage that keeps a farmer's harvest from going to waste. A faster way to diagnose diseases before they progress. These are the kinds of solutions Hausla Empowered, Kotak Mahindra Bank's founder-focused docuseries, sets out to document in its second season.
The show is part of Kotak BizLabs, the bank's accelerator programme, and this season follows four entrepreneurs building in that ecosystem: Pradivya AI, working on railway safety; Lifespark Technologies, focused on Parkinson's care; SabjiKothi, addressing post-harvest farm losses; and Easiofy Solutions, developing solutions for earlier disease detection.
The series is streaming on MX Player, Prime Video, and Kotak's digital platforms.
What the founders are building
Each of the four featured startups addresses a distinct, tangible problem.
Pradivya AI is working on AI-powered predictive track inspection aimed at improving railway safety. Lifespark Technologies is developing technology-led support for people living with Parkinson's disease. SabjiKothi is building cold-storage innovation designed to reduce post-harvest losses for farmers.
Easiofy Solutions is developing AI-enabled healthcare tools linked to earlier diagnosis and treatment planning.
Together, these four stories span mobility, healthcare, and agriculture, showcasing how technology is being used to address real-world challenges. Hausla Empowered spotlights founders whose innovations are creating meaningful impact on everyday life.
Rohit Bhasin, Head - Business Banking and Chief Marketing Officer at Kotak Mahindra Bank, said the series is meant to highlight the conviction behind the founders' work. “Hausla is the courage to turn an idea into action. These four founders are using technology and innovation to address challenges that affect people’s everyday lives, from safer railways and better Parkinson’s care to reducing farm losses and enabling earlier diagnosis. Through Hausla Empowered, we want more people to be inspired through the conviction behind these solutions and the entrepreneurs building them”
The bigger picture
The first season of Hausla Empowered premiered in October 2025, featuring four founders from the Kotak BizLabs Accelerate Programme ecosystem. It garnered more than 30 million views across platforms. Season 2 follows the same format: a launch film followed by four episodes, each documenting one founder's journey.
Hausla Empowered is driven by Kotak BizLabs, the bank's CSR-driven accelerator programme that supports early-revenue startups through mentorship, incubation, networking and funding. The docuseries format gives founders from the programme's cohort a platform beyond the accelerator itself, connecting their work to a wider audience and showing real-world impact.
The four founders featured in Season 2 continue that approach, illustrating how the BizLabs ecosystem supports ventures across sectors that are solving real problems by using technology and innovation.

articles.title: Apple patches CoreGraphics zero-day flaw exploited in attacks
articles.text:
Apple released security updates to fix a zero-day vulnerability exploited in "extremely sophisticated" targeted attacks on iOS devices.
Tracked as CVE-2026-20700, this flaw stems from an out-of-bounds write weakness discovered by Meta Product Security in CoreGraphics, a framework used for two-dimensional vector graphics, image rendering, and text drawing across iOS, macOS, iPadOS, watchOS, and tvOS.
Successful exploitation of out-of-bounds write vulnerabilities can let attackers crash a program, corrupt data, or, in the worst case, gain remote code execution by writing data outside the allocated memory buffer.
"Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27," it warned on Monday.
"Processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution. An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved bounds checking."
The complete list of devices impacted by this zero-day is extensive, as it impacts both older and newer models, including:
- iPhone 11 and later, iPad Pro 12.9-inch 3rd generation and later, iPad Pro 11-inch 1st generation and later, iPad Air 3rd generation and later, iPad 8th generation and later, and iPad mini 5th generation and later
- and Macs running macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 and Tahoe 26.7.1
Apple has addressed this issue with improved bounds checking to prevent exploitation in iOS 26.7.1 and iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1.
While this flaw is likely exploited only in highly targeted attacks, it is strongly advised to install these security updates promptly to prevent potential ongoing attacks.
With this vulnerability, Apple has fixed two zero-days exploited in the wild since the start of the year. The other one, an arbitrary code execution vulnerability in dyld (the Dynamic Link Editor used by Apple operating systems) tracked as CVE-2026-20700 and also exploited in extremely sophisticated targeted attacks, was patched in February.
Earlier this year, it also addressed a high-severity Beats Studio Buds flaw (CVE-2025-20701) that lets attackers in Bluetooth range spy on users' conversations, and patched older iPhones and iPads against four vulnerabilities targeted in cyberespionage and crypto-theft attacks using the Coruna exploit kit.
Last year, Apple fixed seven more zero-days exploited in the wild, the first in January (CVE-2025-24085), the second in February (CVE-2025-24200), a third in March (CVE-2025-24201), two more in April (CVE-2025-31200 and CVE-2025-31201), and two others in December (CVE-2025-43529 and CVE-2025-14174).
Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks
Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed.

articles.title: El mando de PlayStation permitiría hacer compras con NFC: la nueva patente de Sony
articles.text:
Sony presentó una patente para que el mando de PlayStation gestione pagos mediante NFC, una tecnología inalámbrica de corto alcance, con el objetivo de realizar compras en los servicios de la consola sin introducir los datos directamente en ella.
La solicitud se inició en marzo de 2025 y fue publicada el 17 de septiembre de 2026; el sistema permitiría acercar un teléfono, una tarjeta bancaria o una tarjeta regalo a la parte trasera del control, según Dexerto.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo se podrían realizar pagos desdel mando del PlayStation
La patente, titulada “Video Game Controller-Driven Information Transfer”, propone que la consola active un evento de compra y avise al mando para detectar un dispositivo cercano. Esa identificación podría realizarse mediante NFC, Bluetooth, sensores de proximidad, señales de sonido o luz, o un código QR.
Después de confirmar la conexión, el teléfono respondería a través de una aplicación del fabricante de la consola. El mando reuniría los datos de pago y los enviaría a PlayStation para completar la operación.
El mecanismo contemplaría usos que van más allá de una compra convencional: canjear tarjetas regalo, adquirir un videojuego después de probar una demostración, transferir una tarjeta de identificación de jugador, sumarse a una partida multijugador o enviar contenido de una partida al teléfono.
PUBLICIDAD
Qué otras novedades hay para usuarios de PlayStation
Algunos usuarios de PlayStation en Estados Unidos podrían recibir una compensación tras el acuerdo alcanzado por Sony Interactive Entertainment para resolver una demanda colectiva vinculada con la venta de videojuegos digitales.
El convenio prevé un fondo de 7,85 millones de dólares, aunque el monto individual aún no fue definido y probablemente será de unos pocos dólares. El pago no será en efectivo. Cuando el tribunal apruebe de forma definitiva el acuerdo, los consumidores que reúnan los requisitos recibirán el importe en su billetera de PlayStation Network.
El caso, identificado como Caccuri v. Sony Interactive Entertainment, acusa a la compañía de haber aplicado prácticas anticompetitivas para conservar el control sobre la venta de determinados títulos digitales de PlayStation.
PUBLICIDAD
La compensación se relaciona con compras realizadas después de que Sony dejara de vender ciertos cupones que permitían adquirir juegos en tiendas digitales alternativas.
Los posibles beneficiarios deben estar vivos, residir en Estados Unidos o alguno de sus territorios y haber comprado videojuegos digitales seleccionados a través de PlayStation Store.
Asimismo, los pagos deben haberse realizado entre el 1 de abril de 2019 y el 31 de diciembre de 2023, y quienes cumplan las condiciones deberían haber recibido una notificación sobre el acuerdo.
Cuál fue el impacto de las protestas contra Sony por el fin de los juegos físicos
La protesta contra el fin de la fabricación de juegos físicos se desarrolló del 23 al 30 de agosto de 2026, impulsada por el grupo dedicado a la preservación Does It Play?
PUBLICIDAD
Los organizadores pidieron a los usuarios que no iniciaran sesión, no jugaran y no hicieran compras en la tienda digital, en títulos adquiridos en línea ni en suscripciones como PS Plus. La consigna fue “sin disco, no hay compra”, en rechazo a la decisión de Sony de abandonar el formato físico para 2028.
Dos semanas después de finalizada la protesta contra PlayStation, Mat Piscatella, analista de videojuegos de Circana, respondió en Bluesky a una consulta sobre sus efectos: “No hubo ningún cambio significativo en absoluto en el número de jugadores ni en la actividad que monitorizamos”.
El registro de Circana se limita a Estados Unidos, el principal mercado de Sony por ingresos, y mide usuarios activos semanales, no jugadores concurrentes en tiempo real.
PUBLICIDAD
Por ese alcance, la firma no puede determinar cuántas personas participaron de la campaña, aunque sus datos no mostraron una alteración perceptible en los hábitos generales de uso.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Google a fait planter des milliers d'applications iOS sans le vouloir — Frandroid
articles.text:
Des milliers de développeurs d’applications iOS ont vécu des heures extrêmement stressantes. D’un seul coup, le nombre de plantages de leurs applications a explosé. Chez certains, il était plus de 5 000 fois supérieur à la normale, selon Android Authority.
Certains dépensent de nombreux tokens IA, la « monnaie » qui permet de se servir d’un modèle, à la recherche d’une cause. D’autres parviennent à trouver la source du problème, sans toutefois pouvoir faire quoi que ce soit. C’est Google Analytics pour Firebase sur iOS qui a buggé.
Un produit Google bugge, les applications iOS trinquent
Google Analytics, c’est l’outil permettant de mesurer et analyser le trafic d’un site web ou, ici, d’une application mobile. Firebase, toujours de Google, est une plateforme de développement d’applis mobiles et web. L’un de ses intérêts, en plus de sa gratuité, est l’intégration de plusieurs outils clés en main.
Or, de nombreux développeurs d’applis pour iOS se servent de Firebase et de sa partie Analytics. Quand le bug est survenu, celles qui reposaient dessus ont commencé à crasher simultanément.
Google explique sur GitHub que le souci a été rapidement résolu. Cependant, « en raison du comportement de mise en cache, certaines instances de l’application peuvent encore subir des plantages jusqu’à 4 heures après la fin du déploiement ».
Les développeurs sont venus dire qu’en effet, le nombre de plantages a grandement diminué suite au correctif. Selon Google, tout est rentré à la normale au plus tard le mardi 29 septembre 2026 à 08h52, heure de Paris. Des commentaires montrent cependant que ce n’est pas encore le cas pour tout le monde. Au moment de publier cet article, la cause de l’incident n’a pas été précisée.
