articles.title: AMD is acquiring AI company World Labs in a deal worth more than $8 billion
articles.text:
AMD announced today that it’s acquiring World Labs, an AI research lab co-founded by the prominent researcher Dr. Fei-Fei Li, in an all-stock deal worth approximately $8.2 billion. World Labs launched in 2024 and was valued at $1 billion in a matter of months. The startup launched its first commercial product, a world generation model called Marble that lets users make interactive 3D worlds from a prompt, in 2025.
AMD is acquiring AI company World Labs in a deal worth more than $8 billion
World Labs’ co-founder and CEO will become AMD’s chief scientist.
The deal is expected to close by the end of the year. Li will become EVP and chief scientist at AMD, reporting to AMD CEO Lisa Su, while the World Labs team will “continue to focus on advancing AI model research.” AMD also notes that the acquisition will strengthen “its ability to develop AI hardware, software and systems around the needs of emerging models and applications.”
“Just like I knew it was time to do a startup to jumpstart the work of creating foundation models beyond LLMs and achieve the most impact in AI, it’s again very clear that the right path for myself and World Labs is to continue our mission as a part of AMD,” Li says in a post on her Substack. “Together we’re committed to keep pushing the frontier of AI to solve real problems, and doing so openly with the community and the entire ecosystem.”
“Building the compute platforms for the next generation of AI requires a deep understanding of how models are evolving,” Su says in a statement. “Fei-Fei and the World Labs team bring exceptional research leadership and model expertise. Together, we can use that insight to develop the hardware, software and systems that will power the next generation of AI and strengthen the open AI ecosystem.”
The World Labs deal is just the latest multi-billion dollar AI-related acquisition as of late, with Nvidia announcing earlier this month that it would be acquiring Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion.

articles.title: KI-Modell handelt auf eigene Initiative: OpenAI stoppt Veröffentlichung von GPT 6.1 Astra
articles.text:
KI-Modell handelt auf eigene Initiative: OpenAI stoppt Veröffentlichung von GPT 6.1 Astra
OpenAI hat wegen Sicherheitsbedenken die Veröffentlichung eines neuen KI-Modells gestrichen. Unter anderem habe die Software in Tests Nutzer nicht immer ehrlich darüber informiert, welche Aktionen sie unternommen oder nicht unternommen habe, sagte die für Sicherheitssysteme zuständige OpenAI-Managerin Saachi Jain dem Wall Street Journal. Außerdem habe das KI-Modell zum Teil auf eigene Initiative gehandelt, ohne eine Nutzererlaubnis einzuholen. Das Modell mit dem Namen GPT 6.1 Astra sollte demnach in den kommenden Tagen oder Wochen herauskommen.
OpenAI setzt Training seiner Modelle aus
Eigenmächtige Aktionen fortgeschrittener Künstlicher Intelligenz von OpenAI hatten in den vergangenen Wochen wiederholt für Negativ-Schlagzeilen gesorgt. Erst am Wochenende wurde bekannt, dass die Firma nach einem neuen Zwischenfall das Training seiner leistungsstärksten KI-Modelle aussetzte. Bei dem Vorfall schaffte es ein KI-Modell in einem Test, Antworten von einem externen Chatbot zu bekommen, obwohl es eigentlich keinen Internetzugang haben sollte.
Die Software habe jedoch eine Lücke in den Netzwerkeinstellungen gefunden und ausgenutzt, wie OpenAI in einem Blogeintrag berichtete. Das Training solle nun erst wieder aufgenommen werden, wenn man sich sicher sei, dass die Lücke geschlossen ist. Bei dem betroffenen KI-Modell habe es sich nicht um GPT 6.1 Astra gehandelt.
Hack durch KI als Warnsignal
In dem bisher aufsehenerregendsten Fall brach Künstliche Intelligenz des ChatGPT-Entwicklers aus einer abgesicherten Testumgebung aus und hackte sich ungeplant in Computer einer anderen KI-Firma, der Plattform Hugging Face. Wie sich danach herausstellte, drang auch KI anderer Entwickler – des OpenAI-Rivalen Anthropic sowie von Google und dem Facebook-Konzern Meta – bei Tests in Systeme anderer Unternehmen ein.
Der Bundesstaat Florida, der bereits eine Klage gegen OpenAI eingereicht hatte, legte nun mit dem Antrag auf eine einstweilige Verfügung nach. Zu den Forderungen gehöre, dass es keine Entwicklung neuer KI-Modelle ohne zusätzliche Leitplanken geben solle, sagte Floridas Generalstaatsanwalt James Uthmeier.

articles.title: Neue EU-Regeln gegen Greenwashing: Was sich beim Einkaufen jetzt ändert
articles.text:
Neue EU-Regeln gegen Greenwashing: Was sich beim Einkaufen jetzt ändert
Der Kaffee ist „klimaneutral“, das T-Shirt „nachhaltig“ und auf dem Shampoo prangt ein grünes Siegel mit einem Blatt. Wer einkauft, begegnet solchen Versprechen inzwischen fast überall – doch was sie tatsächlich bedeuten, ist häufig deutlich weniger klar. Seit dem 27. September 2026 gelten deshalb neue Regeln. Unternehmen dürfen viele pauschale Umweltversprechen nicht mehr so unreflektiert verwenden wie das bisher der Fall war. Gleichzeitig sollen die Verbraucher:innen besser erkennen können, wie lange Produkte halten, ob und wie einfach sie reparierbar sind und welche Rechte sie haben, wenn ein Produkt kaputtgeht.
Die Regeln gehen auf die sogenannte EmpCo-Richtlinie der EU zurück und wurden in Deutschland unter anderem im Gesetz gegen den unlauteren Wettbewerb (UWG) umgesetzt. Darin finden sich nun etwa strengere Vorgaben für Umweltwerbung, Nachhaltigkeitssiegel und Aussagen über Haltbarkeit und Reparierbarkeit.
Für die Verbraucher:innen bedeutet das nicht, dass grüne Werbung komplett verschwindet – wohl aber das als Greenwashing bekannte unreflektierte Werben mit nicht nachvollziehbaren Begriffen. Werbeversprechen sollen so konkreter und überprüfbarer werden. Und manche Aussagen, die bisher auf Verpackungen im Handel vor Ort oder in Onlineshops selbstverständlich wirkten, sind damit ausdrücklich verboten.
Aussagen müssen objektiv überprüfbar sein
Egal ob „nachhaltig“, „umweltfreundlich“, „grün“ oder „ökologisch“: Allgemeine Aussagen und Versprechen sind künftig deutlich schwieriger, denn ein Hersteller kann ein Produkt nicht einfach mit einem allgemeinen grünen Versprechen versehen, ohne dass es dafür eine entsprechend belastbare Grundlage gibt. Das deutsche Gesetz gegen den unlauteren Wettbewerb (UWG) verbietet bestimmte allgemeine Umweltaussagen ausdrücklich, wenn keine anerkannte hervorragende Umweltleistung nachgewiesen werden kann.
Für Verbraucher dürfte sich dadurch vor allem die Sprache verändern. Denn statt ein T-Shirt einfach als „nachhaltig“ zu beschreiben, wird es darauf ankommen, ob ein bestimmter Anteil des Materials aus recycelten Fasern besteht. Und auch wenn von einer „umweltfreundlichen Verpackung“ die Rede ist, muss erkennbar sein, ob sich das beispielsweise auf weniger Material, einen bestimmten Recyclinganteil oder die Wiederverwertbarkeit bezieht.
Dabei muss auch der Bezug eines Umweltversprechens stimmen. Ein Unternehmen darf etwa nicht den Eindruck erwecken, ein komplettes Produkt sei besonders umweltfreundlich, wenn sich der beworbene Vorteil tatsächlich nur auf einen kleinen Teil davon bezieht. Denn eine Verpackung aus Recyclingmaterial kann durchaus ein Umweltvorteil sein, bedeutet aber nicht automatisch, dass auch das darin enthaltene Produkt besonders nachhaltig hergestellt wurde.
„Klimaneutral“ durch CO₂-Ausgleich wird zum Problem
Besonders kritisch sieht der Gesetzgeber inzwischen das Thema Klimaneutralität. So wurden in der Vergangenheit Produkte als klimaneutral beschrieben, für deren Emissionen im Nachhinein einfach Klimaschutzprojekte finanziert oder entsprechende Zertifikate erworben wurden. Das darf in Zukunft nicht mehr sein, zumindest darf daraus bei einem Produkt nun nicht mehr die Behauptung entstehen, dieses habe aufgrund einer Kompensation neutrale, verringerte oder positive Auswirkungen auf die Umwelt. Solche Praktiken stehen mittlerweile auf der Liste der gegenüber Verbraucher:innen unzulässigen Geschäftspraktiken. Allerdings kann der Hersteller weiter darauf verweisen, dass er Klimaschutzprojekte finanziert oder bestimmte Emissionen kompensiert. Das ist aber etwas anderes als die Aussage, die Packung Kaffee, der Flug oder das T-Shirt selbst sei deshalb klimaneutral.
Kritischer geht der Gesetzgeber in Zukunft auch mit erfundenen Öko- oder Umweltsiegeln um. Bislang war für Käufer:innen nicht immer zu erkennen, ob ein Symbol auf einer Verpackung auf eine unabhängige Zertifizierung zurückgeht oder ob es sich um ein nicht nachvollziehbares Siegel mit unklaren Kriterien handelt. Solche firmeneigenen Nachhaltigkeitssiegel werden zukünftig erheblich schwieriger, denn nach dem neuen UWG ist ein Nachhaltigkeitssiegel grundsätzlich unzulässig, wenn es weder auf einem Zertifizierungssystem beruht noch von einer staatlichen Stelle festgesetzt wurde. Kund:innen sollten daher in jedem Fall fragen, wer hinter einem Siegel steht und wie es zustande kommt.
Strenger werden die Regeln auch, wenn Unternehmen mit einer besonders grünen Zukunft werben. Wer beispielsweise „klimaneutral bis 2030“ oder vergleichbare Aussagen zur künftigen Umweltleistung verwendet, benötigt nach dem neuen UWG klare, objektive, öffentlich einsehbare und überprüfbare Verpflichtungen. Diese müssen in einem realistischen Plan festgelegt sein, messbare und zeitgebundene Ziele enthalten und regelmäßig von einem unabhängigen externen Sachverständigen überprüft werden.
Haltbarkeit und Reparierbarkeit kennzeichnen
Der andere Schwerpunkt betrifft Haltbarkeit und Reparierbarkeit. Verbraucher sollen stärker erkennen können, ob ein Produkt langfristig genutzt werden kann und welche Zusagen der Hersteller dazu macht. Besonders interessant wird das bei Herstellergarantien. Gibt ein Hersteller für ein Produkt kostenlos eine Haltbarkeitsgarantie von mehr als zwei Jahren, kann künftig eine eigens dafür entwickelte EU-Kennzeichnung zum Einsatz kommen (auf die Händler:innen kommen hier neue Pflichten zu). Für sie hat die EU eine einheitliche Gestaltung festgelegt. Die entsprechende Verordnung gilt ebenfalls seit dem 27. September 2026. Für die gesetzliche Gewährleistung gibt es seit diesem Zeitpunkt ebenfalls eine EU-weit einheitliche Mitteilung. Das ist durchaus relevant, weil Gewährleistung und Garantie häufig miteinander verwechselt werden.
Die EU möchte zudem erreichen, dass Verbraucher:innen Produkte stärker danach auswählen können, wie gut sie sich später reparieren lassen. Für einzelne Produktgruppen – insbesondere bei Elektronik und Haushaltsgeräten – fließen deshalb Informationen über einen Reparierbarkeitswert oder andere Angaben rund um Reparaturen und Ersatzteile stärker in den Kaufprozess ein.
Mehr Klarheit, doch der Kunde muss es prüfen
Letztlich verschiebt sich damit der Maßstab, nach dem Produkte beworben und verglichen werden, sodass Verbraucher:innen konkrete Eigenschaften aufgezeigt bekommen. Das kann das Einkaufsverhalten zwar längerfristig verändern, weil Haltbarkeit, Reparierbarkeit und nachvollziehbare Umweltangaben stärker in den Vordergrund gestellt werden und besser nachvollziehbar ist, wie genau diese umgesetzt werden. Doch ob die neuen Regeln Greenwashing tatsächlich spürbar eindämmen, wird auch davon abhängen, wie konsequent Verstöße kontrolliert und geahndet werden.

articles.title: Singapore lab builds connections, drives frontier research in year one
articles.text:
On July 24, 2025, Microsoft Research Asia – Singapore (MSRA – Singapore) opened its doors as Microsoft’s first research lab in Southeast Asia. The launch built on more than two decades of collaboration between Microsoft Research Asia and Singapore’s universities, research institutes, and government agencies. It marked a shift to a closer, more integrated relationship aimed at supporting Singapore’s innovation ecosystem and advancing the development and beneficial use of AI.
Established in 1998, MSRA has a presence in Beijing, Shanghai, Vancouver, and Tokyo, along with Singapore. The Singapore lab strengthens the collaboration with local partners and extends the scientific and societal impact of Microsoft’s global research community.
Over the past year, the Singapore lab has grown its team, deepened partnerships, and explored how frontier AI research can create real-world value. Guided by its mission to advance frontier AI for humanity, its work spans four pillars: next-generation AI models and agentic systems, domain-specific AI for real-world impact, AI-native research practices, and ecosystem and talent development.
From frontier research to real-world impact – and back
Research has its greatest impact when it moves beyond the laboratory into practice: in health and medicine, enterprises, and the daily operations of organizations solving real problems. MSRA – Singapore aims to do just that through a two-way exchange: partners bring domain expertise, real-world data, and operational challenges, while the lab contributes frontier research and engineering capabilities. Together, they translate fundamental advances into practical solutions, while surfacing new questions that feed back into research in a kind of research-to-impact flywheel. Advances in AI foundations enable more capable models and agentic systems that can reason, plan, use tools, and collaborate with people. These capabilities create new opportunities for AI-native innovation. In turn, real-world applications reveal limitations and generate new questions, feeding insights back into foundational research and sustaining a continuous cycle of discovery, application, and learning.
Healthcare offers an early example of the lab’s research-to-impact model. Research on multimodal healthcare AI and self-evolving diagnostic agents is deployed and extended through partnerships across Singapore’s healthcare ecosystem. The lab is collaborating on multimodal and agentic AI approaches to support clinical decision-making, unlock insights from complex medical data, and advance research in disease diagnosis, risk assessment, and personalized care, with the longer-term goal of enabling meaningful real-world use.
Beyond healthcare, the lab is working with organizations across financial services, education, and technology to explore how frontier AI can address sector-specific needs and operational challenges.
Singapore has made AI a national priority through its National AI Strategy 2.0 (opens in new tab), which focuses on deploying industry-transforming AI, advancing frontier research in AI foundations, and developing responsible, socially beneficial applications. These priorities span areas including healthcare, education, finance, and Smart Nation (opens in new tab) services. MSRA – Singapore’s research portfolio aligns with these priorities, with a particular focus on building AI systems that are reliable and trustworthy across Southeast Asian contexts.
The Singapore Economic Development Board (EDB) has been a foundational partner. It supported the lab’s establishment and continues to support joint PhD training through the Industrial Postgraduate Programme (IPP). The relationship has since grown into strategic collaboration. In February 2026, EDB co-hosted an Executive Roundtable on AI in Logistics and Transportation, bringing together more than ten regional industry leaders to explore sectoral challenges.
Government engagement extends beyond EDB. In July 2025, IMDA (opens in new tab) co-hosted Microsoft Research Asia Singapore Day (opens in new tab) — Advancing Industrial AI, a full-day event spanning healthcare AI, interactive world simulators, AI agents, and societal AI. MSRA – Singapore has also engaged with the Ministry of Trade and Industry and the Ministry of Health.
From enduring partnerships to shared discovery
In addition to its deep ties with government agencies, MSRA has built strong connections with Singapore’s academic community, supporting more than 75 research projects with Singapore institutions since 2004. The opening of the Singapore lab has brought new engagements, with nine new projects in its first year with National University of Singapore (NUS) and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU) across healthcare AI, robotics, AI systems, and multi-agent systems.
A landmark example is the five-year Framework Research Agreement (opens in new tab) with NUS, announced in 2025, which provides a platform for joint AI research, talent development, and academic exchange. It defines shared research priorities in healthcare, societal AI, spatial intelligence, and data-intensive computing alongside an annual NUS–MSRA Academic Symposium that brings researchers from both organizations together to shape the collaboration agenda.
The collaboration is already producing concrete research across several frontier areas. NUS Assistant Professor Mike Shou and MSRA’s Xinxing Xu are developing unified multimodal AI for healthcare. NUS assistant professor Yang You and MSRA distinguished scientist Furu Wei are studying systems foundations for diffusion-based language models. NUS assistant professor Jialin Li is working with MSRA on rigorous distributed agreement in multi-agent systems and verifiable machine learning systems.
The NUS–Microsoft Research Asia AI Summer School has reached more than 300 students since its launch in 2025, attracting participants from Singapore, Southeast Asia, and beyond. Through three days of lectures, hands-on workshops, and small-group discussions, the program creates a forum for researchers and students to engage with emerging AI questions and scholars shaping the field. The 2025 program featured a keynote by Doug Burger, technical fellow and corporate vice president of Microsoft, on the AI revolution. Ahead of the 2026 Summer School, Lidong Zhou delivered a lecture on system intelligence, helping frame the conversations that followed.
Beyond NUS, Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore has built connections across Singapore’s research community, including with NTU, Singapore Management University (SMU) (opens in new tab), Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), and other institutions. Research arising from these partnerships has already been published at leading venues, including the International Conference on Learning Representations (opens in new tab) (ICLR) and the Conference on Language Modeling (opens in new tab) (COLM).
From early exposure to research leadership: Cultivating Singapore’s next generation of AI talent
For Microsoft Research Asia, talent development is not a standalone program but a long-term investment in Singapore’s research and innovation capacity, supporting a comprehensive talent pipeline spanning internships, joint PhD supervision, visiting scholar programs, and fellowship initiatives. Through these opportunities, students and early-career researchers gain access to world-class mentorship, a curiosity-driven culture, frontier research challenges, and a global network connecting academia, industry, and real-world applications.
What makes this model distinctive is its continuity. Students may engage with Microsoft Research Asia through workshops or summer schools, gain hands-on experience through its flagship research initiative, Microsoft Research Asia Stars of Tomorrow Internship Program, or pursue doctoral research through joint PhD programs. Some participants later return as faculty collaborators, mentors, or research leaders. Together, these programs form a connected pathway that supports researchers at successive stages of development.
The IPP represents a sustained form of collaboration, enabling PhD students to conduct long-term research under joint mentorship from academia and industry. Qiming Huang, the first IPP student at MSRA — Singapore, is co-supervised by NUS professor Mike Shou and MSRA researcher Xinxing Xu. Through the program, Huang worked closely with researchers from both institutions, gaining exposure to academic rigor and industry-driven research. At CVPR 2026 (opens in new tab), one of the world’s leading conferences in AI and computer vision, Qiming Huang’s paper on RobotSeg – a foundation model for robot segmentation in image and video – was selected for an oral presentation.
NTU assistant professor Jianfei Yang, embodies the continuous collaborative opportunities enabled by Microsoft Research Asia. As a student, Yang’s team won the Beauty of Programming competition, an experience that inspired him to pursue a PhD and begin an academic career. Over the years, he watched many of his classmates and close friends grow into outstanding researchers through MSRA programs. Today, he collaborates with MSRA researchers in robotics and jointly supervises students through the IPP, creating for the next generation the same opportunities that inspired his own journey.
NTU associate professor Ziwei Liu, himself a former MSRA intern, recently saw one of his students become the only Asia-based recipient of the Microsoft Research global Fellowship award for 2025–2026.
The Stars of Tomorrow Internship Program has engaged more than 90 students from Singapore-based institutions over the years. For many students, these internships serve as a gateway to frontier research and help bridge the gap between academic study and real-world innovation.
For exceptional doctoral students, the Microsoft Research Asia Fellowship provides another pathway for growth, recognition, mentorship, and access to Microsoft’s global research community. Since the program began, 13 students from Singapore-based universities have received the fellowship, many of whom have gone on to become professors, industry research leaders, and technology entrepreneurs around the world.
The next phase: Scaling what works
As Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore enters its second year, the focus is shifting from building foundations to scaling the strongest models of collaboration and demonstrating their impact more broadly.
One year ago, the lab opened with a mission to advance frontier AI in close partnership with the ecosystem around it. That mission is already taking shape through joint research, talent development, and the first partnerships connecting lab work to real-world challenges.
The year ahead is about scaling what works. By deepening these connections, Microsoft Research Asia — Singapore can bring more frontier research into practice and create meaningful value for Singapore, the wider region, industry, and society.

articles.title: Windows 11 : Microsoft a mis en pause cette mise à jour car elle désactive les licences Office
articles.text:
En ce moment, chez Microsoft, les mises à jour se suivent, et se ressemblent malheureusement. Après avoir essuyé son lot de bugs avec le Patch Tuesday de septembre sur Windows 11, Microsoft doit à présent régler d’importants problèmes causés par une mise à jour de Microsoft 365.
Celle-ci devait à l’origine permettre aux versions obsolètes des applications Microsoft 365 de reprendre leur cycle de mise à jour automatique. Proposée via Windows update, cette mise à jour était néanmoins optionnelle et ne s’installait donc pas automatiquement.
Malheureusement, pour les utilisateurs ayant fait le choix de l’installer sur leur machine, tout ne s’est pas passé comme prévu. En effet, certains d’entre eux ont été confrontés à un bug particulièrement gênant.
Une mise à jour qui désactive les licences Office
Après avoir installé cette mise à jour, des utilisateurs se sont en effet retrouvé avec des licences perpétuelles pour Office 2016 et Office 2019 désactivées. Chez certains utilisateurs, les applications office se sont soudainement retrouvées à afficher un message indiquant qu’elles n’avaient plus de licence.
Chez d’autres, la mise à jour a tout bonnement désinstallé la suite Office avant de tenter une réinstallation qui échouait, laissant les utilisateurs sans suite Office.
« Microsoft a reçu des rapports faisant état de résultats inattendus sur certains appareils exécutant Office 2016 ou Office 2019 après l’installation de cette mise à jour. Cette mise à jour était destinée à résoudre les problèmes liés aux appareils ne recevant pas de mises à jour des applications Microsoft 365. Dans le cadre de l’action de réparation appliquée par cette mise à jour, certains appareils se sont retrouvés sans versions fonctionnelles de Microsoft 365 Apps ou Office. Pour éviter que des appareils supplémentaires ne soient affectés, nous avons suspendu le déploiement de cette mise à jour. » a ainsi expliqué Microsoft sur la page de support dédiée à cette mise à jour.
Surtout, bien que cette mise à jour proposée par Microsoft était à l’origine optionnelle, il semble que celle-ci se soit installée automatiquement sur les PC d’après les retours de plusieurs administrateurs de parc informatiques.
Face aux nombreux problèmes remontés par les utilisateurs sur les forums de Microsoft, mais également sur Reddit, la firme de Redmond a officiellement suspendu la mise à jour KB5002907 et a indiqué mener une enquête pour tenter de comprendre les causes de ces problèmes.
En attendant un correctif, Microsoft suggère aux utilisateurs dont la licence a été désactivée de saisir de nouveau la clé de produit originale, ou de se connecter au compte Microsoft associé à la licence pour réactiver le produit. Pour ceux dont la suite Office a été désinstallée, Microsoft indique tout simplement de retélécharger et réinstaller la copie d’Office acquise à l’origine puis de réactiver celle-ci avec la clé de licence idoine.

articles.title: AWS Introduces Foreign Key Constraints in Aurora DSQL
articles.text:
AWS recently announced that Aurora DSQL now supports foreign key constraints, allowing applications to enforce referential integrity directly in the database, including CASCADE, SET NULL, and other referential actions. The addition addresses a long-standing gap that users had explicitly called out as an adoption blocker.
Aurora DSQL is a serverless, distributed, PostgreSQL-compatible SQL database designed for highly available, scalable applications. According to the documentation, Aurora DSQL enforces referential integrity through snapshot verification during transactions and conflict detection at commit time. The service checks foreign key relationships against a consistent transaction snapshot without locking tables, allowing concurrent operations, and uses implicit KEY SHARE checks at commit to detect conflicting changes; transactions that would violate a constraint are rejected with a serialization error.
Applications should implement retry logic because concurrent conflicts result in transaction failures rather than waits. For heavily referenced rows, AWS suggests avoiding frequently changing key columns; instead, keep referenced keys stable and move changing values to non-key columns to reduce transaction conflicts.
Marc Brooker, VP and Distinguished Engineer at AWS, highlights that Aurora DSQL uses the Adjudicator and PostgreSQL's KEY SHARE mechanism to detect changes to relevant rows at commit time without blocking concurrent reads:
No blocking, no change in scaling for non-FKC reads, FKC readers never cause other readers to abort, and great FKC scaling for well-distributed workloads.
On LinkedIn, Luc van Donkersgoed, principal engineer at Nederlandse Spoorwegen and creator of AWS News Feed, comments:
They did it! Aurora DSQL now supports foreign key constraints. Lack of FKs was the biggest gap between DSQL and ‘normal’ Postgres, blocking many migrations. This change makes DSQL much more viable for brownfield environments.
In the "Amazon wasted their time building DSQL" thread, the lack of foreign key constraints was mentioned as one of the main blockers for the adoption of the PostgreSQL-compatible distributed database. Marc Bowes, senior principal engineer at AWS, acknowledged at the time:
And yes, foreign keys are coming. We heard ya.
When the service was announced at re:Invent 2024, many practitioners highlighted the lack of foreign key constraints among the many missing features at launch. User SteveTabernacle2 wrote:
Then "Postgres-compatible" is misleading. Foreign keys is such a big part of RDBMS. You can't truly have "relational" data without foreign keys.
The reaction of the community to the new feature has been largely positive, but a user questions on Reddit:
I know this feature was quoted as one of the main adoption blockers, but it slows things down a lot. I'm not sure how good this is going to be considering DSQL's architecture.
AWS notes that all DML operations on referenced or referencing tables incur additional reads to maintain referential integrity and that customers should benchmark the workload before adding a foreign key constraint to a table.
Foreign key constraints were not the only new capability recently added to DSQL, with AWS also adding CloudWatch Database Insights for per-statement, cluster-level performance monitoring and troubleshooting.

articles.title: The new Firefox design: More modern, more flexible, still Firefox | The Mozilla Blog
articles.text:
More modern. More flexible. Still Firefox.
What comes to mind when you think of Firefox? Is it our best-in-class privacy features and ad blocking capabilities? Our partnerships with Wrexham, NVIDIA or Mistral? Or maybe our adorable mascot Kit?
If you’ve been following Firefox this year, you’ve seen us add new ways to get things done while giving you more choice over how you browse. That includes browsing two pages side by side, adding an extra layer of privacy with built-in VPN, blocking trackers for smoother scrolling and faster load times, and deciding how AI shows up in Firefox.
For the past few months, many of you have also been trying out our new Firefox design in Nightly and sharing your thoughts with us as we continued to refine the experience.
Today, we’re rolling out that design with FX 157 to everyone using Firefox across desktop and mobile devices. Firefox has done a lot of growing over the last year; now it looks the part.
A more modern Firefox
When we first shared our plans to design Firefox for the future, we said we wanted Firefox to feel “current, but not generic. Warm, but still precise.”
That design ethos now carries across all of Firefox. We’ve refreshed the colors, icons and themes throughout the browser, from the tabs and toolbars you use every day to your New Tab page, Private Browsing experience and more, with no cost to your browser performance.
This shared design language across desktop and mobile gives Firefox a consistent foundation for new features and experiences, while keeping the personality that makes Firefox unique.
Make Firefox yours
We’ve added more choices for how Firefox looks and works, including the return of a feature many of you asked for:
Compact Mode is back. As people started trying the new design, we heard from many of you who wanted to fit more into your browser window. Compact Mode reduces the size of your tabs and toolbar to give more of your screen to the web, with an auto-compact option for smaller screens.
Find your look. A new theme picker makes it easier to explore different looks for Firefox, with new themes and wallpapers to choose from.
Set up New Tab your way. Choose what you want to see on your homepage. Now, you can pin a shortcut so a site you use all the time stays put.
Refined, not reinvented
Themes and wallpapers may change over time, but the things that made people choose Firefox in the first place are still the same. We’re still independent and open source, with privacy protections built into the browser and controls that put you in charge of how Firefox works for you.
This carries through everything we build, from the height of your toolbars and what belongs on your New Tab page to which AI features show up in your browser, which model you choose and what context you want it to have.
Today’s Firefox is a renewal, grounded in the same principles that have shaped it from the beginning, with a new design built to carry Firefox forward.
For those who have come with us on this journey, thank you for helping us shape the future of Firefox.
If you’ve been away on hiatus, welcome back. Try the latest Firefox and let us know what you think.
This post is also available in: Deutsch (German) Français (French)

articles.title: Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster
articles.text:
Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster
A new quantum computing method can make advanced operations more than 1,000 times faster, potentially removing a major barrier to reliable quantum machines.
- Date:
- September 11, 2026
- Source:
- Chalmers University of Technology
- Summary:
- Researchers have found a way to perform certain quantum operations more than 1,000 times faster, cutting thousands of repeated control cycles down to just one. The advance could reduce errors and bring reliable, fault-tolerant quantum computers closer to reality.
- Share:
Quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings. The longer a quantum operation takes to complete, the more time there is for those errors to build up. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have now developed a method that can perform a broad range of advanced quantum operations more than a thousand times faster. The advance tackles a major obstacle in the field and could help move quantum computing closer to becoming fault-tolerant.
Quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics. Before that can happen, however, these machines need to become much more dependable.
Why Quantum Computers Are So Error-Prone
A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects. Electrical noise, cosmic radiation, and overheating can all introduce errors while information is being processed.
Traditional computers can experience errors too, but decades of development have produced reliable error correction methods that can quickly detect and repair them. Quantum systems are much harder to protect because the information they use is extraordinarily delicate.
"The fundamental building blocks of quantum computers, known as qubits, are so sensitive that even the smallest disturbance can cause the quantum state to deviate from the target, resulting in the loss of information. If too many errors accumulate before they can be corrected, the computation can fail," says Lei Du, researcher in Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, and lead author of the theoretical study published in the journal Physical Review Letters.
A Different Way to Protect Quantum Information
To make quantum computing more resilient and eventually fault-tolerant, researchers are investigating new ways to shield quantum information from errors. One promising strategy uses so-called bosonic quantum codes*.
Instead of assigning quantum information to individual qubits, this approach stores it in microwave fields inside superconducting circuits.
"Rather than storing quantum information in individual qubits, bosonic codes encode information in the microwave fields found within superconducting circuits. This approach has been shown to provide stronger protection against certain types of errors," explains Tangyou Huang, researcher in Quantum Technology at Chalmers and co-author of the study.
Quantum Operations More Than 1,000 Times Faster
Working with bosonic quantum codes is not simple. Creating and controlling the required quantum states has traditionally involved guiding a quantum system through thousands of repeated driving cycles.
That process can take considerable time, and every additional cycle creates another opportunity for outside disturbances to interfere with the calculation. In quantum computing, speed is therefore closely tied to reliability.
Chalmers researchers Lei Du and Tangyou Huang have now proposed a different strategy. Rather than constructing the desired quantum states one small piece at a time, their method can perform a wide variety of operations much faster.
"Our method shows that a diverse range of quantum operations on bosonic states can be completed within a single driving cycle, rather than the several thousand cycles that have been required previously. This makes the operations both faster and more efficient, while reducing the risk that disturbances will corrupt the information before the process is finished. It represents an important step towards fault-tolerant quantum computers," says Lei Du.
Quantum Lattice Gates Provide a Shortcut
The new approach is built around Quantum lattice gates, a recently proposed universal set of quantum gates developed by the same research team.
These gates act somewhat like shortcuts. Instead of requiring a long sequence of repeated control steps, they can allow the intended quantum operation to be completed in just one driving cycle. That could make the process faster, simpler, and less vulnerable to errors.
"You can think of it like building a large Lego castle. Instead of assembling it brick by brick and risking mistakes along the way, quantum lattice gates act like pre-built Lego modules that can be connected quickly and efficiently," says Tangyou Huang.
Designed for Superconducting Quantum Computers
The technique is especially well suited to superconducting quantum computers, which are among the most prominent technologies being developed in the international push toward large-scale quantum computing.
Chalmers University of Technology is also using superconducting technology as it develops a 100-qubit quantum computer.
"A key advantage of our approach is that it can be implemented using existing superconducting quantum circuit platforms. We are already discussing possible experimental realizations with colleagues at Chalmers, and we hope to see a demonstration of the method in the near future," says Tangyou Huang.
The researchers say the work addresses a central problem facing the field: efficiently producing and controlling quantum states that are capable of helping correct errors.
"Our results address one of the major bottlenecks in the field: how to quickly and reliably create and control the error-correcting quantum states that could play an important role in future quantum computers," says Lei Du.
More About Bosonic Codes, Quantum Lattice Gates and Floquet Control
*Bosonic quantum codes store quantum information in the states of, for example, microwave or optical resonators rather than in individual qubits. They are considered a promising tool for quantum error correction because they can provide built-in protection against certain types of errors.
Quantum operations are needed to process that stored information. Quantum lattice gates are a recently proposed collection of basic building blocks that can be used to control bosonic quantum states. By combining and designing these gates, researchers can carry out a wide range of more complicated quantum operations.
One method for implementing these operations is known as Floquet control, which uses periodic control signals to drive a quantum system. Earlier Floquet-based techniques have generally depended on slower processes involving many repeated driving cycles. The approach developed at Chalmers can instead perform quantum lattice gates directly in a single driving cycle, making some operations more than a thousand times faster.
More About the Research
The scientific paper "Single-Period Floquet Control of Bosonic Codes with Quantum Lattice Gates" has been published in Physical Review Letters. The authors are Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, and Lingzhen Guo. The researchers are affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and Tianjin University in China.
The research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT), and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Chalmers University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, Lingzhen Guo. Single-Period Floquet Control of Bosonic Codes with Quantum Lattice Gates. Physical Review Letters, 2026; 137 (6) DOI: 10.1103/tnb8-3m8m

articles.title: Highlights from Git 2.56
articles.text:
The open source Git project just released Git 2.56. Here is GitHub’s look at some of the most interesting features and changes introduced since last time.
The open source Git project just released Git 2.56.0 with features and bug fixes from over 104 contributors, 39 of them new. We last caught up with you on the latest in Git back when 2.55 was released.
To celebrate this most recent release, here is GitHub’s look at some of the most interesting features and changes introduced since last time.
Stage resolved conflicts without staging everything else
Resolving a merge conflict has two distinct parts. First, you edit the working tree until each conflicted path contains the result you want. Then, you stage those paths to tell Git that the conflict is resolved.
Suppose a merge conflicts in recipe.txt, while notes.txt contains an unrelated local edit.
The second step sounds simple, but existing commands make it easy to stage more than you intended. git add -u updates every modified tracked path. During a merge, that may include local changes that are unrelated to the conflict. It can also stage a file that still contains conflict markers if you overlooked one.
Git 2.56 provides a safer workflow:
$ git add --resolved
fatal: the following paths still have conflict markers:
recipe.txt
$ # Edit recipe.txt and remove the conflict markers.
$ git add --resolved
$ git status --short
M notes.txt
M recipe.txt
The new git add --resolved mode is designed specifically for this step. It considers only paths that are currently unmerged in the index. Before staging anything, it scans unmerged regular files for leftover conflict markers. If it finds one, it reports the affected paths and leaves the index unchanged.
The two columns in git status --short distinguish staged and unstaged changes. recipe.txt is staged as resolved, while the unrelated change to notes.txt remains unstaged.
You can also pass a pathspec to limit which unmerged paths are considered. The all-or-nothing marker check still applies within that selection: if any selected regular file contains conflict markers, Git stages none of them. Resolved deletions and binary conflicts do not have textual markers, so Git can stage them normally.
This is intentionally narrower than git add -u or git add -A. --resolved cannot be combined with either mode, and it ignores tracked files that were never conflicted. That makes it a useful safety rail for maintainer workflows where a merge may begin with unrelated local changes already present.
Stop searching history once no more merge bases can exist
Many Git operations need to find the best common ancestor(s) of two commits. Merges use them as the starting point for combining changes, while three-dot diffs use a best common ancestor to decide where a topic branch’s work begins. Repository hosts perform the same calculation for pull request diffs, mergeability checks, review ranges, and other comparisons.
Git finds these common ancestors by walking backward from both tips. Imagine painting commits reachable from one side blue and commits from the other side red. A commit reached by both colors is a merge-base candidate.
Finding one candidate is not necessarily enough. Criss-cross merges can produce multiple merge bases, none of which is an ancestor of another, so Git must keep walking until it knows that it has found all of them. But the old stopping rule could keep processing a long tail of stale, already-common history after another merge base had become impossible.
Git 2.56 tracks how many queued commits remain painted exclusively by each side. The implementation has additional guards around this rule, but at a high level once one exclusive side is exhausted, no new meeting point can appear. Git can stop while still returning every merge base.
The difference can be dramatic when old side branches have been merged into a much longer history. In one real monorepo case, the traversal fell from 0.68 seconds to 0.01 seconds. Production evaluations on two large monorepos found many cases around 70 times faster in one and an average improvement around 20 times in the other.
The final series also fixed a long-standing Linux-kernel performance case. With Git’s default v2 commit-graph, the command git merge-base --all v4.8 v4.9 fell from 167,441 traversal steps and 0.29 seconds to 3,887 steps and 0.01 seconds.
Make smaller path-walk repacks practical for servers
When Git repacks a repository, it searches for similar objects that can be stored efficiently as deltas. The traditional search groups candidates using a name hash. Path-walk repacking instead visits objects by their location in the tree, bringing versions of the same path together and often finding much better delta relationships.
The potential storage savings are substantial. In a benchmark using a recent clone of the Fluent UI repository and forcing Git to recompute deltas, an ordinary bitmapped repack produced a 558.5 MB pack. Repacking with --path-walk produced a 164.4 MB pack, about 71% smaller.
But repository hosts need more than small packs. They commonly use reachability bitmaps to answer object-enumeration queries quickly, and some use delta islands to prevent objects in one group of refs from depending on objects available only in another. Path-walk repacking was incompatible with both, limiting where its storage improvements could be deployed.
Git 2.56 removes those two restrictions. A path-walk repack can now select commits for a new bitmap. Later git pack-objects invocations can reuse an existing bitmap when it answers the request, falling back to the path walk only when necessary.
Path-walk also now performs the bookkeeping required by delta islands: propagating island membership through commits and trees before choosing delta bases. That lets hosts preserve their isolation rules while experimenting with path-walk’s smaller on-disk representation.
These changes do not enable path-walk repacking by default. Instead, they remove two important adoption blockers, making it possible for large repository hosts to evaluate the storage savings without giving up fast bitmap-assisted serving or delta-island constraints.
Those are just a few of the changes in Git 2.56. Here are some other new features and updates worth highlighting.
The experimental git history command continues to grow. Git 2.54 introduced it with reword and split, and Git 2.55 added fixup. Git 2.56 adds:
$ git history drop <commit>
The command removes the selected commit and replays its descendants onto the commit’s parent. If HEAD moves, Git updates the index and working tree while preserving unrelated local changes. It aborts if replaying a descendant would conflict or overwrite a local change. The command remains experimental, cannot operate on a history that contains merge commits, and cannot drop a root or merge commit.
Reference-writing commands have historically been scattered across git update-ref, git symbolic-ref, and other plumbing. Git 2.56 continues consolidating low-level reference management under the git refs toolbox:
Optional old values provide compare-and-swap protection for updates and deletion. These are deliberately low-level commands. In particular, git refs rename moves the ref and its reflog, but does not perform the branch configuration adjustments that git branch -m does.
Cleaning up local topic branches after their work lands upstream can involve comparing each branch to its configured remote-tracking branch. Git 2.56 adds a bulk form:
In this command, origin/* matches branches whose upstream is under origin, topic-* limits the candidates to local branch names beginning with topic-, and --dry-run lists what would be deleted without deleting anything.
When run without --dry-run, Git deletes only branches whose tips are reachable from their matching upstreams. Branches checked out in a worktree, branches with missing upstreams, and several ambiguous push configurations are skipped. branch.<name>.deleteMerged = false can protect a branch from bulk cleanup.
git bisect run is wonderfully effective at finding the commit that introduced a regression, but when it finishes it normally leaves you checked out at the culprit until you run git bisect reset. The new --reset-when-found[=<where>] option combines those steps. Its default is original, which returns to the commit checked out before the bisection began; found cleans up the bisection state but leaves the culprit checked out. The option is unavailable with --no-checkout.
The experimental git replay command can now flatten merge topology with --linearize. Git replays the commits in a single line and drops merge commits, matching the topology produced by git rebase --no-rebase-merges, but without using the working tree. The option cannot be combined with --contained or with replaying multiple branches at once.
Git can now recognize two easy command-line slips and suggest the intended form. Running git push origin/main advises using git push origin main, while git branch --set-upstream-to origin main suggests git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main. Git checks that each correction is plausible before suggesting it, avoiding indiscriminate guesses.
Partial clones omit selected objects initially, but blobs fetched on demand have traditionally remained stored locally forever. Git 2.56 can discard large, recoverable blobs and rely on the promisor remote again:
$ git repack -a --filter=blob:limit=1m --drop-filtered --dry-run $ git repack -a --filter=blob:limit=1m --drop-filtered
The dry run lists candidates; the real repack removes them locally so a later access fetches them again. This is a manual cleanup mechanism, not an automatically bounded cache, and currently supports only blob:limit filters. Git requires a promisor remote and refuses unsafe cases such as dropping an object referenced by the current index. The work was contributed as a GSoC project by Siddharth Shrimali, with Christian Couder and Siddharth Asthana recorded as mentors.
git log --follow can now track a path more reliably through non-linear history. Previously, the command kept one global “current path.” If different parents renamed the path differently, whichever side happened to be visited first could determine what Git followed through the rest of the walk. Git 2.56 records the path separately for each parent, making the result independent of traversal order and fixing cases such as subtree merges.
Graphs with multiple roots can place an unrelated commit directly below a root commit in the same column, making the two appear connected. Git 2.56 indents these "visual roots" when necessary:
* root of one visible history * unrelated commit
This is enabled by default for git log --graph. Use --no-graph-indent for the old rendering, or set log.graphIndent to choose a default.
Several internal changes remove scaling cliffs from otherwise ordinary operations. Reftable writes now avoid redundant reloads after taking the lock, making filesystem-stat calls constant rather than linear in the number of refs. Loading known-new packfiles no longer scans the existing list before every insertion, eliminating an O(N²) regression that made a prompt-related command take 4.5 seconds in a repository with 37,815 packs.
Other changes removed quadratic scans from tombstone-heavy reftables and path-limited working-tree diffs, while making untracked-file collection robustly O(n log n) instead of relying on already-sorted input. The reftable tombstone performance tests fell from about 13 seconds to 0.2 seconds. On a Chromium checkout with roughly 500,000 index entries, one affected git diff improved from about eight minutes to 0.07 seconds.
Elijah Newren is a Staff Software Engineer at GitHub. He is the designer and implementer of merge-ort, Git's default merge strategy since 2.34, author of git-filter-repo—the history rewriting tool the Git project officially recommends—and a driving force behind sparse-checkout.

articles.title: Ce chauffage d'appoint connecté Dreo parfait pour l'hiver chute sous les 50 € sur Amazon — Frandroid
articles.text:
Les soirées plus fraîches sont de retour, et avec elles l’envie d’un peu de chaleur sans relancer le chauffage de toute la maison. Dreo vient justement de présenter sa gamme hiver de chauffages d’appoint. Ici, on s’intéresse plutôt à un modèle déjà en vente. L’Atom 316S est un chauffage d’appoint connecté compact, pensé pour une chambre ou un bureau. Il passe en ce moment sous la barre des 50 euros.
Les forces du Dreo Atom 316S
- Une chauffe céramique PTC de 1 500 watts, sur trois niveaux
- Un thermostat de 5 à 35 °C, réglable degré par degré
- Des protections contre la surchauffe et le basculement
Habituellement affiché à 59 euros, le Dreo Atom 316S tombe à 49 euros sur Amazon.
Un format colonne qui se déplace de pièce en pièce
Avec ses 24,5 cm de haut pour 1,38 kg, le Dreo Atom 316S se glisse facilement au sol près du bureau, au bout du canapé ou dans la chambre. Sa poignée de transport dissimulée à l’arrière permet de le trimballer d’une pièce à l’autre en un geste. Il embarque un écran tactile lisible pour surveiller la température d’un coup d’œil, mais il est aussi possible de le piloter à distance sans quitter votre plaid, depuis votre smartphone et l’application Dreo (en revanche, pas de télécommande dans la boîte).
Sur le papier, Dreo promet un fonctionnement très discret à 34 décibels. Ça reste tout de même un chauffage soufflant : attendez-vous donc à un léger souffle continu lorsque la ventilation s’active. Rien de gênant pour travailler ou regarder un film, mais c’est un détail à garder en tête si vous avez le sommeil très léger et que vous comptez le laisser tourner la nuit à côté du lit.
Une chaleur rapide, à réserver aux petites pièces
Sous son petit gabarit, le Dreo Atom 316S embarque une puissance maximale de 1 500 watts, épaulée par une résistance en céramique PTC. Dreo promet de l’air chaud 2 secondes à peine après l’allumage. Il ne remplacera pas un chauffage principal et atteindra vite ses limites dans un grand séjour. En revanche, sa puissance suffit amplement pour réchauffer un petit bureau, une chambre ou un coin salon.
Ce modèle marque surtout des points avec sa partie connectée. Une fois le chauffage relié au Wi-Fi de la maison, tout devient réglable depuis l’application Dreo : vous pouvez allumer l’appareil à distance avant votre retour du travail, ajuster la température au degré près, jongler entre les 3 niveaux de puissance ou créer des programmes personnalisés pour planifier des créneaux de chauffe automatiques aux heures où vous télétravaillez.
Si vous cherchez plutôt des solutions pour rafraîchir votre intérieur quand les températures grimpent, jetez un œil à notre guide des meilleurs ventilateurs connectés.
